0.title: Proverbs: The Fear of the LORD Is the Beginning of Knowledge
0.overview:
Proverbs is a book about how to live well in God's world. By wisdom it means not cleverness or learning but the skill of living rightly, in money and work, speech and silence, sex and drink, pride and humility, the family and the heart. Few books of the Bible are more practical.

Its motto stands at the door: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge (1:7). Wisdom does not begin with a technique for success but with a posture before the God who made and keeps his people, and it never outgrows that posture. Everything else in the book grows from that root. The motto returns at 9:10 and closes the last poem (31:30).

The book is a collection of collections, and its headings say so. The proverbs of Solomon, son of David, king of Israel (1:1) introduces nine chapters of a father speaking to his son; a second heading (10:1) begins the two-line sayings that fill most of the book. Then come the words of the wise (22:17; 24:23); the proverbs of Solomon which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied (25:1); the words of Agur (30:1); and the words of King Lemuel, taught by his mother (31:1). What we have is God's selection from Solomon's 3,000 proverbs (1 Kgs 4:32) and others, gathered over centuries. How much of chapters 1-9 is Solomon's own is debated, and 22:17-24:22 closely resembles an Egyptian book of instruction; God can take up true observations, reshape them under the fear of the LORD, and make them his word.

A proverb is a compressed truth about how life in God's world ordinarily works, not a promise with a guarantee attached to every case. A child trained early usually keeps to the way (22:6); parents of a wandering child have not been given a broken promise, nor necessarily failed. The book itself sets opposite sayings side by side, Answer not a fool according to his folly, and Answer a fool according to his folly (26:4-5): wisdom is knowing which fits the moment. Job and the Psalms show the righteous suffering too, and Proverbs admits that the poor man's field can be swept away by injustice (13:23).

The New Testament quotes Proverbs as God's word to the church: the Lord's discipline (Heb 12:5, from 3:11), God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble (Jas 4:6; 1 Pet 5:5, from 3:34), feeding a hungry enemy (Rom 12:20, from 25:21-22), the dog returning to its vomit (2 Pet 2:22, from 26:11).

And it shows where this wisdom leads. Jesus said, something greater than Solomon is here (Matt 12:42). Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor 1:24), who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption (1 Cor 1:30), in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col 2:3). The Wisdom who calls in the streets (ch. 1), was beside the LORD at creation (ch. 8) and spreads her table for the simple (ch. 9) is heard in the one who cried out at the feast, If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink (John 7:37). Lady Wisdom is not a code name for Jesus; she is a poetic figure for God's own wisdom. But that wisdom came in person in Christ.

That is why Proverbs is not a burden to the one who reads it with the gospel in hand. No reader will live up to every line: Who can say, "I have made my heart pure; I am clean from my sin"? (20:9). Christ lived the wise and righteous life in our place, and his righteousness is counted as ours; the one who confesses and forsakes his sins will obtain mercy (28:13); the righteous who fall seven times rise again (24:16); and the Spirit he gives is the Spirit of wisdom who makes the way of the wise our own. Proverbs trains the life that grace has begun.

Chapters 1-4, 8, 9 and 31 have more room here, because the whole book stands on them; the sentence proverbs of chapters 10-30 are taken a few verses at a time.

1.title: The Fear of the LORD Is the Beginning of Knowledge

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Why This Book Was Written
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A heading and a purpose statement: wisdom for the simple and the young, and more learning for the wise (vv. 1-6). Then the motto of the whole book (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Wisdom in Proverbs is skill for living in God's world, and it starts not with a technique but with a posture before God.

verseByVerse.quote: The proverbs of Solomon, son of David, king of Israel:
verseByVerse.commentary:
The book opens with a name and a pedigree. Solomon was the king who, when God offered him anything he asked, asked for an understanding mind to govern your people, that I may discern between good and evil (1 Kgs 3:9). God gave it. What we have here is a selection from his sayings and those of others.

The book's authority does not rest on Solomon's brilliance. Solomon himself ended badly, his heart turned by the very things this book warns against. Its authority rests on the God who gave him wisdom and then gave these sayings to his people. The Hebrew word for proverbs, mashal, is a saying that often sets two things side by side so that one throws light on the other.

And there is one more name behind this one. Jesus said of himself, something greater than Solomon is here (Matt 12:42). The queen of the South came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon; the reader of Proverbs has the wiser King close at hand, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col 2:3).
verseByVerse.note: Solomon is credited with 3,000 proverbs. The book also gathers sayings of “the wise,” proverbs copied by Hezekiah’s men, and the words of Agur and Lemuel.

verseByVerse.quote: To know wisdom and instruction, to understand words of insight, to receive instruction in wise dealing, in righteousness, justice, and equity; to give prudence to the simple, knowledge and discretion to the youth—
verseByVerse.commentary:
The purpose is stacked up word on word, and inside the list sit righteousness, justice, and equity. Wisdom in this book is not cleverness; a con man can be clever. Wisdom here is the skill of living rightly, and it is never separated from being good.

The word instruction appears twice. Wisdom is not only information received; it is a shaping that sometimes hurts, like the Lord's discipline of his sons in 3:11, quoted in Hebrews 12.

Two audiences are named. The simple are not the mentally slow. They are a door that swings with any wind, believing whatever they hear last. The youth stands at the start of life with every road open. Proverbs is written for the person who does not yet know which voices to trust: teenagers, and every adult honest about how easily he is still persuaded.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the wise hear and increase in learning, and the one who understands obtain guidance, to understand a proverb and a saying, the words of the wise and their riddles.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In case the wise reader thinks the book is for other people, the purpose statement turns to him. One mark of wisdom is that it knows it has not arrived. The fool in this book is always sure; the wise man is always learning.

Try it as a test. When did you last change your mind about something important because someone corrected you? If you cannot remember, the verse is aimed at you.

Proverbs have to be understood, not merely memorised: a compressed truth about how life usually goes, not a guarantee, which is why 26:4 and 26:5 can sit side by side and say opposite things about answering a fool.

verseByVerse.quote: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge; fools despise wisdom and instruction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The motto of the whole book returns in almost the same words at 9:10, and the rest of Scripture repeats it: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom (Ps 111:10), and Job's great poem on the search for wisdom ends, Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom (Job 28:28).

What is the fear of the LORD? It is not cringing terror, as though God were a tyrant. Nor is it only respect, as though he were a distinguished elder. It is the settled awareness that the God of Israel, the LORD, is really there, is holy, sees everything, and is the one you will answer to. It is the reverence of a child who loves his father and would not for the world grieve him, and who also knows his father is not to be trifled with. Both together.

And it is the beginning, a Hebrew word meaning both the first step and the chief part. You cannot start being wise without it, and you never graduate beyond it. A person can be highly educated and successful and still not have begun. The first question Proverbs asks is not how smart you are but where you stand before God.

The fool in Proverbs is not stupid. He is someone who will not be told; the problem is not in his head but in his will.

For a Christian the motto has a face. God has made Christ wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption (1 Cor 1:30). To fear the LORD now is to bow before the Son, and that is where real knowledge begins.
verseByVerse.note: The book closes on the same note: a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised (31:30).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A father speaks. The first danger he names is a gang offering belonging and easy money (vv. 8-19).
verseByVerse.theology: The first temptation in the book is not lust but belonging, and the first lie is that greed can be shared without cost.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear, my son, your father's instruction, and forsake not your mother's teaching, for they are a graceful garland for your head and pendants for your neck.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From here to the end of chapter 9, most of the book is a father speaking to his son. Wisdom is taught first at the kitchen table, and in a world where a mother's voice could be discounted, the book gives your mother's teaching the same weight as the father's.

Timothy knew what that looks like. Paul reminds him of the faith that dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice (2 Tim 1:5), and that from childhood you have been acquainted with the sacred writings (2 Tim 3:15). A mother reading Scripture to a child is doing the work of Proverbs 1.

Parental instruction is not a weight hung round the neck but jewellery. A young man often feels it as a chain; the father says it is a crown. The picture returns in 4:9.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent. If they say, "Come with us, let us lie in wait for blood; let us ambush the innocent without reason; like Sheol let us swallow them alive, and whole, like those who go down to the pit; we shall find all precious goods, we shall fill our houses with plunder; throw in your lot among us; we will all have one purse"—
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first warning in the book is short and plain: do not consent. Temptation is not sin; the son cannot stop sinners from asking, but he can answer no. The whole battle comes down to one word. He does not say it alone: he speaks as a son, with a father's love and the LORD's covenant behind him, and for the Christian the grace that saves also trains us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions (Titus 2:12), by the Spirit who gives the strength to refuse.

The father puts the gang's pitch in their own words, so that his son will recognise it. The first word is Come with us. Before it is an offer of money, it is an offer of belonging. A lonely young man is offered a crew.

They speak of swallowing people alive, and whole. It sounds exciting said quickly; said slowly, it is the language of murderers. Then the money, and the clinching promise of one purse: shared risk, shared reward, loyalty.

The Gospels show how that purse ends. Among the Twelve, Judas was the one having charge of the moneybag, and he used to help himself to what was put into it (John 12:6). He sold innocent blood for thirty pieces of silver, then came back saying, I have sinned by betraying innocent blood. The priests who had paid him answered, What is that to us? See to it yourself (Matt 27:4). That is the loyalty of the one purse. The gang that promises to share everything leaves you alone with the guilt.

verseByVerse.quote: my son, do not walk in the way with them; hold back your foot from their paths, for their feet run to evil, and they make haste to shed blood. For in vain is a net spread in the sight of any bird, but these men lie in wait for their own blood; they set an ambush for their own lives. Such are the ways of everyone who is greedy for unjust gain; it takes away the life of its possessors.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The counsel is physical: hold back your foot. Sin is usually reached by steps, not leaps. Some temptations are resisted by debate; most are resisted by not being there.

Isaiah says nearly the same of a whole nation, Their feet run to evil, and they are swift to shed innocent blood (Isa 59:7), and Paul gathers those words into his indictment of the human race: Their feet are swift to shed blood (Rom 3:15). The gang in Proverbs 1 is not an unusual kind of human being. It is what every heart is capable of when greed and company run together. That is why the son needs more than good advice: he needs Christ, who was tempted in every way and did not sin (Hebrews 4:15), who obeyed in his place, and whose mercy meets the one who has already gone with the gang.

A bird that sees the net spread will not fly into it; these men are building the trap and walk into it anyway. Their greed does not merely cost them their money; it owns them and then kills them. Judas again: he acquired a field with the reward of his wickedness, and died in it (Acts 1:18).

Paul says the same about the respectable version of this sin: those who desire to be rich fall into temptation, into a snare (1 Tim 6:9). The snare is the same in an alley or an office. Is there any gain in my life that I could only have by someone else's loss? That is the net, and I can see it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–33 — Wisdom Cries Aloud in the Street
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wisdom shouts in the streets, pleads with the simple to turn, and warns that the time of calling ends (vv. 20-33).
verseByVerse.theology: The same voice that pleads also warns that the day of pleading ends. The New Testament hears that voice in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Wisdom cries aloud in the street, in the markets she raises her voice; at the head of the noisy streets she cries out; at the entrance of the city gates she speaks:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now a new voice. Wisdom speaks not in a temple or a hermit's cave but in the market and at the city gate where business and lawsuits were settled. The sinners of verse 11 called the young man in the street; Wisdom shouts in the same street, over the traffic. She goes where the gang goes. Nobody in this chapter perishes because the truth was hidden from him.

The New Testament hears this voice in Jesus. On the last day of the feast, the great day, Jesus stood up and cried out, "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink" (John 7:37). He described himself in Wisdom's terms: wisdom is justified by her deeds (Matt 11:19). And where Luke records the Wisdom of God said, I will send them prophets and apostles (Luke 11:49), Matthew records Jesus saying in his own person, Therefore I send you prophets and wise men and scribes (Matt 23:34). Wisdom in this poem is a figure of speech, not a secret name for Jesus; but the wisdom of God she gives a voice to took flesh in him and walked into the same streets.

Why is Wisdom a woman? The Hebrew word for wisdom is feminine, and Proverbs personifies it as a woman calling in the streets, set against another woman, Folly (9:13–18). Wisdom is not a goddess but God’s own wisdom given a voice; the New Testament finds its fullness in Christ, the wisdom of God (1 Cor 1:24).
verseByVerse.note: Wisdom speaks again, at greater length, in 8:1-36 and 9:1-6.

verseByVerse.quote: "How long, O simple ones, will you love being simple? How long will scoffers delight in their scoffing and fools hate knowledge? If you turn at my reproof, behold, I will pour out my spirit to you; I will make my words known to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three kinds of people, a descending staircase: the simple drift, scoffers mock what they have not considered, fools hate knowledge. The chilling word is love: the simple prefer their ignorance, because staying unformed means staying uncommitted. How long? is the impatience of love, like a mother calling a child in from the road.

Wisdom does not ask the simple to become wise first and then come. She asks them to turn, and then she will give herself: her spirit and her words. The turning is repentance; the gift is grace.

In its own setting the line probably means that Wisdom will pour out her mind and heart in words, as the parallel line says (the Hebrew word for spirit can mean that). But read with the whole Bible open, it has a fuller echo. God said through Joel, I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh (Joel 2:28), and Peter declared it fulfilled at Pentecost (Acts 2:17). Jesus' cry at the feast was about exactly this: Now this he said about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive (John 7:39). What Wisdom offers in the street, Christ, the wisdom of God, poured out on his people.

verseByVerse.quote: Because I have called and you refused to listen, have stretched out my hand and no one has heeded, because you have ignored all my counsel and would have none of my reproof, I also will laugh at your calamity; I will mock when terror strikes you, when terror strikes you like a storm and your calamity comes like a whirlwind, when distress and anguish come upon you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the tone is frightening. Wisdom stretched out my hand, reaching to pull a person out of danger. Paul uses the same picture of God with Israel: All day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people (Rom 10:21).

How can Wisdom laugh at anyone's disaster? It sounds cruel until you see what is being laughed at. It is not the suffering person but the folly that thought it could defy God and win. Psalm 2 uses the same figure of the kings who plot against the LORD and his Anointed: He who sits in the heavens laughs (Ps 2:4). The laughter is the absurdity of rebellion exposed. Every warning the fool dismissed as overcautious has come true.

The consequences of folly arrive like weather, suddenly and from every side: a marriage that ends, a career that collapses in a week, after years of warnings ignored.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they will call upon me, but I will not answer; they will seek me diligently but will not find me. Because they hated knowledge and did not choose the fear of the LORD, would have none of my counsel and despised all my reproof, therefore they shall eat the fruit of their way, and have their fill of their own devices.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A hard sentence. Proverbs 8 promises, those who seek me diligently find me (8:17); here the same seeking finds nothing. The difference is what they are seeking. Verse 29 explains: they hated knowledge and did not choose the fear of the LORD. They want the consequences removed, not the heart changed. It is the cry of Esau, who found no chance to repent, though he sought it with tears (Heb 12:17). He wanted the blessing back, not the God of the blessing.

There is a real then. Jesus told of the master of the house who has risen and shut the door, and those outside knocking and calling Lord, open to us (Luke 13:25). The door does not stay open forever. That is why the Bible's urgency always falls on the present: Seek the LORD while he may be found (Isa 55:6); behold, now is the day of salvation (2 Cor 6:2).

Pastorally, it matters to say this plainly: if you are anxious that you have sought God too late, your anxiety is itself evidence that you are not the person of verse 29. The people in this verse do not grieve that they hated the fear of the LORD. They only grieve the storm.

The verb is choose. The fool was not unlucky; he decided, again and again, until the decisions became who he was. God's judgment here is being given what they chose, in full. They wanted their own devices; now they have their fill of them. The worst thing God can do to a person who insists on his own way is to let him have it.

verseByVerse.quote: For the simple are killed by their turning away, and the complacency of fools destroys them; but whoever listens to me will dwell secure and will be at ease, without dread of disaster."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two killers are named, and neither is dramatic. Turning away: not open rebellion, just walking off when Wisdom is talking. And complacency: the ease of a person who assumes tomorrow will look like today. Jesus told of a rich man who said to his soul, relax, eat, drink, be merry. But God said to him, Fool! This night your soul is required of you (Luke 12:19-20). Most people are destroyed not by one great act of defiance but by being comfortable.

The chapter ends on the other side, and the promise is rest. The fool was at ease in a false way and destroyed by it. The one who listens to Wisdom is truly at ease, without dread of disaster. Not without disaster, necessarily. Without dread of it. His security rests on something the storm cannot take.

Wisdom called in the street; Christ called in the same way, with the same offer: Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matt 11:28). Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts (Heb 3:15). The whole book is an invitation to be the person of verse 33, and it begins by bowing before the Lord who is himself the wisdom of God.

1.overview: Proverbs opens with its heading and purpose, wisdom for the simple and growth for the wise (vv. 1-6), and its motto, the fear of the LORD as the beginning of knowledge (v. 7). A father warns his son about a gang whose ambush is set for themselves (vv. 8-19). Then Wisdom shouts in the streets, pleading with the simple to turn and promising security to all who listen (vv. 20-33).
1.theology:
Wisdom begins with the fear of the LORD, the reverent and loving awareness of the holy God (v. 7; 9:10; Ps 111:10). Folly is a matter of the will, not the intellect: fools despise wisdom. Wisdom is inseparable from righteousness, justice and equity (v. 3).

Temptation offers belonging before it offers gain, and sin is self-destructive: the ambush is set for the ambushers (vv. 10-19; Rom 3:15; 1 Tim 6:9).

Wisdom calls publicly and freely, offers her spirit to those who turn (v. 23; Acts 2:17), and warns that the time of calling ends (vv. 24-31; Luke 13:25). The New Testament presents Christ as the Wisdom of God who cries out and gives rest (Luke 11:49; John 7:37; 1 Cor 1:24, 30; Col 2:3).
1.examples: A teenager invited into a group chat that mocks someone, or a colleague offered a cut of a scheme everyone else is in on, hears the gang's first words, Come with us, and can learn to answer no. A mother reading Scripture to a child at bedtime is doing what Lois and Eunice did. And someone carrying an anxious fear of having left it too late can take heart from verse 33: the promise is not a life without disaster, but a life without dread of it.

2.title: If You Seek It Like Silver

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Search and the Gift
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: If the son searches for wisdom like silver, he will find the knowledge of God, because the LORD gives wisdom (vv. 1-11).
verseByVerse.theology: The effort is ours and the gift is God's, and neither cancels the other.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, if you receive my words and treasure up my commandments with you, making your ear attentive to wisdom and inclining your heart to understanding; yes, if you call out for insight and raise your voice for understanding, if you seek it like silver and search for it as for hidden treasures,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Proverbs 2 is, in Hebrew, a single long sentence of twenty-two verses, built as a chain: if this, then that. The conditions climb. A word heard and forgotten has not been received; to treasure up is to store it somewhere safe, where you can get at it again. Inclining your heart is leaning toward a speaker so as not to miss a word: hearing that goes inward.

In chapter 1, Wisdom raises her voice in the street (1:20). Now the son is to raise his voice for her. She calls; he calls back. Wisdom is a conversation, and the one who wants it must ask out loud, which means admitting he lacks it. If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God (Jas 1:5).

Now the governing image. Men have searched for silver with tunnels cut into rock, lamps lowered into shafts, and years spent on the hope of a seam. Job 28 describes exactly that, Surely there is a mine for silver, and then asks, But where shall wisdom be found? (Job 28:1, 12).

What do you search for with that kind of energy? A promotion, a house, a relationship? The verse does not say those are wrong; it says wisdom deserves at least as much. Jesus told of a man who found treasure hidden in a field, Then in his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field (Matt 13:44). For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also (Matt 6:21).

verseByVerse.quote: then you will understand the fear of the LORD and find the knowledge of God. For the LORD gives wisdom; from his mouth come knowledge and understanding; he stores up sound wisdom for the upright; he is a shield to those who walk in integrity, guarding the paths of justice and watching over the way of his saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the then: the searcher went looking for wisdom and found God. The fear of the LORD is where wisdom begins (1:7) and where the search ends. The treasure at the bottom of the mine is not a technique for living but the knowledge of God: not facts about him, but knowing him.

Verse 6 is the hinge of the chapter, and it turns everything the right way round. After four verses of digging, the reason anyone finds wisdom is that the LORD gives it. The search is real, but it is not a wage; nobody earns wisdom the way a miner earns silver. It is a gift, and it comes from his mouth, which means it comes by his word.

The New Testament keeps both halves in the same way: work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure (Phil 2:12-13). The effort does not cancel the grace, and the grace does not make the effort pointless. God gives his wisdom to people who want it badly enough to dig. Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find (Matt 7:7).

The son was to treasure up the father's words (v. 1); here God stores up wisdom for the upright. He lays up a supply for his people before they need it, and he is their shield. The son on this road is not walking it alone.

His saints are not an elite of especially holy people, but those bound to God in his covenant love. Every believer walking the path of justice has God on watch over that path.

verseByVerse.quote: Then you will understand righteousness and justice and equity, every good path; for wisdom will come into your heart, and knowledge will be pleasant to your soul; discretion will watch over you, understanding will guard you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second then is about knowing how to live, and the order matters. Proverbs never offers moral skill cut off from God; it comes after, and out of, knowing him. Righteousness and justice and equity are the same three words from the book's purpose statement (1:3). This is where the book was heading. And every good path is generous: wisdom does not only tell a person what to avoid; it opens up every good road there is.

Something changes inside. At first the son searches for wisdom as a duty, digging because his father told him to. But wisdom will come into your heart, and then it becomes pleasant. What was hard work becomes a taste. This is what God, by his Spirit, does to the desires of those he teaches. The psalmist could say, The law of your mouth is better to me than thousands of gold and silver pieces (Ps 119:72). The search for silver ends with the searcher preferring what he found to silver.

If obedience still feels like a mine shaft to you, keep digging. The promise is that it will not always feel that way.

God watched over the way of his saints (v. 8); now the wisdom he gave watches from inside. Discretion is the ability to see a situation for what it is before you are in the middle of it: to recognise the smooth voice on the first sentence rather than the fifth. That is what the rest of the chapter needs.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–22 — Delivered from Two Ways of Death
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wisdom delivers from two smooth-speaking dangers, crooked men and the forbidden woman whose house sinks to death, and keeps the upright in the land (vv. 12-22).
verseByVerse.theology: The two great seductions of a young man, crooked company and illicit sex, both speak smoothly and both lead down.

verseByVerse.quote: delivering you from the way of evil, from men of perverted speech, who forsake the paths of uprightness to walk in the ways of darkness, who rejoice in doing evil and delight in the perverseness of evil, men whose paths are crooked, and who are devious in their ways.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom's first rescue is from a kind of man identified by his speech: talk that twists things, that makes the wrong sound reasonable and the right sound naive. The gang of chapter 1 was dangerous because of what it said: Come with us. Most young people are not dragged into evil. They are talked into it.

These men once knew the paths of uprightness; they walked away, and prefer darkness, where they cannot be seen.

Here is the last stage of corruption: not doing evil reluctantly, but enjoying it, and enjoying it in others. Paul describes the same end of the road: they not only do them but give approval to those who practice them (Rom 1:32). When a group laughs together about wrongdoing, that is the verse.

On a crooked path you cannot see where it bends next; wisdom lets you see the bend before you take it.

verseByVerse.quote: So you will be delivered from the forbidden woman, from the adulteress with her smooth words, who forsakes the companion of her youth and forgets the covenant of her God;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom's second rescue. She may be an Israelite by birth; she is "strange" and "foreign" (see the note) because she stands outside the boundary God set around marriage. Like the men of verse 12, she works by speech: smooth words. Chapter 5 will say her lips drip honey and her speech is smoother than oil (5:3). Sexual temptation almost never introduces itself as adultery. It introduces itself as being understood, admired, listened to. The discretion of verse 11 is what hears the flattery for what it is.

Both dangers in this chapter work through words, which means both are defeated by a better word: the father's commandments treasured up in the heart (v. 1). A man who has Scripture stored away has something to answer the smooth voice with.

She has left her husband, and forgotten the covenant of her God. Marriage in the Bible is never merely a private arrangement between two people. God is party to it. Malachi says it outright: the LORD was witness between you and the wife of your youth, to whom you have been faithless, though she is your companion and your wife by covenant (Mal 2:14).

So adultery is not a sin against one person. It breaks faith with a spouse and with God at the same time. Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled (Heb 13:4).

The forbidden woman is a real danger: adultery, plainly warned against. She is also the dark counterpart of Lady Wisdom, and in chapter 9 she reappears as Folly herself. The warning is literal, and it also stands for every voice that lures us away from God’s wisdom.
verseByVerse.note: “Forbidden woman” is literally “strange woman,” and “adulteress” is literally “foreign woman” (ESV notes).

verseByVerse.quote: for her house sinks down to death, and her paths to the departed; none who go to her come back, nor do they regain the paths of life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Her house looks like a house, with a door, a bed, perfume. The father sees what the young man cannot: the whole building is sinking. The ESV notes that the departed is in Hebrew "the Rephaim", the shades of the dead, whom Sheol rouses to greet a fallen king in Isaiah (Isa 14:9). Chapter 7 ends with the same picture: Her house is the way to Sheol (7:27).

This is a warning about where the road goes, and it is meant to frighten. Adultery rarely stays one act. It rewires a person's desires, breaks trust that is almost never fully rebuilt, wrecks children, and often ends a life's direction. Many who go down that road never come back to where they were. He who commits adultery lacks sense; he who does it destroys himself (6:32).

But a reader who has already been down that road needs to hear the rest of the Bible too. Proverbs describes the destination of the path, not the limit of God's mercy. David went to another man's wife and took her. When Nathan confronted him, David said to Nathan, "I have sinned against the LORD." And Nathan said to David, "The LORD also has put away your sin; you shall not die" (2 Sam 12:13). Paul wrote to Corinthians who had been adulterers, And such were some of you. But you were washed (1 Cor 6:11). No one regains the paths of life by his own strength. Christ brings people back who could not come back.

verseByVerse.quote: So you will walk in the way of the good and keep to the paths of the righteous. For the upright will inhabit the land, and those with integrity will remain in it, but the wicked will be cut off from the land, and the treacherous will be rooted out of it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the two warnings, the positive goal: wisdom puts a person on a road with good company. The best protection against bad company is good company. Flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace, along with those who call on the Lord from a pure heart (2 Tim 2:22).

For an Israelite, the land meant the inheritance God had promised Abraham, the place of God's blessing and presence. To be cut off from it was to lose everything the covenant offered. Psalm 37 says the same, The righteous shall inherit the land and dwell upon it forever (Ps 37:29).

Jesus took that promise and widened it: Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth (Matt 5:5). Proverbs is not promising here that every upright person will keep his house or farm; it describes where the two roads finally end. The land was always a picture of something larger, the whole creation renewed and given to God's people.

Two futures: the treacherous are rooted out like a plant that looked established and had no hold; the upright remain. The world is passing away along with its desires, but whoever does the will of God abides forever (1 John 2:17). The silver the young man was told to dig for turns out to be a place in God's world forever.

2.text: <sup>1</sup>My son, if you receive my words and treasure up my commandments with you,<sup>2</sup>making your ear attentive to wisdom and inclining your heart to understanding;<sup>3</sup>yes, if you call out for insight and raise your voice for understanding,<sup>4</sup>if you seek it like silver and search for it as for hidden treasures,<sup>5</sup>then you will understand the fear of the LORD and find the knowledge of God.<sup>6</sup>For the LORD gives wisdom; from his mouth come knowledge and understanding;<sup>7</sup>he stores up sound wisdom for the upright; he is a shield to those who walk in integrity,<sup>8</sup>guarding the paths of justice and watching over the way of his saints.<sup>9</sup>Then you will understand righteousness and justice and equity, every good path;<sup>10</sup>for wisdom will come into your heart, and knowledge will be pleasant to your soul;<sup>11</sup>discretion will watch over you, understanding will guard you,<sup>12</sup>delivering you from the way of evil, from men of perverted speech,<sup>13</sup>who forsake the paths of uprightness to walk in the ways of darkness,<sup>14</sup>who rejoice in doing evil and delight in the perverseness of evil,<sup>15</sup>men whose paths are crooked, and who are devious in their ways.<sup>16</sup>So you will be delivered from the forbidden woman, from the adulteress with her smooth words,<sup>17</sup>who forsakes the companion of her youth and forgets the covenant of her God;<sup>18</sup>for her house sinks down to death, and her paths to the departed;<sup>19</sup>none who go to her come back, nor do they regain the paths of life.<sup>20</sup>So you will walk in the way of the good and keep to the paths of the righteous.<sup>21</sup>For the upright will inhabit the land, and those with integrity will remain in it,<sup>22</sup>but the wicked will be cut off from the land, and the treacherous will be rooted out of it.
2.overview: Proverbs 2 is one long conditional argument. If the son searches for wisdom like silver (vv. 1-4), he will find the knowledge of God, who gives wisdom and guards his saints (vv. 5-8), and wisdom will become pleasant and guard him (vv. 9-11): from men of perverted speech (vv. 12-15) and from the forbidden woman whose house sinks down to death (vv. 16-19). The upright will remain in the land (vv. 20-22).
2.theology:
The search for wisdom requires real effort (vv. 1-4), yet wisdom is God's gift from his mouth (v. 6); human seeking and divine giving work together (Phil 2:12-13; Jas 1:5). Its goal is knowing God himself (v. 5), and moral understanding follows from that (v. 9). God changes desire, so that wisdom becomes pleasant (v. 10).

Evil and sexual sin both work through deceptive speech (vv. 12, 16). Marriage is a covenant before God, so adultery breaks faith with God as well as a spouse (v. 17; Mal 2:14). The road of adultery leads to death (vv. 18-19), but the gospel restores the repentant (2 Sam 12:13; 1 Cor 6:11). The inheritance of the land anticipates the meek inheriting the earth (v. 21; Matt 5:5).
2.examples: A student who gives an hour a day to Scripture with the energy others give to exams is digging in the right mine, and may find that what began as duty becomes a taste. Someone who notices a colleague's flattery beginning to feel like being understood can recognise the smooth voice of verse 16 on the first sentence rather than the fifth. And the person who has already gone down that road can read David's story and Paul's such were some of you: the end of the path is not the limit of mercy.

3.title: Trust in the LORD with All Your Heart

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Trust, Honour and the Father's Discipline
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Trust the LORD with all your heart, honour him with the firstfruits, and do not despise his loving discipline (vv. 1-12).
verseByVerse.theology: Every line in this section is about the heart's posture toward God: trusting him, honouring him, and not resenting him when he corrects.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, do not forget my teaching, but let your heart keep my commandments, for length of days and years of life and peace they will add to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The father begins with memory and the heart. Most people who abandon what they were taught do not reject it in one decision; they forget it slowly, by not returning to it. So the teaching is to be kept in the heart, where it shapes what a person wants and not just what he knows.

The reason given is life, and peace, shalom, life that is well in every part. The commandments are not a fence to keep good things out; they are the shape of life as God made it to work.

Is this a promise that every godly person lives to old age? The book itself does not read it that way, and neither does the rest of Scripture. Proverbs gives patterns, not promises: it describes how God's world generally runs, and a life of honesty, self-control and peace with neighbours tends to be longer and fuller than a life of drunkenness, violence and deceit. Abel was righteous and died young. The deepest fulfilment of length of days lies beyond this life, in the one who promises eternal life to all who trust him.

verseByVerse.quote: Let not steadfast love and faithfulness forsake you; bind them around your neck; write them on the tablet of your heart. So you will find favor and good success in the sight of God and man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Steadfast love and faithfulness are two of the richest words in the Old Testament, hesed and emet. They are the words God used of himself before Moses, abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness (Exod 34:6): the son is to bear the character of the God who first showed it to him.

They are kept outside, around your neck, and inside, on the tablet of your heart. What God wrote on stone at Sinai, the father wants written on his son's heart. That is precisely what God promised to do in the new covenant: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts (Jer 31:33). Paul told the Corinthians they were a letter written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts (2 Cor 3:3).

And when the Word became flesh, John saw the two words walking in a human life: full of grace and truth (John 1:14).

The ESV notes that good success may be rendered "repute": a good name. Luke says the boy Jesus increased in favor with God and man (Luke 2:52), the clearest picture there is of this verse lived.

verseByVerse.quote: Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make straight your paths.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Trust means to rely on, to put your weight down on something. With all your heart excludes the divided trust that relies on God for eternity and on itself for Tuesday, the same wholeness as the great command, You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart (Deut 6:5).

It does not say, do not use your understanding; Proverbs is full of commands to think and plan. It says, do not lean on it. Your understanding is a useful tool and a terrible foundation: limited, because you do not know tomorrow, and bent, because your heart tilts it toward what you want.

And when you find you have not trusted with all your heart, as every believer does, this verse is not the end of you. Christ trusted the Father perfectly in our place, even on the cross (Luke 23:46), and his Spirit renews trust in those who are his.

Acknowledge translates the ordinary Hebrew word for know. It means more than a nod to God before doing what you had already decided: it means bringing him into the career and the conversation at lunch, the budget and the marriage.

The picture is of a road being levelled, as in Isaiah's highway where the uneven ground shall become level (Isa 40:4). It does not promise a map of the whole journey, a road without hills, or an inner voice naming which job to take. It promises that God clears the way ahead of the one who trusts him, and gets him where he is meant to go. The heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps (16:9).

verseByVerse.quote: Be not wise in your own eyes; fear the LORD, and turn away from evil. It will be healing to your flesh and refreshment to your bones.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Verse 7 says negatively what verse 5 said positively. Leaning on your own understanding looks like the man who does not ask advice because he already knows, and does not pray about a decision because it is obvious. Isaiah pronounced a woe on exactly him: Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes (Isa 5:21). Paul told the Romans, Never be wise in your own sight (Rom 12:16).

The cure is fear the LORD, the beginning of knowledge (1:7), and it shows itself practically: turn away from evil. A person who says he trusts God and keeps walking toward evil is still wise in his own eyes. Yet the way back is open: he who confesses and forsakes his sins will obtain mercy (28:13).

The ESV notes that flesh is literally "navel" and healing may be "medicine". Either way, humility before God is good for body as well as soul: a person not carrying the burden of being his own god carries less strain. Pride is exhausting.

verseByVerse.quote: Honor the LORD with your wealth and with the firstfruits of all your produce; then your barns will be filled with plenty, and your vats will be bursting with wine.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Trust in God shows up in the bank account. Under the law, Israel brought the first and best of the harvest to God: The best of the firstfruits of your ground you shall bring into the house of the LORD your God (Exod 23:19). The firstfruits were given before the farmer knew how big the harvest would be, an act of trust; giving God what is left over after the bills requires no faith at all. For a Christian the principle stands: giving to God first and gladly, as people who have received everything from him. Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver (2 Cor 9:7).

Is this the prosperity gospel, give to get? No. God is no man's debtor, but Proverbs describes how his world generally works, not a formula to manipulate him. Job feared God, gave to the poor, and lost everything in a day, and said, The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD (Job 1:21).

Paul gives the New Testament form of the promise, and says what the abundance is for: God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that having all sufficiency in all things at all times, you may abound in every good work (2 Cor 9:8). The full barn is given so that the giving can continue.

Does this bind Christians to a tithe? Firstfruits and tithes belonged to Israel’s law. The New Testament does not set a percentage; it calls for giving that is regular, proportionate and cheerful (1 Cor 16:2; 2 Cor 9:6–7), and many find a tenth a good place to begin. If you have given faithfully and are still struggling, God has not broken his word to you; the richest return on a gift to him is himself, and treasure in heaven that no thief can reach (Matt 6:20).

verseByVerse.quote: My son, do not despise the LORD's discipline or be weary of his reproof, for the LORD reproves him whom he loves, as a father the son in whom he delights.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having promised full barns, the father faces the other side: what about when life hurts? To despise discipline is to shrug off hardship and learn nothing; to be weary of it is to be crushed and give up. Neither is right, because discipline is love. A father who never corrects his son cares about him less, not more.

The letter to the Hebrews quotes these two verses to Christians who were suffering and ready to give up: My son, do not regard lightly the discipline of the Lord, nor be weary when reproved by him. For the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and chastises every son whom he receives (Heb 12:5-6). Hebrews follows the Septuagint here; the sense is the same as the Hebrew. Discipline is for our good, that we may share his holiness (Heb 12:10), and later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness (Heb 12:11). The risen Christ says the same to a lukewarm church: Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline (Rev 3:19).

Not all suffering is punishment for a specific sin, and Job is the Bible's long proof of that. All of a believer's suffering is in the hands of a Father who loves him, and it is right to ask what he may be teaching. But lament is also faithful: Psalm 88 ends in darkness, Job poured out his complaint, and both stand in Scripture. Not every sorrow is a lesson you are failing to learn; sometimes the Father's word in it is simply that he is with you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–26 — Blessed Is the One Who Finds Wisdom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wisdom is worth more than any treasure, a tree of life, the wisdom by which the LORD founded the earth; kept, she gives security by day and sweet sleep by night (vv. 13-26).
verseByVerse.theology: The wisdom that holds the universe together is offered to a young man to hold his life together.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed is the one who finds wisdom, and the one who gets understanding, for the gain from her is better than gain from silver and her profit better than gold. She is more precious than jewels, and nothing you desire can compare with her.
verseByVerse.commentary: A new section opens with a beatitude: blessed, truly well off, whatever the circumstances. The language is commercial: compare the returns, the father says to a young man about to enter the market. Nothing you desire compares with her: not the house, the salary, the reputation or the retirement. Paul agrees: godliness is of value in every way, as it holds promise for the present life and also for the life to come (1 Tim 4:8).

verseByVerse.quote: Long life is in her right hand; in her left hand are riches and honor. Her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace. She is a tree of life to those who lay hold of her; those who hold her fast are called blessed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom is pictured holding gifts in both hands. In her right hand, the hand of greater honour, is long life; in her left, riches and honor. Life comes first, and riches second: the man who chases riches directly often loses them, and the one who pursues wisdom finds them added. Jesus put it in the same order: But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you (Matt 6:33).

Many imagine a godly life as dreary. The paths of folly are exciting at the start and full of regret; the paths of wisdom are sometimes hard at the start and full of peace.

A tree of life takes the reader back to Eden. After the fall, God guarded that tree lest he reach out his hand and take also of the tree of life and eat, and live forever (Gen 3:22). Now wisdom is a tree of life to those who lay hold of her, the very reaching out that was barred in Eden.

The Bible ends where it began, with the tree restored: on either side of the river, the tree of life with its twelve kinds of fruit, and The leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations (Rev 22:2). The way back to the tree is through the one who is the wisdom of God.

Does wisdom guarantee riches and long life? No more than verse 2 guarantees old age: Lazarus was poor (Luke 16:20). The full gift of wisdom’s long life is eternal.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD by wisdom founded the earth; by understanding he established the heavens; by his knowledge the deeps broke open, and the clouds drop down the dew.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the father lifts his son's eyes from the marketplace to the universe: the wisdom he urges is the wisdom by which God built the world. O LORD, how manifold are your works! In wisdom have you made them all (Ps 104:24).

Wisdom is not an arbitrary set of rules laid over a neutral world. It is the grain of the universe, from the great deeps to the morning dew; folly goes against it, and creation pushes back.

The New Testament names this creative wisdom. All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made (John 1:3). For by him all things were created, and in him all things hold together (Col 1:16-17). Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor 1:24). Chapter 8 develops this at length.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, do not lose sight of these— keep sound wisdom and discretion, and they will be life for your soul and adornment for your neck. Then you will walk on your way securely, and your foot will not stumble. If you lie down, you will not be afraid; when you lie down, your sleep will be sweet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the cosmic view, back to the son: good judgment and the ability to plan well are life inside and adornment outside, the double picture of verse 3.

By day, security. The wise are not immune from difficulty, but many disasters that wreck lives are the foreseeable results of choices, and wisdom removes a great many stones from the road.

By night, against the small hours of racing over the debt or the lie that might come out, the verse promises what money cannot buy: sweet sleep. In peace I will both lie down and sleep; for you alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety (Ps 4:8). For he gives to his beloved sleep (Ps 127:2). If you are a believer who lies awake through insomnia, illness or grief, this is not a rebuke: the verse describes a pattern, and the God who gives sleep also keeps watch with you through the night, for he will neither slumber nor sleep (Ps 121:4).

The most vivid picture of this verse in the Bible is a boat in a storm on Galilee. While the disciples were terrified, Jesus was in the stern, asleep on the cushion (Mark 4:38), because he trusted his Father completely. Those who belong to him can learn to sleep the same way.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be afraid of sudden terror or of the ruin of the wicked, when it comes, for the LORD will be your confidence and will keep your foot from being caught.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ESV notes that ruin is literally "storm". It is the same storm as in chapter 1, where terror strikes the fool like a storm (1:27). The storm will come; it will not sweep the wise away.

The ground of his safety is finally not his own wisdom but the LORD. The chapter began with trust (v. 5) and returns to it: the LORD will be your confidence. The wise man trusts not his wisdom but the God who gave it, and his foot is kept because God watches over his steps.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wisdom turns outward: do not withhold or postpone good, plot against a neighbour or envy the violent, for the LORD scorns the scorners and gives favour to the humble (vv. 27-35).
verseByVerse.theology: Trust in God that does not open the hand to a neighbour is not the trust of verse 5.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not withhold good from those to whom it is due, when it is in your power to do it. Do not say to your neighbor, "Go, and come again, tomorrow I will give it"—when you have it with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter turns to the neighbour: faith in God (v. 5) and honouring him with wealth (v. 9) are tested at the front door. The Hebrew, as the ESV's footnote records, reads Do not withhold good "from its owners". The good you could do for someone who needs it belongs, in a sense, to him: to hold back wages owed or help you could easily give is a kind of theft. The God who has not withheld good from us asks not that you meet every need in the world, but that you not refuse the one in front of you that is in your power to meet. So then, as we have opportunity, let us do good to everyone (Gal 6:10). Owe no one anything, except to love each other (Rom 13:8).

Postponement is the polite way of withholding good. It sounds generous and costs nothing today, but the need is today, and tomorrow is not promised. Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring (27:1).

James saw the same thing in the church: a brother or sister without food, and a believer saying, Go in peace, be warmed and filled, without giving them the things needed for the body, what good is that? (Jas 2:16). Is there a need you have been saying "tomorrow" to?

verseByVerse.quote: Do not plan evil against your neighbor, who dwells trustingly beside you. Do not contend with a man for no reason, when he has done you no harm.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your neighbour dwells trustingly beside you, assuming you are safe. To plot against someone who is not on guard is a particular evil: the friendly colleague quietly positioning against you, the partner moving the money.

Some people pick fights, arguing for the pleasure of winning. If he has done you no harm, leave him alone. If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all (Rom 12:18).

verseByVerse.quote: Do not envy a man of violence and do not choose any of his ways, for the devious person is an abomination to the LORD, but the upright are in his confidence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why would anyone envy a violent man? Because he often seems to win: he gets his way and takes what he wants. Psalm 73 is the long confession of a believer who nearly slipped this way: For I was envious of the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked (Ps 73:3). Envy is the first step toward choosing his ways.

Here is what the envious young man cannot see. The devious person is an abomination to the LORD, one of the strongest words of revulsion in the Old Testament. And the upright are in his confidence: in the close circle of friends who share secrets. The friendship of the LORD is for those who fear him, and he makes known to them his covenant (Ps 25:14).

The violent man has power; the upright man has God's friendship. Jesus said to his disciples, but I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you (John 15:15).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD's curse is on the house of the wicked, but he blesses the dwelling of the righteous. Toward the scorners he is scornful, but to the humble he gives favor. The wise will inherit honor, but fools get disgrace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three closing contrasts. The wicked man's house may be large and the righteous man's small; what matters is whether God's curse or blessing rests on it. God answers people in kind: the scorner is mocked, the humble are lifted. The ESV notes that favor may be rendered "grace", and that is exactly how the verse passed into the New Testament, where it is quoted twice: God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble (Jas 4:6; 1 Pet 5:5). James introduces it with the words But he gives more grace.

This is the gospel in a proverb. Grace is not given to the deserving. It is given to the humble, the people who know they are not deserving. The door to God is low, and only those who bend can get through it.

The chapter that began with trusting God with all your heart ends by showing where that trust leads.

The wise inherit honour as a gift; the fool who grasped at it gets disgrace (the ESV notes the Hebrew behind get is uncertain).

when you lie down, your sleep will be sweet.<sup>25</sup>Do not be afraid of sudden terror or of the ruin of the wicked, when it comes,<sup>26</sup>for the LORD will be your confidence and will keep your foot from being caught.<sup>27</sup>Do not withhold good from those to whom it is due, when it is in your power to do it.<sup>28</sup>Do not say to your neighbor, "Go, and come again, tomorrow I will give it"—when you have it with you.<sup>29</sup>Do not plan evil against your neighbor, who dwells trustingly beside you.<sup>30</sup>Do not contend with a man for no reason, when he has done you no harm.<sup>31</sup>Do not envy a man of violence and do not choose any of his ways,<sup>32</sup>for the devious person is an abomination to the LORD, but the upright are in his confidence.<sup>33</sup>The LORD's curse is on the house of the wicked, but he blesses the dwelling of the righteous.<sup>34</sup>Toward the scorners he is scornful, but to the humble he gives favor.<sup>35</sup>The wise will inherit honor, but fools get disgrace.
3.overview: The father urges his son to keep his teaching, to trust the LORD with all his heart rather than lean on his own understanding, to honour him with the firstfruits, and not to despise his fatherly discipline (vv. 1-12). Wisdom is worth more than any treasure, a tree of life, the wisdom by which the LORD founded the earth (vv. 13-26). And wisdom turns outward: it does not withhold good from a neighbour, and it receives the grace God gives to the humble (vv. 27-35).
3.theology:
Trust in God is wholehearted reliance that does not rest its weight on human understanding (vv. 5-6), and it is expressed in humility (v. 7), generosity (vv. 9-10) and acceptance of discipline (vv. 11-12). God's discipline is evidence of his fatherly love (Heb 12:5-11).

The wisdom by which God created the world (vv. 19-20) is fulfilled in Christ, through whom all things were made (John 1:3; Col 1:16-17). Wisdom is a tree of life, restoring what was lost in Eden (v. 18; Gen 3:22; Rev 22:2).

Love of neighbour is the proof of trust in God (vv. 27-30). God gives grace to the humble (v. 34; Jas 4:6; 1 Pet 5:5). The promises of long life and prosperity describe the general pattern of God's world, not a formula (Job 1:21).
3.examples: A couple choosing whether to move for a new job can pray about it, take advice, think hard, and still not lean their whole weight on their own reading of the future; God promises to level the road, not to show them the map. A family that sets aside its giving at the start of the month, before the bills, is bringing firstfruits. A believer in a hard season need neither shrug it off nor be crushed by it, and may also simply lament. And a neighbour who asks for help today should not hear Come back tomorrow if the help is in our hands now.

4.title: Keep Your Heart with All Vigilance

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A father passes on what his own father taught him as a boy: hold fast my words and live; get wisdom above all, and she will guard and crown you (vv. 1-9).
verseByVerse.theology: Wisdom is handed down from grandfather to father to son, and the first step toward it is simply wanting it more than anything else.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear, O sons, a father's instruction, and be attentive, that you may gain insight, for I give you good precepts; do not forsake my teaching.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The address has widened from my son to O sons. The private word to one boy is now for every reader, daughters as surely as sons. The ESV notes that gain insight is literally "know insight": wisdom is known the way a person knows a friend.

The father makes a simple claim: what I am giving you is good, not merely strict or traditional. A young person often assumes that his parents' instruction is there to limit him. The father asks him to consider that it might be a gift, and then warns him not to forsake it, as the men of chapter 2 forsook the paths of uprightness (2:13).

verseByVerse.quote: When I was a son with my father, tender, the only one in the sight of my mother, he taught me and said to me, "Let your heart hold fast my words; keep my commandments, and live. Get wisdom; get insight; do not forget, and do not turn away from the words of my mouth. Do not forsake her, and she will keep you; love her, and she will guard you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the father tells a story about himself. He was once a tender boy too, cherished by his mother, and he asks nothing he did not have to learn himself.

If the father speaking is Solomon, the grandfather is David, and we have a record of the kind of thing he said: And you, Solomon my son, know the God of your father and serve him with a whole heart and with a willing mind (1 Chr 28:9).

Three generations: the grandfather who taught, the father who remembers, the son who hears. Wisdom is meant to travel that way, from one generation's mouth to the next generation's heart, in words short enough for a boy to carry. What sentences will your children quote to theirs? Not most of what you say; a few things said often and lived out in front of them.

Wisdom is something to be acquired at a cost, and then someone to love, who in return will guard you. The son who guards her is guarded by her. That is the shape of every relationship with God's wisdom: what you hold on to ends up holding you.

verseByVerse.quote: The beginning of wisdom is this: Get wisdom, and whatever you get, get insight. Prize her highly, and she will exalt you; she will honor you if you embrace her. She will place on your head a graceful garland; she will bestow on you a beautiful crown."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This sounds circular: the beginning of wisdom is to get wisdom. But that is the point. The first step toward wisdom is not cleverness or experience. It is deciding that you want it above everything else. The fool never starts, because he does not think he needs it.

Whatever you get ranks degrees, money, friends and experience beneath this one thing. Jesus told of a merchant who, on finding one pearl of great value, went and sold all that he had and bought it (Matt 13:46). The kingdom and the wisdom of God are not an add-on to a life already full of other priorities. They are worth the whole purse.

A practical test: if someone looked at how you spend your money and your hours, would they conclude that wisdom is what you are trying to get?

Prize her, and she will exalt you. The language is almost that of courtship, and the grandfather's words end with a coronation. The person who treasures wisdom is not diminished by submitting to it; he is made royal.

Paul saw a crown at the end of his own race: Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award to me on that day, and not only to me but also to all who have loved his appearing (2 Tim 4:8).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two paths: do not set foot on the way of the wicked, who feed on violence, for the path of the righteous grows like the dawn while the way of the wicked is deep darkness (vv. 10-19).
verseByVerse.theology: One road grows lighter with every step; the other grows darker until a person cannot see what trips him.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear, my son, and accept my words, that the years of your life may be many. I have taught you the way of wisdom; I have led you in the paths of uprightness. When you walk, your step will not be hampered, and if you run, you will not stumble. Keep hold of instruction; do not let go; guard her, for she is your life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The father returns to one son. Accept is stronger than hear: taking a gift into your hands. He has not only taught but led: instruction without example is a map; with example it is a guide. The father can say I have led you because he has been on the road himself.

There are seasons that are steady and seasons at a sprint, when decisions come fast. Wisdom learned in the walking seasons keeps a person from falling in the running ones. A man who has thought through his convictions before the crisis does not have to invent them in it.

The grip language is urgent: the father talks about instruction the way a man hanging over a cliff talks about a rope. For she is your life. Moses said the same of God's word: For it is no empty word for you, but your very life (Deut 32:47).

verseByVerse.quote: Do not enter the path of the wicked, and do not walk in the way of the evil. Avoid it; do not go on it; turn away from it and pass on. For they cannot sleep unless they have done wrong; they are robbed of sleep unless they have made someone stumble. For they eat the bread of wickedness and drink the wine of violence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Six ways of saying one thing. The commands come from a father who has already led his son on straight paths (v. 11), and they are not repetitive by accident: the danger lies less in a single decision to become wicked than in the first step onto the path, and the second, and then the discovery that one is a long way down it.

The counsel is not "walk down the path a little way to understand it". It is avoid it. Some evil is best understood from a distance: films not to watch, websites not to open, parties not to attend, conversations to walk out of. Pass on.

A chilling picture of what evil does over time. At first a wicked act keeps a man awake with guilt; in the end, not doing it keeps him awake. Evil has become an appetite. Micah pronounced woe on those who devise wickedness and work evil on their beds! When the morning dawns, they perform it (Mic 2:1).

Compare the sweet sleep promised to the wise in 3:24. Both kinds of people lie awake or sleep according to what their hearts love.

Wickedness is their food. Jesus described what fed him in exactly the opposite terms: My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work (John 4:34). Every person lives on something. The question is what.

verseByVerse.quote: But the path of the righteous is like the light of dawn, which shines brighter and brighter until full day. The way of the wicked is like deep darkness; they do not know over what they stumble.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Dawn begins as a grey line on the horizon, then colour, then the sun's edge, then, steadily, full day. The righteous life is not bright all at once; it grows. That encourages anyone whose faith feels still at the grey-line stage. It is supposed to start there; the question is not how bright the light is but which direction it is moving. Paul describes the Christian life in the same way: we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another (2 Cor 3:18).

And the light has a source. Jesus said, I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life (John 8:12). The righteous path grows brighter because it leads toward him.

The other path runs the other way, into deep darkness. And the worst of it is not the stumbling but the not knowing why. The broken marriages, the friendships that end: they blame luck, other people, the system, and cannot see that the obstacle is their own path. The one who walks in the darkness does not know where he is going (John 12:35).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The father's words are life and healing. Keep your heart with all vigilance, for it is the spring of life, and then guard the mouth, the eyes and the feet, swerving neither right nor left (vv. 20-27).
verseByVerse.theology: The whole person is kept by keeping the heart, and the heart is kept by what the mouth, eyes and feet are allowed to do.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, be attentive to my words; incline your ear to my sayings. Let them not escape from your sight; keep them within your heart. For they are life to those who find them, and healing to all their flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last section moves through the body: ear, eyes, heart, then mouth, eyes and feet. The father wants his words to reach every part of his son.

Let them not escape from your sight is a warning about how easily truth slips away. It does not need to be refuted. It only needs to be not looked at for long enough. A Bible left closed for a month does not argue with you; it just fades.

The ESV notes that the Hebrew reads all "his" flesh, individualising the promise: each person who finds these words finds them to be life and healing for himself. The father's words are not only rules; they are medicine.

verseByVerse.quote: Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The centre of the chapter, and perhaps the most important single verse for understanding how Proverbs thinks about a person. In the Bible the heart is not only feelings but the control room of a person, where he thinks, chooses, loves and believes, and life flows out of it like water from a spring. If the spring is poisoned, every stream downstream is poisoned too.

Jesus taught exactly this: For from within, out of the heart of man, come evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery (Mark 7:21). And again, out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks (Luke 6:45). The problem with human beings is not first their circumstances or their behaviour. It is their hearts.

Guarding the heart with all vigilance is not protecting your feelings from being hurt. It means watching what goes into it, what it is allowed to love, what it dwells on, and what it is being trained to want. A man does not wake up one day an adulterer; he has let his heart dwell on another woman for months. A person does not become bitter overnight; he rehearsed the grievance a thousand times.

What have you allowed into your heart this week, through your eyes, your phone, your thoughts before sleep? Those are the springs your life will flow from next week.

And there is a limit to what anyone can do. No one can make his own heart new. That is what God promises to do: to give a new heart and put his Spirit within (Ezek 36:26-27). The command to keep the heart is given to people whose hearts God has already begun to change, and when they find they have not kept it, they look to Christ, whose heart was wholly pure in their place, and come back by confession to the mercy that is new every morning.

verseByVerse.quote: Put away from you crooked speech, and put devious talk far from you. Let your eyes look directly forward, and your gaze be straight before you. Ponder the path of your feet; then all your ways will be sure. Do not swerve to the right or to the left; turn your foot away from evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the heart, the mouth, because the mouth is where the heart comes out first. Words that twist are flattery, half-truths, gossip dressed up as concern, sarcasm that wounds: put them as far away as poison. Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up (Eph 4:29).

Then the eyes, like a man on a narrow road not glancing at every distraction; much temptation begins with the eyes lingering. And the Christian knows what to look at: let us run with endurance the race that is set before us, looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith (Heb 12:1-2). No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God (Luke 9:62).

Then the feet. Ponder means to think carefully about where the next step goes. The ESV notes it may be rendered "Make level", and that is the form in which the verse is quoted in the New Testament: and make straight paths for your feet, so that what is lame may not be put out of joint but rather be healed (Heb 12:13). There the point is that a Christian's steady walk helps the weaker believers walking behind him.

The chapter ends with the language Moses used to Israel: You shall not turn aside to the right hand or to the left (Deut 5:32). There are two ditches, careless sin on one side and proud rule-keeping on the other, and the wise person keeps walking straight ahead, heart guarded, mouth clean, eyes forward, on the road that grows brighter until full day.
