4.overview: A father passes on what his own father taught him: hold fast to my words and live; get wisdom above everything, and she will guard and crown you (vv. 1-9). He urges his son not to set foot on the path of the wicked; the path of the righteous is like the dawn, growing brighter until full day, while the way of the wicked is deep darkness (vv. 10-19). Above all he is to keep his heart, the spring of life, and guard his mouth, eyes and feet (vv. 20-27).
4.theology:
Wisdom is passed down through the generations in the family (vv. 3-4; 1 Chr 28:9). The first step toward wisdom is to desire it above all else (v. 7; Matt 13:45-46).

Sin is progressive and becomes an appetite (vv. 16-17); righteousness is progressive and grows toward full light (v. 18; 2 Cor 3:18; John 8:12).

The heart is the source of all of life, so it must be guarded above all (v. 23; Mark 7:21-23; Luke 6:45). The guarding of heart, mouth, eyes and feet belongs together (vv. 24-27), and the New Testament applies verse 26 to walking steadily for the sake of weaker believers (Heb 12:13).
4.examples: A grandmother who has told her grandchildren the same few sentences about God for years has done what David did for Solomon. A young Christian discouraged that his faith is only a grey line on the horizon can remember that dawn always starts that way. And someone who notices a resentment he has rehearsed for months, or a screen he keeps returning to late at night, has found exactly where verse 23 asks him to stand guard, and where Christ's mercy meets him when he has not.

5.title: Drink Water from Your Own Cistern

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Honey That Turns to Wormwood
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The forbidden woman's lips drip honey, but in the end she is bitter as wormwood (vv. 1-6).
verseByVerse.theology: Adultery is sweet at the beginning and bitter at the end, and the one who leads others astray is lost herself.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, be attentive to my wisdom; incline your ear to my understanding, that you may keep discretion, and your lips may guard knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Chapter 2 warned about the forbidden woman in four verses; chapters 5 and 7 give her a chapter each. The father knows which temptation is most likely to wreck his son.

He wants his son's lips to guard knowledge, because the danger in this chapter comes through lips too. Her lips drip honey (v. 3). His lips must be full of something better. A man whose mouth is stocked with truth has an answer ready when flattery comes.

verseByVerse.quote: For the lips of a forbidden woman drip honey, and her speech is smoother than oil, but in the end she is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a two-edged sword. Her feet go down to death; her steps follow the path to Sheol; she does not ponder the path of life; her ways wander, and she does not know it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ESV notes that forbidden is literally "strange", and speech is "palate". The father does not pretend temptation is ugly. If he told his son that sin looks disgusting, the son would conclude on the first attractive temptation that his father did not know what he was talking about. So he admits it: it is sweet.

Then the two words that change everything: in the end. Wormwood, a plant so bitter that the Bible uses it for grief and judgment, is what the honey becomes, and the smooth speech becomes a sword that cuts both ways. Temptation sells the beginning and hides the end. Before any choice, ask how this tastes in the end. Think past the evening to the morning, past the affair to the divorce court, past the secret to the moment it comes out.

The ESV notes that her steps "lay hold of" Sheol, as if grasping at the grave. The tragedy of verse 6 is that she herself is lost: not a mastermind, but wandering without knowing it. The person who leads others into sexual sin is usually someone who has never stopped to think where she is going. Compare the command to the son in 4:26, Ponder the path of your feet.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Keep far from her door: adultery costs honour, years and wealth, and ends in regret (vv. 7-14).
verseByVerse.theology: The father makes his son hear, in advance, the words he will say at the end if he does not listen now.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, O sons, listen to me, and do not depart from the words of my mouth. Keep your way far from her, and do not go near the door of her house,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now: the description is over, and no young man is exempt. The instruction is about distance: not "go to her door and resist", but do not go near it. The strongest men in Scripture fell when they put themselves in reach. Paul's word is the same, Flee from sexual immorality (1 Cor 6:18). You do not negotiate with this temptation; you leave the building. Paul wrote that to people whose bodies are already a temple of the Holy Spirit, bought with a price, and the Spirit who lives in them is the strength to leave the building.

Practically, that means identifying the doors. The late-night conversation with a colleague that has become personal. The social media account you check. The trip where no one knows you. The app on the phone. Do not go near the door.

verseByVerse.quote: lest you give your honor to others and your years to the merciless, lest strangers take their fill of your strength, and your labors go to the house of a foreigner, and at the end of your life you groan, when your flesh and body are consumed,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the father reads out the bill: reputation, the best years, money and work, all going to the house of a foreigner. Adultery has always been expensive. Today the bill arrives as legal fees, divided property, maintenance payments, and a family home sold.

And at the end, the body. Sexual sin has physical consequences, sometimes in disease, always in the wearing out of a life spent on it. Paul says, the sexually immoral person sins against his own body (1 Cor 6:18). The groan at the end of life is the sound of a man who has discovered too late what he spent.

verseByVerse.quote: and you say, "How I hated discipline, and my heart despised reproof! I did not listen to the voice of my teachers or incline my ear to my instructors. I am at the brink of utter ruin in the assembled congregation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The father lets his son hear his own future regret, the words he will say decades later if he does not listen now. The regret is not only about the woman. It is about not listening. The root sin was despising correction; the adultery was the fruit.

Every older person who has wrecked his life has some version of this speech. Most of them could name the teachers who warned them. A young reader can take this as a gift: here is the speech; you do not have to give it. And if you have already given it, it need not be your last word. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins (1 John 1:9). A husband or wife who has been betrayed should hear plainly that the unfaithfulness was not their fault.

The ruin is public. In the assembled congregation means before the whole community of God's people. Sexual sin is conducted in secret, but it rarely stays there, and when it comes out it damages not only the man but the congregation that trusted him. That is especially sobering for anyone who leads in a church.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–23 — Rejoice in the Wife of Your Youth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Drink from your own cistern and rejoice in the wife of your youth, for the LORD sees every path (vv. 15-23).
verseByVerse.theology: The best defence against forbidden pleasure is not less pleasure but delight in the gift God has given.

verseByVerse.quote: Drink water from your own cistern, flowing water from your own well. Should your springs be scattered abroad, streams of water in the streets? Let them be for yourself alone, and not for strangers with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the father turns from warning to invitation. In a dry land a man's own cistern, dug with labour, kept his household alive. The image is of a man's wife and the delight of sexual love within marriage. The Song of Songs uses the same picture of a bride: a garden fountain, a well of living water (Song 4:15), a spring locked, a fountain sealed (Song 4:12).

The father does not say that sexual desire is shameful, or to be suppressed. He says: drink. From your own well.

The picture reverses: promiscuity spills on the public road what was meant to water one home. Sexual love is designed to be exclusive, for yourself alone. That is not a restriction on its joy; it is the condition of it.

verseByVerse.quote: Let your fountain be blessed, and rejoice in the wife of your youth, a lovely deer, a graceful doe. Let her breasts fill you at all times with delight; be intoxicated always in her love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rejoice is a command to be glad in the woman he married young, who will grow old with him. Malachi uses the same phrase in warning men who were abandoning their first wives: let none of you be faithless to the wife of your youth (Mal 2:15). The law even gave a newly married man a year's exemption from military service so that he could be happy with his wife whom he has taken (Deut 24:5).

Here the Bible speaks with a frankness that surprises some readers. God is not embarrassed by the marriage bed; he designed it. Paul says married couples are not to deprive one another (1 Cor 7:5).

And the ESV notes a striking thing: be intoxicated is literally "be led astray". The same verb that describes a man wandering off to sin (v. 23) is used here of being carried away by love for his own wife. The father is saying: be led astray, but at home. Let her love be the thing that takes you out of yourself.

verseByVerse.quote: Why should you be intoxicated, my son, with a forbidden woman and embrace the bosom of an adulteress? For a man's ways are before the eyes of the LORD, and he ponders all his paths.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why would a man leave that for this? The word is the same again, "led astray", and adulteress is literally "a foreign woman", as the ESV notes. Why be led astray by a stranger, when you could be led astray by your wife?

This is the strategy of the whole chapter. The best defence against forbidden pleasure is not grim willpower but a greater delight. A husband who keeps pursuing and enjoying his wife has far less appetite for honey from other lips; spouses who neglect each other leave the gate open.

A word for readers for whom this is painful: the single, the widowed, those whose marriages are cold or broken. The chapter's command to flee still stands for you, and so does its promise that God sees every path (v. 21). The deepest fulfilment of the love the chapter describes is not found in any human marriage but in Christ, who loved the church and gave himself up for her (Eph 5:25). That love is offered to every believer, married or not.

And here is the reason beneath all the others. Adultery depends on secrecy. But nothing is secret. No creature is hidden from his sight, but all are naked and exposed to the eyes of him to whom we must give account (Heb 4:13). The woman of verse 6 did not ponder her path. The LORD ponders every path, and the ESV notes that the word may mean he "makes level" them. He sees the road and he governs where it leads.

verseByVerse.quote: The iniquities of the wicked ensnare him, and he is held fast in the cords of his sin. He dies for lack of discipline, and because of his great folly he is led astray.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wicked man thinks he is free, doing what he wants. In fact he is tied up, and the ropes are his own sins. Every indulgence adds another cord. Jesus said, everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin (John 8:34). Anyone who has fought a pornography habit knows how true this is. It began as a choice and became a cord.

The chapter ends with the word it has been playing on: led astray. The man who would not be led astray by his wife's love is led astray by his own folly, all the way to death. And the cause is named, lack of discipline, the thing he confessed at verse 12 that he hated. Desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death (Jas 1:15).

But the cords can be cut. Jesus, having said that whoever practises sin is its slave, went on: So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed (John 8:36). You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body (1 Cor 6:19-20).

5.text: <sup>1</sup>My son, be attentive to my wisdom; incline your ear to my understanding,<sup>2</sup>that you may keep discretion, and your lips may guard knowledge.<sup>3</sup>For the lips of a forbidden woman drip honey, and her speech is smoother than oil,<sup>4</sup>but in the end she is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a two-edged sword.<sup>5</sup>Her feet go down to death; her steps follow the path to Sheol;<sup>6</sup>she does not ponder the path of life; her ways wander, and she does not know it.<sup>7</sup>And now, O sons, listen to me, and do not depart from the words of my mouth.<sup>8</sup>Keep your way far from her, and do not go near the door of her house,<sup>9</sup>lest you give your honor to others and your years to the merciless,<sup>10</sup>lest strangers take their fill of your strength, and your labors go to the house of a foreigner,<sup>11</sup>and at the end of your life you groan, when your flesh and body are consumed,<sup>12</sup>and you say, "How I hated discipline, and my heart despised reproof!<sup>13</sup>I did not listen to the voice of my teachers or incline my ear to my instructors.<sup>14</sup>I am at the brink of utter ruin in the assembled congregation."<sup>15</sup>Drink water from your own cistern, flowing water from your own well.<sup>16</sup>Should your springs be scattered abroad, streams of water in the streets?<sup>17</sup>Let them be for yourself alone, and not for strangers with you.<sup>18</sup>Let your fountain be blessed, and rejoice in the wife of your youth,<sup>19</sup>a lovely deer, a graceful doe. Let her breasts fill you at all times with delight; be intoxicated always in her love.<sup>20</sup>Why should you be intoxicated, my son, with a forbidden woman and embrace the bosom of an adulteress?<sup>21</sup>For a man's ways are before the eyes of the LORD, and he ponders all his paths.<sup>22</sup>The iniquities of the wicked ensnare him, and he is held fast in the cords of his sin.<sup>23</sup>He dies for lack of discipline, and because of his great folly he is led astray.
5.overview: The father warns his son about the forbidden woman, whose lips drip honey but who is bitter as wormwood in the end, wandering toward death without knowing it (vv. 1-6). He must keep far from her door, for adultery costs honour, years and wealth and ends in regret and public ruin (vv. 7-14). Instead he is to drink from his own well and rejoice in the wife of his youth (vv. 15-20). The LORD sees every path, and the wicked are bound by the cords of their own sin (vv. 21-23).
5.theology:
Temptation offers sweetness at the start and hides its bitter end (vv. 3-4). Sexual sin is costly in every part of life, and at root it grows from despising correction (vv. 9-14).

Sexual delight within marriage is God's gift and is commanded (vv. 15-19; 1 Cor 7:3-5); delight in that gift is the positive defence against adultery (v. 20). God sees all human ways (v. 21; Heb 4:13), and sin enslaves (v. 22; John 8:34). Marriage points beyond itself to Christ's love for the church (Eph 5:25, 31-32).
5.examples: A married man who notices that a friendship at work has become the place he feels most understood has found one of the doors the father names, and the wise thing is to walk away from it before it opens. A couple who keep making time for each other, years into marriage, are doing what verse 19 commands. And a husband or wife who has already fallen, or been betrayed, should hear both the chapter's warnings and the gospel beyond them: the cords can be cut, and Christ sets free.

6.title: Go to the Ant, O Sluggard

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Rash Pledge and the Lazy Hand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two traps with money: a rash pledge for a neighbour's debt, to be escaped at once, and the sluggard's little sleep, which the ant's diligence rebukes and poverty follows (vv. 1-11).
verseByVerse.theology: Wisdom avoids reckless promises and idle hands alike, and both begin as small, pleasant decisions.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, if you have put up security for your neighbor, have given your pledge for a stranger, if you are snared in the words of your mouth, caught in the words of your mouth,
verseByVerse.commentary:
A very practical piece of financial advice: security and pledge describe co-signing a loan, a handshake promising to pay if the borrower does not. The Bible does not forbid lending, generosity or bearing another's burden (Bear one another's burdens, Gal 6:2). What it warns against, here and repeatedly in Proverbs, is binding yourself to an open-ended obligation you cannot control. A wise rule many Christians follow: never guarantee more than you could afford to give away outright, and where you can, give rather than guarantee.

The trap was made of words. Many people have lost their homes through a moment's eagerness to help a friend or look generous; the words took a second, the debt took years.
verseByVerse.note: Proverbs returns to guaranteeing debts at 11:15, 17:18, 20:16 and 22:26-27.

verseByVerse.quote: then do this, my son, and save yourself, for you have come into the hand of your neighbor: go, hasten, and plead urgently with your neighbor. Give your eyes no sleep and your eyelids no slumber; save yourself like a gazelle from the hand of the hunter, like a bird from the hand of the fowler.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The remedy is urgent and humbling. You have come into the hand of your neighbor: your future now belongs to someone else's choices. So go, hurry, and plead with him to release you. The ESV notes that plead urgently may be rendered "humble yourself". Pride will want to keep the promise rather than admit it was foolish. The father says: swallow your pride and get out.

A gazelle does not negotiate with the hunter; it runs. Some problems grow quietly while we sleep, and a debt obligation is one of them.

There is a striking reversal of this warning in the New Testament. The one pledge Proverbs tells a son never to make, Christ made for us. He bound himself to pay the debt of people who could not pay. Judah once said to his father about Benjamin, I will be a pledge of his safety (Gen 43:9). Hebrews says that Jesus is the guarantor of a better covenant (Heb 7:22). He did not run from the obligation; he paid it in full.

verseByVerse.quote: Go to the ant, O sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise. Without having any chief, officer, or ruler, she prepares her bread in summer and gathers her food in harvest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From the man who promises too much to the man who does too little. The sluggard appears again and again in Proverbs, usually in comic scenes. Here a grown man is sent to school, and the teacher is an insect. Wisdom is written into creation for anyone willing to consider. Agur will return to the ants later: the ants are a people not strong, yet they provide their food in the summer (30:25).

Two lessons. First, the ant works without a supervisor. Many people work hard only when someone is watching. Paul told Christian workers to labour heartily, as for the Lord and not for men (Col 3:23), serving a Master who has already promised them the inheritance, and that changes why anyone works.

Second, the ant works ahead, gathering in summer for winter. Wisdom plans for seasons that have not yet arrived.

verseByVerse.quote: How long will you lie there, O sluggard? When will you arise from your sleep? A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest, and poverty will come upon you like a robber, and want like an armed man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It sounds like a parent at a bedroom door late in the morning: How long? The sluggard does not say, I intend to ruin my life. He says, five more minutes. The word little comes three times; laziness never presents itself as a life decision, and that is what makes it dangerous.

The little decisions add up to a sudden arrival, like a robber, and the sluggard is surprised. He should not be. These two verses appear again, word for word, at the end of the sluggard's vineyard in 24:33-34, as if the lesson needed saying twice.

The New Testament is equally plain: If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat (2 Thess 3:10). Work is not a curse; it is how God provides for us and lets us provide for others, so that he may have something to share with anyone in need (Eph 4:28). A word of care is needed too: the depressed, the exhausted and the sick are not sluggards, and this proverb is not aimed at them. It is aimed at the man who could get up and chooses not to.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The worthless man signals, schemes and sows discord, and will be broken suddenly; the LORD hates seven things, ending with one who sows discord among brothers (vv. 12-19).
verseByVerse.theology: God's hatred is aimed at what destroys people and community, and the list starts with pride and ends with division.

verseByVerse.quote: A worthless person, a wicked man, goes about with crooked speech, winks with his eyes, signals with his feet, points with his finger, with perverted heart devises evil, continually sowing discord; therefore calamity will come upon him suddenly; in a moment he will be broken beyond healing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now a troublemaker who works in code: crooked speech, a wink, a movement of the feet (the ESV notes the Hebrew is "scrapes"), a pointing finger, signals to allies behind the backs of his targets. Psalm 35 prays against enemies who wink the eye (Ps 35:19). Every office and every church has seen this man: the raised eyebrow in a meeting, the knowing look, the whispered aside.

Beneath the signals is a heart that devises evil, and its product is discord: a suspicion planted here, a remark repeated there, friendships split, continually.

He works slowly and secretly, but his end is sudden: in a moment. The man who broke others will be broken beyond healing. God's patience is not indifference. While people are saying, "There is peace and security," then sudden destruction will come upon them (1 Thess 5:3).

verseByVerse.quote: There are six things that the LORD hates, seven that are an abomination to him: haughty eyes, a lying tongue, and hands that shed innocent blood, a heart that devises wicked plans, feet that make haste to run to evil, a false witness who breathes out lies, and one who sows discord among brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The pattern "six things, seven" is a Hebrew way of building to a climax; the seventh item is the one the list is aiming at. And the language is strong. The LORD hates. Some readers are uncomfortable with a God who hates. But a God who loved people and did not hate what destroys them would not be good. A doctor who loves his patient hates the cancer.

The list moves down the body: eyes, tongue, hands, heart, feet. The whole person can be put to the service of evil.

It begins with haughty eyes, the look of a person who sees himself above others. Pride is first, because pride is where most of the others start. Jesus told of a Pharisee who looked down on a tax collector, and ended, everyone who exalts himself will be humbled (Luke 18:14). Then a lying tongue, and hands that shed innocent blood. Some readers find it strange that pride stands in the same list as murder. God does not.

The scheming heart and the eager feet. These are the same as the troublemaker of verse 14 and the gang of chapter 1, whose feet run to evil (1:16).

The last two are about destroying community. A false witness destroys justice. And the climactic seventh is one who sows discord among brothers, picking up the sowing discord of verse 14. The section began and ends with discord. God hates it most because it attacks what he loves most: the unity of his people.

Does God hate people, or only sins? The last two items on the list are persons, a false witness and a sower of discord, and the Psalms can say that God hates evildoers (Ps 5:5). Scripture means his settled opposition to those who persist in evil, and it is no contradiction of his love, for he shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Rom 5:8). Every one of these seven sins was laid on Christ, so that liars, the proud and dividers of churches who turn to him are forgiven and made peacemakers.

That should give every church member pause. Gossip, faction, the whispered complaint about the elders, the stirring up of one group against another, all belong on this list. Paul says, watch out for those who cause divisions (Rom 16:17). And Jesus pronounced the opposite blessing: Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God (Matt 5:9). Ask which of the two your words this week have been.
verseByVerse.note: Other numerical sayings: 30:15-31, and the "three transgressions, and for four" of Amos 1-2.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–35 — Fire Carried in the Lap
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Parents' teaching is a lamp that guards from the adulteress; adultery is fire carried next to the chest (vv. 20-35).
verseByVerse.theology: Adultery is not a private risk but playing with fire, and it provokes a wound that money cannot settle.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, keep your father's commandment, and forsake not your mother's teaching. Bind them on your heart always; tie them around your neck. When you walk, they will lead you; when you lie down, they will watch over you; and when you awake, they will talk with you. For the commandment is a lamp and the teaching a light, and the reproofs of discipline are the way of life,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The father returns to his great theme, and the language echoes Moses: these words that I command you today shall be on your heart, and You shall bind them as a sign on your hand (Deut 6:6, 8). Parental teaching in Proverbs carries the weight of God's law because it passes on God's law.

The ESV notes that the Hebrew says "it" three times, as if the teaching were a single companion that walks with the son by day, watches at night, and talks to him when he wakes. That is Scripture stored in the heart. Walking into a meeting, it guides; lying awake, it guards; and on waking, the first thought can be God's word rather than the day's anxiety.

Moses had described the same three moments: when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise (Deut 6:7).

A lamp shows the next step in the dark. Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path (Ps 119:105). And the father adds something less comfortable: the reproofs of discipline are the way of life. Correction is part of the light. The person who wants God's guidance but not his rebukes wants a lamp that shows only pleasant things.

verseByVerse.quote: to preserve you from the evil woman, from the smooth tongue of the adulteress. Do not desire her beauty in your heart, and do not let her capture you with her eyelashes; for the price of a prostitute is only a loaf of bread, but a married woman hunts down a precious life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is where the lamp is most needed. The ESV notes that by a change of vowels the Hebrew may read "from the wife of a neighbor", and that adulteress is literally "the foreign woman". The warning of chapters 2 and 5 returns.

The battle is located precisely: in your heart. Adultery is not first an act; it is a desire entertained. Jesus said the same: everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart (Matt 5:28). David's fall began with a look from a rooftop at a woman bathing; and the woman was very beautiful (2 Sam 11:2).

The weapon named is small, her eyelashes: a look held a second too long. The father wants his son to know how little it takes.

The verse is a comparison of costs, and the ESV notes that it may also be read, "for a prostitute leaves a man with nothing but a loaf of bread". Either way, the point is the same: sin with a prostitute is costly and degrading, but sin with another man's wife (the Hebrew is "a man's wife") costs far more. It hunts down a precious life. The verse is not approving of prostitution. Paul answers anyone who thinks it harmless: Do you not know that he who is joined to a prostitute becomes one body with her? (1 Cor 6:16).

verseByVerse.quote: Can a man carry fire next to his chest and his clothes not be burned? Or can one walk on hot coals and his feet not be scorched? So is he who goes in to his neighbor's wife; none who touches her will go unpunished.
verseByVerse.commentary: Two questions that answer themselves, so that the son reaches the conclusion himself. Every man who begins an affair believes he will be the exception, keeping it secret and keeping his marriage. He is carrying fire in his shirt and insisting it will not burn. The consequences may be slow or quick, public or private, but there are no exceptions.

verseByVerse.quote: People do not despise a thief if he steals to satisfy his appetite when he is hungry, but if he is caught, he will pay sevenfold; he will give all the goods of his house. He who commits adultery lacks sense; he who does it destroys himself. He will get wounds and dishonor, and his disgrace will not be wiped away. For jealousy makes a man furious, and he will not spare when he takes revenge. He will accept no compensation; he will refuse though you multiply gifts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now a comparison with theft. A starving man who steals bread gets a measure of sympathy. Still, he must repay sevenfold, a number for full and complete restitution. (The law required fourfold or fivefold for stolen livestock, Exod 22:1, and Zacchaeus promised fourfold, Luke 19:8.) It may cost all the goods of his house. But it can be paid. The debt has a limit.

Adultery is different. The thief was hungry; the adulterer had a wife. He lacks sense, and the damage is not to his purse but to himself: he who does it destroys himself.

Even when forgiven, and it can be, the adulterer's reputation carries a mark for years. Many a gifted man has discovered that he cannot return to the place of trust he once held.

And here is the final difference from theft. You can repay a thief's victim. But you cannot pay off a husband whose wife you have taken. He will accept no compensation. What was stolen was not property; it was a one-flesh union. The Song of Songs says jealousy is fierce as the grave (Song 8:6).

That is a sobering place to end the chapter, and it is meant to be. But it also shows why the gospel is such good news. The sins that no human compensation can cover, the blood of Christ can. He did not pay in gifts or goods; he paid with his life, and what money could never wipe away, his cleansing does.

The law prescribed death for adultery (Lev 20:10), but these verses describe the husband’s fury and the adulterer’s ruin, not a court. That civil penalty belonged to Israel’s theocracy; in Christ there is forgiveness for adulterers who repent (John 8:11; 1 Cor 6:9–11).

he who does it destroys himself.<sup>33</sup>He will get wounds and dishonor, and his disgrace will not be wiped away.<sup>34</sup>For jealousy makes a man furious, and he will not spare when he takes revenge.<sup>35</sup>He will accept no compensation; he will refuse though you multiply gifts.
6.overview: A son who has rashly guaranteed a neighbour's debt must get free at once (vv. 1-5), and the sluggard must learn from the ant (vv. 6-11). The LORD hates seven things, from haughty eyes to one who sows discord among brothers (vv. 12-19). Parental teaching guards against the adulteress, for adultery is carrying fire and destroys the man who does it (vv. 20-35).
6.theology:
Wisdom governs money: avoiding reckless financial obligations (vv. 1-5) and working diligently without supervision (vv. 6-11; 2 Thess 3:10; Col 3:23). The one pledge Proverbs warns against, Christ made as the guarantor of the new covenant (Heb 7:22).

God hates what destroys people, and the list of seven begins with pride and ends with discord among brothers (vv. 16-19; Luke 18:14; Rom 16:17). God's word, stored in the heart, accompanies the believer at every moment (vv. 20-23; Deut 6:6-8).

Adultery begins in the heart (v. 25; Matt 5:28), always burns (vv. 27-29), and does damage that cannot be repaid by human means (vv. 30-35).
6.examples: A young adult asked by a friend to co-sign a car loan can say no kindly, or give what he can afford to lose, rather than hand his future to someone else's choices. Someone who works hard only when the manager is in the office can learn from the ant, and from Paul: we work for a Master who sees. A church member tempted to pass on a complaint about the elders can recognise the seventh thing the LORD hates, and choose to be a peacemaker instead.

7.title: The Young Man Lacking Sense

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Keep My Words as the Apple of Your Eye
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Guard my teaching like the pupil of your eye, and make wisdom your sister, to keep you from the forbidden woman (vv. 1-5).
verseByVerse.theology: The father's defence against seduction is a closer relationship with wisdom than the seductress can offer.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, keep my words and treasure up my commandments with you; keep my commandments and live; keep my teaching as the apple of your eye; bind them on your fingers; write them on the tablet of your heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last major warning about the forbidden woman opens with the grandfather's sentence from 4:4, keep my commandments and live, passed on word for word.

The apple of your eye is the pupil, so sensitive that anything near it makes you blink. Moses said God kept Israel as the apple of his eye (Deut 32:10). The father wants his son to guard God's teaching with that same reflex, flinching at anything that threatens it.

Fingers and heart: action and affection. A man who has God's word only on his fingers keeps rules he does not love; a man who has it only in his heart has feelings that never become obedience. The father wants both.

verseByVerse.quote: Say to wisdom, "You are my sister," and call insight your intimate friend, to keep you from the forbidden woman, from the adulteress with her smooth words.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is a strategy. Wisdom is to be the son's sister and intimate friend. In the Song of Songs "my sister" is a term of tender affection for a bride. The father is not asking his son merely to know about wisdom. He is asking him to be close to her, to love her, to be at home with her. The best defence against a false intimacy is a true one.

The ESV notes again that these are "the strange" and "the foreign" woman. And again, her weapon is smooth words. A young man who has made wisdom his closest friend will recognise a counterfeit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–23 — What the Father Saw from His Window
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: From his window the father watches a young man lacking sense walk toward her corner at dusk, and follow her like an ox to the slaughter (vv. 6-23).
verseByVerse.theology: The fall is not sudden; it is a walk that began with a young man choosing which street to take at dusk.

verseByVerse.quote: For at the window of my house I have looked out through my lattice, and I have seen among the simple, I have perceived among the youths, a young man lacking sense, passing along the street near her corner, taking the road to her house in the twilight, in the evening, at the time of night and darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now a story. The father looks through the lattice, a wooden screen that let a person see out without being seen; what follows he has watched happen. The young man he picks out is not a hardened criminal. He is simple, one of the open-door people of chapter 1, and lacking sense, literally lacking heart. There is nothing at his centre holding him steady. That is the most dangerous condition a young person can be in: not rebellious, just empty.

Watch his feet. He does not go to her house, not yet; he is just walking near where sin lives. Maybe he tells himself it is the shorter route. This is how most falls happen: no one wakes up planning adultery, but he chooses the street. It may be the lingering conversation, the website opened "just to see", the drink with a colleague after everyone else has gone home. Paul's counsel is to make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires (Rom 13:14). Do not walk near her corner.

The light fades as he walks, and so does his judgment. Sin prefers the dark, where no one sees. People loved the darkness rather than the light because their works were evil (John 3:19).

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, the woman meets him, dressed as a prostitute, wily of heart. She is loud and wayward; her feet do not stay at home; now in the street, now in the market, and at every corner she lies in wait.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And behold: the father's voice tightens, as if he wants to shout through the window. Her clothing announces what she is, and her heart is wily. The ESV notes the Hebrew is "guarded in heart". She shows everything on the outside and hides everything on the inside. He is exposed; she is calculating.

She is restless, never settled, always out. And she is hunting: at every corner she lies in wait. The same verb was used of the gang in chapter 1 who lie in wait for blood (1:11). The seductress and the violent man are hunters of the same kind. Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour (1 Pet 5:8).

verseByVerse.quote: She seizes him and kisses him, and with bold face she says to him, "I had to offer sacrifices, and today I have paid my vows; so now I have come out to meet you, to seek you eagerly, and I have found you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She seizes and kisses him before he has said a word. Temptation often works this way: it moves before the person has had time to think, and it acts as if what is happening is perfectly normal.

Her opening line is religious. The ESV notes the sacrifices were "peace offerings", and under the law the meat of such an offering had to be eaten that day or the next (Lev 7:15-16). There is a feast at home, and she has done her duty to God: religion becomes the cover for sin. Some of the most destructive affairs have been conducted by people who never missed church.

Then flattery: to seek you eagerly, and I have found you. You, specifically. For an empty young man, nothing is more intoxicating than being wanted.

verseByVerse.quote: I have spread my couch with coverings, colored linens from Egyptian linen; I have perfumed my bed with myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon. Come, let us take our fill of love till morning; let us delight ourselves with love. For my husband is not at home; he has gone on a long journey; he took a bag of money with him; at full moon he will come home."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything about the bed is luxurious and imported; she appeals to every sense, and she has prepared.

Myrrh and aloes appear elsewhere in Scripture in two very different places. The king in Psalm 45 has robes fragrant with myrrh and aloes and cassia on his wedding day (Ps 45:8). And when Jesus was buried, Nicodemus brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about seventy-five pounds in weight (John 19:39). The same scents belong to a wedding and a burial. Her bed smells like a wedding. It is a grave.

She calls it love. It is not. Chapter 5 described love: rejoicing in the wife of your youth, delighted in her always (5:18-19). She offers a night, till morning. Love is measured in decades; this is measured in hours.

Finally the reassurance: the husband is away on a long trip, and no one will find out. Every affair is built on the belief that it will stay hidden. She refers to him coldly, not as "my love" but my husband, a man to be timed around.

verseByVerse.quote: With much seductive speech she persuades him; with her smooth talk she compels him. All at once he follows her, as an ox goes to the slaughter, or as a stag is caught fast till an arrow pierces its liver; as a bird rushes into a snare; he does not know that it will cost him his life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She keeps talking, and every sentence removes an objection. By the end he is not so much persuaded as compelled. There comes a point in temptation where resistance feels impossible. The time to resist was back on the street, one corner ago.

Three animals, and each one tells the same truth. An ox walks placidly to the slaughterhouse, thinking it is going to pasture. A stag is caught and waits for the arrow. A bird rushes into a snare, eagerly. (The ESV notes that the Hebrew of the middle line is difficult, and gives the probable reading.) None of them knows what is happening. He does not know that it will cost him his life.

The Bible has its own case study. Samson laid his head on Delilah's knees, and his strength left him (Judg 16:19). And it has its counter-example. When Potiphar's wife caught Joseph by his garment and said, Lie with me, he left his garment in her hand and fled and got out of the house (Gen 39:12). Joseph lost a coat and kept his life. The young man in Proverbs 7 kept his coat and lost everything.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–27 — Many a Victim Has She Laid Low
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Let not your heart turn aside to her: many have fallen, and her house is the way to death (vv. 24-27).
verseByVerse.theology: The strong have fallen here too, so no reader may assume he is the exception.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, O sons, listen to me, and be attentive to the words of my mouth. Let not your heart turn aside to her ways; do not stray into her paths,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The story is over, and the father turns from the window to his sons. Once more, O sons. He has not told the story to entertain them but to arm them.

Two steps again: first the heart turns aside, then the feet stray. The fall begins inside. James describes the same order: each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire (Jas 1:14). This is why the father spent so much of the book on the heart. Guard it, and the feet will follow.

Practically, that means paying attention to where the heart's imagination drifts, and turning it back early. It means friends who ask hard questions: exhort one another every day, that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin (Heb 3:13). And it means prayer, because Jesus said, Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak (Matt 26:41). He said it as one who knew temptation from the inside: he was in every respect tempted as we are, yet without sin (Heb 4:15). The young man at the window had no one; the believer has a High Priest who stood where he stands and did not fall, and who gives mercy and grace in time of need (Heb 4:16).

verseByVerse.quote: for many a victim has she laid low, and all her slain are a mighty throng. Her house is the way to Sheol, going down to the chambers of death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The final warning is statistical. Many have fallen here, and her slain are a mighty throng. She has brought down people who were stronger, wiser and more gifted than the young man on the street. Samson was strong; David was a man after God's own heart. No one is too strong for this temptation. Therefore let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall (1 Cor 10:12).

The chapter that began with a perfumed bed ends in the chambers of death. The bedroom was the graveyard's front room.

But the last word of the Bible on temptation is not death. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape (1 Cor 10:13). There is always a door out, and very often it is the door of your own house, which you can walk back through before dark. And for those who have already gone into her house, the Christ who went down into death for sinners came up again, and brings back with him all who turn to him.

7.text: <sup>1</sup>My son, keep my words and treasure up my commandments with you;<sup>2</sup>keep my commandments and live; keep my teaching as the apple of your eye;<sup>3</sup>bind them on your fingers; write them on the tablet of your heart.<sup>4</sup>Say to wisdom, "You are my sister," and call insight your intimate friend,<sup>5</sup>to keep you from the forbidden woman, from the adulteress with her smooth words.<sup>6</sup>For at the window of my house I have looked out through my lattice,<sup>7</sup>and I have seen among the simple, I have perceived among the youths, a young man lacking sense,<sup>8</sup>passing along the street near her corner, taking the road to her house<sup>9</sup>in the twilight, in the evening, at the time of night and darkness.<sup>10</sup>And behold, the woman meets him, dressed as a prostitute, wily of heart.<sup>11</sup>She is loud and wayward; her feet do not stay at home;<sup>12</sup>now in the street, now in the market, and at every corner she lies in wait.<sup>13</sup>She seizes him and kisses him, and with bold face she says to him,<sup>14</sup>"I had to offer sacrifices, and today I have paid my vows;<sup>15</sup>so now I have come out to meet you, to seek you eagerly, and I have found you.<sup>16</sup>I have spread my couch with coverings, colored linens from Egyptian linen;<sup>17</sup>I have perfumed my bed with myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon.<sup>18</sup>Come, let us take our fill of love till morning; let us delight ourselves with love.<sup>19</sup>For my husband is not at home; he has gone on a long journey;<sup>20</sup>he took a bag of money with him; at full moon he will come home."<sup>21</sup>With much seductive speech she persuades him; with her smooth talk she compels him.<sup>22</sup>All at once he follows her, as an ox goes to the slaughter, or as a stag is caught fast<sup>23</sup>till an arrow pierces its liver; as a bird rushes into a snare; he does not know that it will cost him his life.<sup>24</sup>And now, O sons, listen to me, and be attentive to the words of my mouth.<sup>25</sup>Let not your heart turn aside to her ways; do not stray into her paths,<sup>26</sup>for many a victim has she laid low, and all her slain are a mighty throng.<sup>27</sup>Her house is the way to Sheol, going down to the chambers of death.
7.overview: The father urges his son to guard his teaching like the pupil of the eye and make wisdom his sister, as protection from the forbidden woman (vv. 1-5). From his window he tells of a young man lacking sense walking at dusk near her corner; she meets him, kisses him, offers a feast, a perfumed bed and the assurance that her husband is away, and he follows her like an ox to the slaughter (vv. 6-23). The father warns his sons not to let their hearts turn toward her, for her house leads down to death (vv. 24-27).
7.theology:
Sin works gradually and through small choices: a street chosen at dusk (vv. 8-9). Temptation appeals to every sense, flatters, uses religion as cover, and promises secrecy (vv. 13-20). The heart turns before the feet stray (v. 25; Jas 1:14).

The defence against false intimacy is a true intimacy with wisdom (v. 4), God's word treasured and written on the heart (vv. 1-3), flight rather than negotiation (Gen 39:12), watchful prayer (Matt 26:41), and the faithfulness of God who provides a way of escape (1 Cor 10:13). No one is strong enough to be safe from this sin (v. 26; 1 Cor 10:12).
7.examples: A young man who notices that his evening walks, or his late-night scrolling, keep taking him past the same corner can change the route before he has to fight the battle at the door. A Christian who finds himself using church language to excuse what he knows is wrong has met the woman with the peace offerings. And anyone who has already gone through her door can go back through his own: the way of escape is real, and the Christ who rose from death brings home those who turn to him.

8.title: Wisdom Calls: I Was Beside Him

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Wisdom Calls at the Crossroads
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wisdom calls in public to everyone, even the simple and the fool, with words that are straight and worth more than silver or jewels (vv. 1-11).
verseByVerse.theology: The seductress of chapter 7 whispered at a corner in the dark; Wisdom calls in the open, to everyone, and has nothing to hide.

verseByVerse.quote: Does not wisdom call? Does not understanding raise her voice? On the heights beside the way, at the crossroads she takes her stand; beside the gates in front of the town, at the entrance of the portals she cries aloud:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Does not wisdom call? Does not understanding raise her voice? Chapter 7 ended in the chambers of death. The young man lacking sense went looking for a voice at dusk and found the wrong one. Wisdom was calling all along.

On the heights. The seductress was at every corner lying in wait (7:12), in the twilight. Wisdom stands on the heights, where she can be seen, at the crossroads, where decisions are made, and beside the gates, where everyone passes. One whispers in the dark; the other calls aloud in the open. Every reader stands at that crossroads, and the question is whether he is listening.

verseByVerse.quote: "To you, O men, I call, and my cry is to the children of man. O simple ones, learn prudence; O fools, learn sense.
verseByVerse.commentary: To the children of man. Wisdom's call is universal, and she calls the very people who seem least likely to respond: the simple and the fools. She does not wait for them to improve before she invites them. The invitation is precisely for those who lack what she offers. This is the shape of grace. Jesus said he came to call not the righteous but sinners, and Wisdom's voice sounds exactly like his.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear, for I will speak noble things, and from my lips will come what is right, for my mouth will utter truth; wickedness is an abomination to my lips. All the words of my mouth are righteous; there is nothing twisted or crooked in them. They are all straight to him who understands, and right to those who find knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every word Wisdom uses of her speech contrasts with the seductress. Hers were smooth words and flattery; Wisdom's are noble things, what is right, truth. The lips of the forbidden woman dripped honey (5:3). Wisdom's lips find wickedness disgusting.

There is nothing twisted in them: you never have to read Wisdom's words twice to find the trick. And they are straight to him who understands. The words are clear, but it takes an understanding heart to see how clear they are. To the proud they seem foolish or narrow; to the humble, obvious.

Here is a test for any voice, whether a friend, an advertisement or your own desires: does it need to hide its ending, as the seductress hid the chambers of death? Wisdom never does.

verseByVerse.quote: Take my instruction instead of silver, and knowledge rather than choice gold, for wisdom is better than jewels, and all that you may desire cannot compare with her.
verseByVerse.commentary: As in 3:14-15, the key word is instead. She is not saying, have both. She is saying, if you must choose, choose me. The honest businessman who loses a deal because he would not lie has taken instruction instead of silver. The student who will not cheat for a grade has taken knowledge rather than gold. Wisdom says they have the better bargain.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wisdom hates pride, gives rulers their just rule, and loves and enriches those who love her (vv. 12-21).
verseByVerse.theology: Every just ruler governs by a wisdom that is not his own, and that wisdom gives herself to anyone who loves her.

verseByVerse.quote: "I, wisdom, dwell with prudence, and I find knowledge and discretion. The fear of the LORD is hatred of evil. Pride and arrogance and the way of evil and perverted speech I hate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Prudence, knowledge and discretion are Wisdom's companions, and whoever takes her in finds she brings her family: good sense, foresight, the ability to plan well.

Hatred of evil. Here is a definition that should surprise anyone who thinks of the fear of the LORD as merely a feeling. You cannot revere God and be comfortable with what he hates. A person who says he fears God but enjoys cruelty, lies easily and laughs at purity has not understood the words. Abhor what is evil; hold fast to what is good (Rom 12:9).

And the first things on Wisdom's hate list are pride and arrogance, just as haughty eyes stood first among the seven things the LORD hates (6:17). Pride is the opposite of wisdom because pride will not learn.

verseByVerse.quote: I have counsel and sound wisdom; I have insight; I have strength. By me kings reign, and rulers decree what is just; by me princes rule, and nobles, all who govern justly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom is not weak. Many people think of goodness as soft and of power as belonging to the ruthless. Wisdom says she holds both the counsel and the strength.

By me kings reign. Every just government has ruled by wisdom not its own. The ESV notes that many manuscripts read all who "govern the earth". Kings think their power comes from armies, elections or birth. It comes from God. He removes kings and sets up kings; he gives wisdom to the wise (Dan 2:21). There is no authority except from God (Rom 13:1).

That is a humbling truth for anyone in authority, whether a president, a manager, an elder or a parent. The wisdom to rule well is borrowed. And it is a comforting truth for everyone under authority: no ruler is outside the rule of the one whose robe bears the name King of kings and Lord of lords (Rev 19:16).

verseByVerse.quote: I love those who love me, and those who seek me diligently find me. Riches and honor are with me, enduring wealth and righteousness. My fruit is better than gold, even fine gold, and my yield than choice silver. I walk in the way of righteousness, in the paths of justice, granting an inheritance to those who love me, and filling their treasuries.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I love those who love me. Wisdom is not a cold principle but someone who returns love. Put this beside chapter 1, where those who ignored Wisdom's call will seek me diligently but will not find me (1:28). The same words, opposite outcomes. The difference is the heart. The people of chapter 1 sought rescue from the storm; the people of chapter 8 seek Wisdom because they love her. Anyone who seeks God for God's sake will find him.

Wisdom does bring riches and honour, but look at the adjective: enduring wealth. And it stands beside righteousness. The riches of folly are quick and passing; Wisdom's are slow and lasting. Her fruit and her yield are the language of a harvest, something that grows over seasons.

She fills treasuries, but only by walking in the paths of justice. Wisdom never makes anyone rich by crooked means. And what she gives is an inheritance, something received as a gift and kept in a family. Isaiah extends the same invitation in the voice of the LORD: Why do you spend your money for that which is not bread, and your labor for that which does not satisfy? Incline your ear, and come to me; hear, that your soul may live (Isa 55:2-3).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–31 — Before the Beginning of the Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before the earth, the depths or the hills, Wisdom was with the LORD, beside him like a master workman, his daily delight and delighting in the children of man (vv. 22-31).
verseByVerse.theology: Wisdom here is a poetic figure, but the New Testament gives her place and work to the eternal Son, through whom all things were made and in whom the Father delights.

verseByVerse.quote: "The LORD possessed me at the beginning of his work, the first of his acts of old. Ages ago I was set up, at the first, before the beginning of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD possessed me. The word possessed stands at the centre of a famous debate in church history. The Hebrew verb usually means to get or acquire, but is sometimes used of God making or bringing forth (Genesis 14:19), so translations differ. The ESV notes that it may be rendered "fathered", and that the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament (the Septuagint) read "created"; it also notes that work is literally "way". In the fourth century Arius and his followers used the Greek "created" to argue that the Son of God was a creature, the first and greatest thing God made. The church rejected that teaching at the Council of Nicaea in 325, and rightly. Arius misused this verse: he took a line of poetry about God's wisdom and turned it into a statement about when the Son began, which it was never meant to be.

First, Proverbs 8 is poetry. Wisdom is personified, as Folly is in chapter 9. She is a poetic figure, a woman calling in the streets, not a direct description of the second person of the Trinity. The point is that God's wisdom is older than the world and that everything was made by it. God was never without his wisdom.

Second, the New Testament leads us from this chapter to Christ, though it never quotes it directly. What Proverbs says of God's wisdom in a poem, the apostles say of the Son plainly. Paul calls Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor 1:24). But the New Testament is careful about how. John does not say the Word was made at the beginning; he says, In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God (John 1:1). The Son is not the first of God's works; he is the one through whom are all things (1 Cor 8:6). When the risen Christ calls himself the beginning of God's creation (Rev 3:14), he means its source and ruler, not its first product. In the same way Paul calls the Son the firstborn of all creation and at once explains, For by him all things were created (Colossians 1:15-16). Firstborn means the heir with the rank (Psalm 89:27), not the first thing made.

Set up. This is the word God uses of his King: I have set my King on Zion (Ps 2:6). Before there was an earth, Wisdom was enthroned. Micah said of the ruler to be born in Bethlehem, whose coming forth is from of old, from ancient days (Mic 5:2). And Jesus prayed, glorify me in your own presence with the glory that I had with you before the world existed (John 17:5).
verseByVerse.note: Wisdom speaks as present with God before creation, language the New Testament echoes of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: When there were no depths I was brought forth, when there were no springs abounding with water. Before the mountains had been shaped, before the hills, I was brought forth, before he had made the earth with its fields, or the first of the dust of the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brought forth. This is birth language. The poem uses it to say that Wisdom did not come after the world. Before the oceans, before a single spring, Wisdom was. The Nicene Creed, the church's fourth-century confession, says of the Son that he is "begotten, not made", and that is the right direction to take this language when it is applied to Christ: not that he had a beginning, but that he is eternally from the Father, as a son is from a father.

The poem goes down the list of the oldest things anyone can imagine. Mountains seem eternal; Wisdom is older. The first of the dust of the world, the very first grain of soil, came after her. Everything a person can see or touch is younger than the wisdom of God.

verseByVerse.quote: When he established the heavens, I was there; when he drew a circle on the face of the deep, when he made firm the skies above, when he established the fountains of the deep, when he assigned to the sea its limit, so that the waters might not transgress his command, when he marked out the foundations of the earth,
verseByVerse.commentary:
I was there. Wisdom was not a spectator in the stands but present at the work. God drew a circle on the face of the deep, the horizon, where the sky seems to meet the waters. Genesis says that at the beginning darkness was over the face of the deep (Gen 1:2). Wisdom saw God mark out order in that darkness. Proverbs 8 is poetry and does not say how long the work took. Genesis does, and this commentary holds that God made all things in six ordinary days (Genesis 1; Exodus 20:11). Faithful Christians who read the days as long ages or as a literary framework do so out of reverence for Scripture too, and deserve respect.

The ESV notes that the meaning of the Hebrew of verse 28 is uncertain, but the picture is clear. To the ancient mind the sea was the great symbol of chaos. God speaks and it stops: Thus far shall you come, and no farther, and here shall your proud waves be stayed (Job 38:11). I placed the sand as the boundary for the sea, a perpetual barrier that it cannot pass (Jer 5:22).

Wisdom does the same in a human life. The commands of God that seem to limit us are like the shoreline: without them, chaos floods everything. A person who throws off every limit does not become free; he becomes a flood.

verseByVerse.quote: then I was beside him, like a master workman, and I was daily his delight, rejoicing before him always, rejoicing in his inhabited world and delighting in the children of man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here the poem reaches its warmest point. Wisdom was beside him, close at God's side, and like a master workman, the skilled craftsman at the builder's elbow. (The rare Hebrew word may instead mean a little child, as the ESV notes.) John says, All things were made through him (John 1:3), and speaks of God the only Son, who is at the Father's side (John 1:18).

And the mood of creation was joy. I was daily his delight, and the ESV notes this may be "daily filled with delight". Wisdom was rejoicing before him always. Creation was not a grim task. It was carried out in delight, the Father delighting in his Wisdom and Wisdom rejoicing before him.

When Jesus was baptised, a voice from heaven said, This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased (Matt 3:17). And Jesus prayed of the glory the Father had given him because you loved me before the foundation of the world (John 17:24). The delight of verse 30 is older than time.

The children of man. Wisdom's delight moved outward, to the inhabited world and above all to the children of man. Of all that God made, Wisdom took special pleasure in human beings.

Read that in the light of the gospel. The Son who was the Father's delight before the world began delighted in the children of man so much that he became one of them. He emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men (Phil 2:7). The Wisdom who rejoiced over the world at creation came into that world to save it. That is how much God's wisdom delights in you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–36 — Whoever Finds Me Finds Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Blessed are those who wait daily at Wisdom's doors, For whoever finds me finds life (vv. 32-36).
verseByVerse.theology: Life and death depend on one thing: whether a person finds wisdom, and in the fullest sense that means finding Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, O sons, listen to me: blessed are those who keep my ways. Hear instruction and be wise, and do not neglect it. Blessed is the one who listens to me, watching daily at my gates, waiting beside my doors.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now. It is the same phrase the father used after the story of the seductress (7:24). After the vision of creation, she comes back to the crossroads, to her sons, and draws the conclusion: listen to me. The wisdom that made the world is the wisdom that will make your life.

The danger for most people is not open rejection of wisdom. It is neglect: letting the voice go unheard because other voices are louder and closer.

The picture in verse 34 is of someone waiting outside a house every morning for the door to open, like a servant waiting for his master, or a lover for the beloved. The blessing belongs to the person who makes seeking wisdom a daily habit, not a crisis measure.

For a Christian, waiting at Wisdom's doors means waiting on Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3). And it is never a wait at a locked house. He has promised, whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37).

verseByVerse.quote: For whoever finds me finds life and obtains favor from the LORD, but he who fails to find me injures himself; all who hate me love death."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever finds me. This is the promise the chapter has been building toward: not only a better life, but life itself. And favor from the LORD, which is grace.

Whoever has the Son has life (1 John 5:12). And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent (John 17:3). I am the way, and the truth, and the life (John 14:6). To find Wisdom, finally, is to find Christ.

And the other side: he who fails to find me injures himself. Rejecting wisdom is self-harm. No one else needs to punish the fool; he wounds himself.

The last phrase is stark. Nobody thinks he loves death. The young man of chapter 7 thought he loved pleasure. But to reject the source of life is, whether one knows it or not, to choose death. Whoever does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him (John 3:36).

So the chapter ends where the book always ends up: at a choice between two ways. But here the choice has a face. The Wisdom who stood beside the Father at creation, delighting in the children of man, stands at the crossroads and calls. Whoever finds him finds life.
