all who hate me love death."
8.overview: Wisdom calls in public to all, even fools (vv. 1-11). By her kings reign, and she loves those who love her (vv. 12-21). She was with the LORD before creation, his delight, and delights in humanity (vv. 22-31). Whoever finds her finds life; all who hate her love death (vv. 32-36).
8.theology:
God's wisdom is universally offered (vv. 4-5), perfectly truthful (vv. 6-9), and the source of all just authority (vv. 15-16; Dan 2:21; Rom 13:1). The fear of the LORD includes hatred of evil (v. 13).

Wisdom existed before creation and was the agent of it (vv. 22-31). She is a poetic personification, not a direct portrait of the Son, but the New Testament gives this language its full meaning in Christ. It identifies Christ as the wisdom of God (1 Cor 1:24; Col 2:3), through whom all things were made (John 1:1-3; Col 1:16-17; Heb 1:2). Verse 22 must not be read, as Arius read it, to make the Son a creature; the Son is eternally with the Father (John 1:1; 17:5), begotten, not made.

The Father's eternal delight in his Wisdom (v. 30; Matt 3:17; John 17:24) overflows in delight in humanity (v. 31), fulfilled in the incarnation (Phil 2:6-7). Finding Wisdom is finding life; rejecting her is loving death (vv. 35-36; John 17:3; 3:36).
8.examples: God's commands work like a shoreline: they look like limits, but they are what keeps the chaos out. And the blessed life is pictured as someone who waits at Wisdom's door every morning, not only when trouble comes.

9.title: Wisdom Has Built Her House

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wisdom has built her house, set her table and sent her young women to call the simple: Leave your simple ways, and live (vv. 1-6).
verseByVerse.theology: Wisdom's invitation is a feast already prepared, offered free to people who have nothing to bring but their need.

verseByVerse.quote: Wisdom has built her house; she has hewn her seven pillars. She has slaughtered her beasts; she has mixed her wine; she has also set her table.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Built her house. The first nine chapters end with a pair of pictures meant to be seen side by side: two women, two houses, two feasts.

Her house is substantial, seven pillars cut from stone, and seven often stands for completeness. Her house is finished, solid, ready; nothing about it is temporary. Proverbs will later say, The wisest of women builds her house (14:1). And Jesus spoke of the wise man who built his house on the rock, the house that did not fall (Matt 7:24-25).

Many Christians have heard a further echo here, though it is an echo and not the verse's own meaning. The New Testament speaks of a house God is building, and Christ Jesus is the cornerstone, in whom the whole structure, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord (Eph 2:20-21). In the end, the house that wisdom builds is the dwelling place of God among his people.

Then the feast. Meat has been slaughtered, wine mixed with spices, the table laid. Everything is ready before a single guest has been invited. The cost has been paid by the host.

Jesus told a parable that sounds almost exactly like this. A king prepared a wedding feast for his son, and sent word: See, I have prepared my dinner, my oxen and my fat calves have been slaughtered, and everything is ready. Come to the wedding feast (Matt 22:4). The gospel is not an invitation to come and help prepare the meal. It is an invitation to a table already set.

verseByVerse.quote: She has sent out her young women to call from the highest places in the town, "Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!" To him who lacks sense she says,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Her young women. Her invitation does not wait for people to find her house; it goes out to find them, calling from the highest places in the town, where the voice carries furthest. In the parable of the great banquet, the master said, Go out quickly to the streets and lanes of the city (Luke 14:21), and then, Go out to the highways and hedges and compel people to come in, that my house may be filled (Luke 14:23).

Every Christian who speaks of Christ to a friend is one of Wisdom's messengers, calling from wherever he stands in the town.

Whoever is simple. That is the young man of chapter 7, exactly, the one who was lacking sense (7:7). Wisdom invites the very person who is most likely to walk into Folly's house. She does not demand that he become wise first. The qualification for her feast is knowing you need it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Come, eat of my bread and drink of the wine I have mixed. Leave your simple ways, and live, and walk in the way of insight."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eat of my bread. Wisdom is not only studied; she is received, taken in, the way food becomes part of a body. Isaiah's great invitation sounds the same: Come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; and he who has no money, come, buy and eat! (Isa 55:1).

And Jesus took the words onto his own lips. I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst (John 6:35). I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever (John 6:51). The poem does not name him, but the gospel shows what this bread finally is: Christ himself, the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24), who gives not only food but his own life. The Bible's last invitation is Wisdom's invitation still: let the one who desires take the water of life without price (Rev 22:17).

Leave your simple ways. The ESV notes that this could be rendered "Leave the company of the simple". Either way, a person cannot sit at Wisdom's table and keep his old life and old companions unchanged. Grace is free, but it is not static: by the Spirit it changes the direction of a life. Three verbs sum up the invitation: leave, live, walk.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: How a person takes correction shows whether he can be taught, for The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom (vv. 7-12).
verseByVerse.theology: How a person takes correction shows which banquet he is heading for.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever corrects a scoffer gets himself abuse, and he who reproves a wicked man incurs injury. Do not reprove a scoffer, or he will hate you; reprove a wise man, and he will love you. Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be still wiser; teach a righteous man, and he will increase in learning.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever corrects a scoffer. These sayings interrupt the two banquets to explain why some accept Wisdom's invitation and others do not: it comes down to how a person takes correction.

The scoffer is the person who mocks what is serious. Correct him, and you will get abuse in return: insults, anger, perhaps worse. Jesus said the same: do not throw your pearls before pigs, lest they trample them underfoot and turn to attack you (Matt 7:6).

Reprove a wise man. The same rebuke produces opposite reactions, and the reaction reveals the heart.

So turn the test on yourself: when someone last pointed out a fault in you, did you love them for it or resent them? A believer can bear correction without despair, because his standing rests on Christ, not on being found faultless. Faithful are the wounds of a friend (27:6). The psalmist could say, Let a righteous man strike me—it is a kindness; let him rebuke me—it is oil for my head (Ps 141:5).

Still wiser. The ESV notes that the Hebrew has no word for instruction; it simply says "give to a wise man". The wise man is not the one who knows the most but the one who keeps learning.

verseByVerse.quote: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and the knowledge of the Holy One is insight. For by me your days will be multiplied, and years will be added to your life. If you are wise, you are wise for yourself; if you scoff, you alone will bear it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fear of the LORD. The motto of 1:7 returns almost word for word, framing the first nine chapters like a door at each end.

And something is added: the knowledge of the Holy One is insight. Wisdom is not only fearing God; it is knowing him, the Holy One, personally. The goal of Proverbs is not a clever life. It is a life that knows God.

Years will be added. Folly's guests are among the dead (v. 18); Wisdom's have years added.

Does wisdom always lengthen life? As a pattern, yes: the wise avoid much that cuts lives short. But Abel, John the Baptist and Stephen died young and righteous, so the proverb states how God's world usually works, not a timetable for each life. Its fullest meaning lies beyond the grave: whoever does the will of God abides forever (1 John 2:17).

Wise for yourself. No one else can be wise for you, and no one else will bear your scoffing. Your parents' faith will not save you, and your friends' folly will not excuse you. The righteousness of the righteous shall be upon himself, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon himself (Ezek 18:20). For each will have to bear his own load (Gal 6:5).

That cuts both ways, and parents need to hear the second half. A son or daughter who scoffs bears it alone; a father or mother who taught faithfully is not made guilty by a child's choices, and may keep praying for that child with hope.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Folly calls from the same heights in the same words, offering stolen water, but her guests are in Sheol (vv. 13-18).
verseByVerse.theology: Folly copies Wisdom's invitation word for word, but her table is set with stolen goods in a house of the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: The woman Folly is loud; she is seductive and knows nothing. She sits at the door of her house; she takes a seat on the highest places of the town, calling to those who pass by, who are going straight on their way,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Folly is loud. Folly is personified just as Wisdom has been, and she looks very much like the forbidden woman of chapter 7, who was also loud (7:11). She is seductive, and she knows nothing. The ESV notes the alternative "full of simpleness". She has a great deal to say and nothing to teach.

She sits. Wisdom built her house, hewn pillars, slaughtered, mixed, set, sent. Six verbs of work. Folly sits. She has built and prepared nothing.

And yet she has found a seat on the highest places of the town, exactly where Wisdom's messengers called (v. 3). Her voice is just as easy to hear.

Going straight on. Her target is not people who are already lost, but those going straight on their way. Folly's business is to pull people off a good road. No one is so far along the straight road that he is beyond her reach.
verseByVerse.note: Folly is pictured as a rival woman, imitating wisdom’s invitation.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!" And to him who lacks sense she says, "Stolen water is sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant." But he does not know that the dead are there, that her guests are in the depths of Sheol.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same invitation. Here is the chilling detail. Folly's invitation is word for word Wisdom's (v. 4), from the same heights, to the same people.

She never announces herself as folly; she uses the language of wisdom. False teaching borrows the vocabulary of the gospel. Sin promises life, freedom, fulfilment, the very things God offers. The simple person cannot tell the two invitations apart by their words. He can only tell them apart by what is served, and by where the house leads.

Stolen water. Here is what is served. Wisdom offered meat and mixed wine. Folly offers water and bread, and it is stolen. She has nothing of her own. Her whole appeal is that it is forbidden: the water is not better water, and the bread is pleasant because it is eaten in secret.

This is the oldest temptation there is. The fruit in Eden was a delight to the eyes, and the woman took it (Gen 3:6); its attraction was sharpened by the fact that God had said no. Paul describes the same perverse effect: sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, produced in me all kinds of covetousness (Rom 7:8). There is a thrill in the forbidden that has nothing to do with the thing itself. An affair, a theft, a secret habit: the secrecy is half the pleasure.

He does not know. The guests at Folly's table look around and see a party. They do not see what the father has been trying to show them since chapter 2: the dead are there. The ESV notes that the word is "Rephaim", the shades of the dead, just as at 2:18. Her guests are already in the depths of Sheol. They think they are dining; they are buried.

For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord (Rom 6:23). That verse is Proverbs 9 in one sentence: stolen water that ends in death, or bread for nothing that ends in life. Both hostesses are calling right now, in the same words, from the same heights. But only one of them has paid for the feast herself. Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb (Rev 19:9).

9.text: <sup>1</sup>Wisdom has built her house; she has hewn her seven pillars.<sup>2</sup>She has slaughtered her beasts; she has mixed her wine; she has also set her table.<sup>3</sup>She has sent out her young women to call from the highest places in the town,<sup>4</sup>"Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!" To him who lacks sense she says,<sup>5</sup>"Come, eat of my bread and drink of the wine I have mixed.<sup>6</sup>Leave your simple ways, and live, and walk in the way of insight."<sup>7</sup>Whoever corrects a scoffer gets himself abuse, and he who reproves a wicked man incurs injury.<sup>8</sup>Do not reprove a scoffer, or he will hate you; reprove a wise man, and he will love you.<sup>9</sup>Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be still wiser; teach a righteous man, and he will increase in learning.<sup>10</sup>The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and the knowledge of the Holy One is insight.<sup>11</sup>For by me your days will be multiplied, and years will be added to your life.<sup>12</sup>If you are wise, you are wise for yourself; if you scoff, you alone will bear it.<sup>13</sup>The woman Folly is loud; she is seductive and knows nothing.<sup>14</sup>She sits at the door of her house; she takes a seat on the highest places of the town,<sup>15</sup>calling to those who pass by, who are going straight on their way,<sup>16</sup>"Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!" And to him who lacks sense she says,<sup>17</sup>"Stolen water is sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant."<sup>18</sup>But he does not know that the dead are there, that her guests are in the depths of Sheol.
9.overview: Wisdom sets a feast and invites the simple to leave their ways and live (vv. 1-6). The scoffer hates correction and the wise love it; the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom (vv. 7-12). Folly copies Wisdom's invitation, but her guests are among the dead (vv. 13-18).
9.theology:
Chapters 1 to 9 close with two invitations. Wisdom's feast is prepared at the host's cost and offered freely to the needy (vv. 1-6), as the gospel banquet is (Matt 22:2-4; Luke 14:16-23; John 6:35; Rev 22:17); accepting it means leaving the old way (v. 6).

The response to correction reveals the heart (vv. 7-9), and the fear of the LORD frames the whole first section (v. 10; 1:7). Each person bears his own response (v. 12; Ezek 18:20).

Folly imitates Wisdom's words (v. 16), offers only what is stolen and secret (v. 17; Gen 3:6; Rom 7:8), and leads to death (v. 18; Rom 6:23).
9.examples: The same rebuke can be hated by one person and loved by another, and the difference shows which table each is heading for. Wisdom works, building and preparing; Folly only sits and calls. And the guests at her table think they are dining when they are already buried.

10.title: The Proverbs of Solomon: Two Ways in Two Lines

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Righteous and the Wicked
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Solomon's sayings begin with the family, the purse and the memory a life leaves: A wise son makes a glad father (vv. 1-7).
verseByVerse.theology: From here the book speaks in two-line contrasts, and the first ones set the two ways side by side in the family, the purse and the memory a life leaves behind.

verseByVerse.quote: The proverbs of Solomon. A wise son makes a glad father, but a foolish son is a sorrow to his mother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With a new heading the book changes shape. After nine chapters of a father's long speeches, from here to the middle of chapter 22 come short sayings, most of them two-line contrasts: the wise and the foolish, the righteous and the wicked, the diligent and the lazy. The first nine chapters were the lecture; these are the tools.

A proverb is meant to be picked up, turned over, carried into the day and tested against life; one or two pondered will do more good than a chapter skimmed.

The first tool is aimed at the family. A son's choices land on his parents; no one's wisdom or folly is private.

Only one Son ever made his Father wholly glad. At the Jordan the Father said of Jesus, with you I am well pleased (Luke 3:22), and Jesus could say, I always do the things that are pleasing to him (John 8:29). He is the wise Son this verse describes, whose obedience is counted to all who trust him (Rom 5:19), and he came for the foolish sons and daughters who grieve their parents and God, as the father running to the prodigal shows (Luke 15:20).

Are the proverbs promises? Mostly they are patterns: short sayings about how God's world usually works, true as a rule, and meant to be weighed beside other proverbs and the rest of Scripture. Proverbs itself shows this. It says the diligent grow rich (v. 4), and also that injustice sweeps away the poor man's harvest (13:23). It says a wise son gladdens his father, and Ezekiel describes a righteous father whose son turns violent (Ezekiel 18:5-13). So a hard-working believer who is still poor has not disproved the book or failed God. And parents whose child has turned away should hear this verse as a description of their sorrow, not a verdict on their parenting. God himself said, Children have I reared and brought up, but they have rebelled against me (Isaiah 1:2). The Bible's certainties rest on God's promises in Christ, not on a formula for children or money.
verseByVerse.note: The first collection of Solomon’s one-verse proverbs (10:1–22:16).

verseByVerse.quote: Treasures gained by wickedness do not profit, but righteousness delivers from death. The LORD does not let the righteous go hungry, but he thwarts the craving of the wicked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Treasures gained by wickedness. Dishonest gain is real money, but it does not profit. It cannot buy what matters, and it cannot save its owner from the one appointment he cannot avoid. Jesus warned, one's life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions (Luke 12:15).

The LORD feeds the righteous. Here the LORD himself first appears in these sayings, and he appears as provider and as judge. The righteous are fed. The wicked have cravings that God thwarts: they get what they wanted and find it does not satisfy, or they never get it at all.

Is it true that no righteous person ever goes hungry? David said, I have been young, and now am old, yet I have not seen the righteous forsaken or his children begging for bread (Ps 37:25). That is the pattern of God's care. Yet Hebrews speaks of the faithful who went about destitute, afflicted, mistreated (Heb 11:37). A proverb states how God's world generally works, not a guarantee against every hardship. But even in hunger, the righteous are never abandoned, and the Father who knows what they need has promised to provide what they truly need (Matt 6:33).

By contrast, righteousness delivers from death. That describes the righteous life, which keeps a man from the violent or shameful ends of the wicked; in the light of the New Testament it points to the righteousness God gives in Christ, which delivers from death itself (Rom 5:17–21). It is not salvation by good works.

verseByVerse.quote: A slack hand causes poverty, but the hand of the diligent makes rich. He who gathers in summer is a prudent son, but he who sleeps in harvest is a son who brings shame.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A slack hand. One hand is loose, not gripping the tool; the other is sharp and working. This is not the only reason people are poor, and Proverbs will say much about the poor who are oppressed and the rich who are unjust. But it is one reason, and a young person can do something about it.

Gathers in summer. Harvest does not wait. There are a few weeks when the crop must be brought in, and a son who sleeps through them has lost the year. Life has harvests too: the years of study, the early career, the season when children are young and must be taught. They do not come back. And the lazy son shames the family that bears his name.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessings are on the head of the righteous, but the mouth of the wicked conceals violence. The memory of the righteous is a blessing, but the name of the wicked will rot.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessings on the head. They rest there visibly, like a crown. The wicked man's mouth, by contrast, hides something. He talks pleasantly, and violence lies behind the words. The ESV notes that the line may also be read, "but violence covers the mouth of the wicked": the violence he planned will come back over his own face.

The memory of the righteous. A righteous person's memory goes on blessing others after he has died: the grandmother whose prayers are still remembered, the father whose honesty is still quoted. Abel was killed at the beginning of history, and through his faith, though he died, he still speaks (Heb 11:4). He will be remembered forever (Ps 112:6).

The name of the wicked will rot, like meat left out. No one names his son after a notorious traitor.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–21 — The Mouth of the Righteous
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Most of these sayings are about speech: The mouth of the righteous is a fountain of life, and love covers all offenses (vv. 8-21).
verseByVerse.theology: What comes out of a person's mouth either gives life to others or does them harm, and restraint is half of wisdom.

verseByVerse.quote: The wise of heart will receive commandments, but a babbling fool will come to ruin. Whoever walks in integrity walks securely, but he who makes his ways crooked will be found out. Whoever winks the eye causes trouble, and a babbling fool will come to ruin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wise of heart. The wise man takes in; the fool pours out. He receives commandments because he knows he needs them. The babbling fool, literally the fool of lips, is too busy talking to hear anything. And he talks himself into ruin.

Integrity. It means being whole, the same person in public and in private. And that person walks securely. He does not have to remember which story he told to whom. The man with a crooked way is living with a time bomb. He will be found out.

Whoever winks the eye. The winking eye is the signal of the schemer we met in 6:13. The second line repeats verse 8 word for word; some truths are worth saying twice within a few lines.

verseByVerse.quote: The mouth of the righteous is a fountain of life, but the mouth of the wicked conceals violence. Hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all offenses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A fountain of life. A fountain in a dry land is where people come to live. The righteous person's speech is like that. People come away from talking with him refreshed, encouraged, set right.

Jesus promised that this fountain would flow from everyone who comes to him: Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water (John 7:38). A believer's mouth can become a fountain of life because the Spirit of life lives in him. The second line repeats verse 6.

Hatred stirs up strife. It stirs, like someone stirring embers back into flame. It keeps old grievances alive. Love covers. It does not pretend the offence did not happen, and it does not cover crimes that must be exposed. But it declines to keep uncovering what has been forgiven. Whoever covers an offense seeks love, but he who repeats a matter separates close friends (17:9).

Peter took this proverb straight into the life of the church: Above all, keep loving one another earnestly, since love covers a multitude of sins (1 Pet 4:8). And behind every Christian's covering love stands the love of God, who covered our sins at the cost of his Son.

Is there an offence you keep stirring? What would it mean to cover it today?

verseByVerse.quote: On the lips of him who has understanding, wisdom is found, but a rod is for the back of him who lacks sense. The wise lay up knowledge, but the mouth of a fool brings ruin near.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A rod for the back. There are two ways to learn. The person with understanding learns through words; wisdom is on his lips because it has gone in through his ears. The person who lacks sense will not learn through words, so he learns through the rod, through pain. The question is whether a person learns from instruction or from consequences.

The wise lay up knowledge. They store it like provisions. The fool spends his words as fast as he gets them, and every sentence brings disaster a step closer. Some people are one remark away from losing a job or a friend, and they make the remark.

verseByVerse.quote: A rich man's wealth is his strong city; the poverty of the poor is their ruin. The wage of the righteous leads to life, the gain of the wicked to sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A rich man's wealth. Money does protect people. The rich can afford lawyers, doctors and a cushion against disaster. The poor have none, and one broken car can ruin them. Proverbs is not naive about that.

But the book does not leave it there. In 18:11 the same first line comes back with a second line added: A rich man's wealth is his strong city, and like a high wall in his imagination. The fortress is real, and it is also partly imaginary. Money protects against many things, but not against death, grief, judgment or a heart that is empty. That is why Paul tells the rich not to be haughty, nor to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but on God (1 Tim 6:17).

The wage of the righteous. The righteous man's wages go toward life: his family fed, his neighbour helped, God honoured. The wicked man's gain leads to more sin: more greed, more indulgence, more distance from God. Money is an amplifier. It makes a person more of what he already is.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever heeds instruction is on the path to life, but he who rejects reproof leads others astray. The one who conceals hatred has lying lips, and whoever utters slander is a fool.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rejecting reproof. A person who will not take correction does not only harm himself. He leads others astray. A father who never admits he was wrong teaches his children to do the same. A leader who will not be corrected takes a whole organisation down with him. Teachability is not a private virtue.

Hidden hatred. Verse 18 names two ways to handle hatred, and both are wrong. Hide it behind a smile, and you are a liar. Let it out as slander, and you are a fool. The only real answer to hatred is not to hide it or voice it, but to have it removed from the heart, which only God can do.

verseByVerse.quote: When words are many, transgression is not lacking, but whoever restrains his lips is prudent. The tongue of the righteous is choice silver; the heart of the wicked is of little worth. The lips of the righteous feed many, but fools die for lack of sense.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When words are many. The more a person talks, the more chances there are to say something wrong. James says, let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger (Jas 1:19), and if anyone does not stumble in what he says, he is a perfect man (Jas 3:2).

The wise person restrains his lips, like reining in a horse, and that self-control is the Spirit's fruit (Gal 5:23), not mere willpower. Ask him for it, and keep a guard on your lips.

Choice silver. The contrast is between the tongue of one and the heart of the other. The righteous man's words are valuable because his heart is; the wicked man's heart is worth little, so his words are too. Speech is only as good as the heart it comes from.

The lips feed many. The righteous person's words are food, and they feed many: counsel, encouragement, truth, the gospel itself. The fool cannot feed even himself, and dies starving for the sense that was on offer.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–32 — The Blessing and the Stronghold
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The blessing of the LORD makes rich; the hope of the righteous brings joy, and they will never be removed (vv. 22-32).
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter ends by looking to the future: what the righteous hope for will come, and what they stand on will hold.

verseByVerse.quote: The blessing of the LORD makes rich, and he adds no sorrow with it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After many proverbs about human diligence, this one sets it in its place. Riches that last come from the blessing of the LORD. And that kind of wealth comes without the sorrow that so often attaches to money: the anxiety, the family fights, the guilt of how it was gained.

The ESV notes that the second line may be read, "and toil adds nothing to it". That does not contradict verse 4, which praised the diligent hand. It says that diligence without God's blessing achieves nothing lasting. It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil; for he gives to his beloved sleep (Ps 127:2). Work hard, and rest in the knowledge that the increase is his. Godliness with contentment is great gain (1 Tim 6:6).

Is this a promise of wealth? No. God’s blessing is the true riches, and it adds no sorrow. Many faithful believers are poor (Luke 6:20; Jas 2:5); the proverb is not a prosperity formula.

verseByVerse.quote: Doing wrong is like a joke to a fool, but wisdom is pleasure to a man of understanding. What the wicked dreads will come upon him, but the desire of the righteous will be granted. When the tempest passes, the wicked is no more, but the righteous is established forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like a joke. What a person laughs at reveals what he loves. For the fool, wrongdoing is entertainment: the prank that humiliates someone, the joke about cheating, the laughter at sin on a screen. For the man of understanding, wisdom is where the pleasure is.

What the wicked dreads. The wicked man pushes down a fear that one day he will answer for it, and he is right. The righteous man's desire will be granted.

When the tempest passes. The storm comes to both; the difference is what is left afterward. Jesus told of two houses in the same storm; one did not fall, because it had been founded on the rock, and the other fell, and great was the fall of it (Matt 7:25, 27).

verseByVerse.quote: Like vinegar to the teeth and smoke to the eyes, so is the sluggard to those who send him. The fear of the LORD prolongs life, but the years of the wicked will be short.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like vinegar. Anyone who has managed people will recognise this comic picture. You send a lazy man on an errand, and the experience is like sour vinegar on your teeth, or smoke in your eyes: irritating, painful, and impossible to ignore. A Christian employee's reliability is part of his witness, whether or not anyone thanks him for it.

Verse 27 states the general pattern again. A life lived in reverence toward God avoids a great many of the things that shorten lives: violence, addiction, reckless living, the stress of guilt. And ultimately the fear of the LORD leads to a life that has no end.

verseByVerse.quote: The hope of the righteous brings joy, but the expectation of the wicked will perish. The way of the LORD is a stronghold to the blameless, but destruction to evildoers. The righteous will never be removed, but the wicked will not dwell in the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hope of the righteous. The wicked expects a future built on his own plans, and it will perish. The righteous hopes in God, and that hope brings joy even now, before it is fulfilled. Hope does not put us to shame, because God's love has been poured into our hearts (Rom 5:5).

A stronghold. The same way of the LORD is two different things to two different people. To the blameless it is a fortress, a place of safety. To evildoers it is destruction. God's ways do not change; people's relationship to them does. The same sun that grows a plant withers one with no roots.

Never removed. The righteous are rooted. Those who trust in the LORD are like Mount Zion, which cannot be moved, but abides forever (Ps 125:1). Circumstances will shake them; they will not be removed from God's hand.

verseByVerse.quote: The mouth of the righteous brings forth wisdom, but the perverse tongue will be cut off. The lips of the righteous know what is acceptable, but the mouth of the wicked, what is perverse.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brings forth wisdom. Wisdom is brought forth as a tree bears fruit; it grows out of the righteous person's mouth naturally. The perverse tongue, the tongue that twists truth, is like a branch that will be cut off.

What is acceptable. The righteous person's lips know what is fitting: when to speak and when to be quiet, what will help and what will wound, how to say a hard thing kindly. That is a skill learned over years of listening to God and to people. The wicked mouth knows only what is twisted. Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person (Col 4:6).

No subject in this chapter gets more attention than the mouth, where wisdom and folly show themselves first and most often.

10.text: <sup>1</sup>The proverbs of Solomon. A wise son makes a glad father, but a foolish son is a sorrow to his mother.<sup>2</sup>Treasures gained by wickedness do not profit, but righteousness delivers from death.<sup>3</sup>The LORD does not let the righteous go hungry, but he thwarts the craving of the wicked.<sup>4</sup>A slack hand causes poverty, but the hand of the diligent makes rich.<sup>5</sup>He who gathers in summer is a prudent son, but he who sleeps in harvest is a son who brings shame.<sup>6</sup>Blessings are on the head of the righteous, but the mouth of the wicked conceals violence.<sup>7</sup>The memory of the righteous is a blessing, but the name of the wicked will rot.<sup>8</sup>The wise of heart will receive commandments, but a babbling fool will come to ruin.<sup>9</sup>Whoever walks in integrity walks securely, but he who makes his ways crooked will be found out.<sup>10</sup>Whoever winks the eye causes trouble, and a babbling fool will come to ruin.<sup>11</sup>The mouth of the righteous is a fountain of life, but the mouth of the wicked conceals violence.<sup>12</sup>Hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all offenses.<sup>13</sup>On the lips of him who has understanding, wisdom is found, but a rod is for the back of him who lacks sense.<sup>14</sup>The wise lay up knowledge, but the mouth of a fool brings ruin near.<sup>15</sup>A rich man's wealth is his strong city; the poverty of the poor is their ruin.<sup>16</sup>The wage of the righteous leads to life, the gain of the wicked to sin.<sup>17</sup>Whoever heeds instruction is on the path to life, but he who rejects reproof leads others astray.<sup>18</sup>The one who conceals hatred has lying lips, and whoever utters slander is a fool.<sup>19</sup>When words are many, transgression is not lacking, but whoever restrains his lips is prudent.<sup>20</sup>The tongue of the righteous is choice silver; the heart of the wicked is of little worth.<sup>21</sup>The lips of the righteous feed many, but fools die for lack of sense.<sup>22</sup>The blessing of the LORD makes rich, and he adds no sorrow with it.<sup>23</sup>Doing wrong is like a joke to a fool, but wisdom is pleasure to a man of understanding.<sup>24</sup>What the wicked dreads will come upon him, but the desire of the righteous will be granted.<sup>25</sup>When the tempest passes, the wicked is no more, but the righteous is established forever.<sup>26</sup>Like vinegar to the teeth and smoke to the eyes, so is the sluggard to those who send him.<sup>27</sup>The fear of the LORD prolongs life, but the years of the wicked will be short.<sup>28</sup>The hope of the righteous brings joy, but the expectation of the wicked will perish.<sup>29</sup>The way of the LORD is a stronghold to the blameless, but destruction to evildoers.<sup>30</sup>The righteous will never be removed, but the wicked will not dwell in the land.<sup>31</sup>The mouth of the righteous brings forth wisdom, but the perverse tongue will be cut off.<sup>32</sup>The lips of the righteous know what is acceptable, but the mouth of the wicked, what is perverse.
10.overview: The main collection of Solomon's proverbs begins, in short two-line contrasts. A wise son gladdens his parents, ill-gotten treasure does not profit, and diligence brings plenty (vv. 1-7). Most of the chapter concerns speech: the righteous mouth is a fountain of life, love covers offences, and many words bring transgression (vv. 8-21). The LORD's blessing makes rich without sorrow, and the righteous will never be removed (vv. 22-32).
10.theology:
The two ways of chapters 1-9 are now applied to everyday life in compressed sayings. Proverbs describe the general pattern of God's world, not guarantees for every case (v. 3; Ps 37:25; Heb 11:37).

Human diligence matters (vv. 4-5), but lasting wealth is the LORD's blessing (v. 22; Ps 127:2). Speech reveals the heart (v. 20) and either gives life or does harm (vv. 11, 21). Love covers offences (v. 12; 1 Pet 4:8). Wealth is a real protection and a false security (v. 15; 18:11). The hope of the righteous will not perish (v. 28; Rom 5:5).
10.examples: Think of the person whose words you go to when you are dry: that is what verse 11 means by a fountain of life. Ask what your name will smell like when you are gone. And try saying less for a day, asking the Spirit for restraint, and notice how much you are glad you did not say.

11.overview: God delights in honest weights; integrity guides the upright, riches fail in the day of wrath, and the righteous bless their city (vv. 1-11). The wise keep secrets, seek counsel and are kind; evil will not go unpunished (vv. 12-22). The generous are enriched, the hoarder is cursed, and the fruit of the righteous is a tree of life (vv. 23-31).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Honest Scales and a Rejoicing City
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Honest scales are the LORD's delight, integrity guides the upright, and By the blessing of the upright a city is exalted (vv. 1-11).
verseByVerse.theology: Righteousness is public: it is measured in the marketplace and felt by a whole city.

verseByVerse.quote: A false balance is an abomination to the LORD, but a just weight is his delight. When pride comes, then comes disgrace, but with the humble is wisdom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A false balance. In the ancient market, goods were weighed on a balance against stones of a set weight. A dishonest trader kept two sets of stones in his bag: a heavy one for buying and a light one for selling. The law had forbidden it, You shall have just balances, just weights (Lev 19:36), and the prophets denounced merchants who were eager to make the ephah small and the shekel great and deal deceitfully with false balances (Amos 8:5).

God calls the rigged scale an abomination, a word often used of idolatry. And he calls an honest weight his delight. God cares about the till at the corner shop. He is pleased by an accurate invoice, an honest tax return, a fair price for a used car. Business is not a secular zone where God's standards do not apply. A just balance and scales are the LORD's (16:11).

What are the scales in your work: the timesheet, the expense claim, the grade you give a student? For those he has already made his own, each of them can be the LORD's delight.

When pride comes. Disgrace follows pride as thunder follows lightning. The humble have wisdom because they are willing to learn. Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted (Luke 14:11).

verseByVerse.quote: The integrity of the upright guides them, but the crookedness of the treacherous destroys them. Riches do not profit in the day of wrath, but righteousness delivers from death. The righteousness of the blameless keeps his way straight, but the wicked falls by his own wickedness. The righteousness of the upright delivers them, but the treacherous are taken captive by their lust.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Integrity guides. A person of integrity has a built-in guide. When a hard decision comes, he does not have to calculate what he can get away with; he already knows what he will do. The treacherous man has no such guide, and his crookedness eventually turns on him.

The day of wrath. The second line repeats 10:2; the first names the moment when riches fail: the day of wrath. Zephaniah said, Neither their silver nor their gold shall be able to deliver them on the day of the wrath of the LORD (Zeph 1:18). There is a day money cannot buy off, and many people spend their lives preparing financially for every day except that one.

Their own wickedness. Verses 5 and 6 make the same point: the wicked are not so much destroyed by God's thunderbolts as by their own choices. Their own cravings become the chains. Sin carries its own punishment inside it.

verseByVerse.quote: When the wicked dies, his hope will perish, and the expectation of wealth perishes too. The righteous is delivered from trouble, and the wicked walks into it instead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the wicked dies. Everything the wicked man hoped for was on this side of the grave, so at the grave it all ends. The ESV notes that wealth may also be read "his strength" or "iniquity". Whether he trusted his money, his strength or his wrongdoing, none of it goes further than the funeral. The righteous man's hope does not stop at death; that is where it is finally realised.

The righteous is delivered. Sometimes the trouble meant for the righteous lands on the wicked. The book of Esther is a whole story built on this proverb: Haman built a gallows for Mordecai, and in the end they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai (Esth 7:10).

verseByVerse.quote: With his mouth the godless man would destroy his neighbor, but by knowledge the righteous are delivered. When it goes well with the righteous, the city rejoices, and when the wicked perish there are shouts of gladness. By the blessing of the upright a city is exalted, but by the mouth of the wicked it is overthrown.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With his mouth. The godless man's weapon is his mouth: slander, lies, rumour. Words can destroy a neighbour's reputation, marriage or career. The defence is knowledge: knowing the truth, knowing God, and being known for integrity, so that the lie does not stick.

The city rejoices. When righteous people prosper, whole communities are better off, and people know it. When a corrupt official falls or a crime boss is jailed, the streets celebrate.

A city is exalted. The upright bless their city: they pay fair wages, keep their word, care for the poor, pray for their leaders. The wicked tear it down, again by the mouth: corruption, propaganda, lies. God told the exiles in Babylon, seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you, for in its welfare you will find your welfare (Jer 29:7). Jesus called his disciples the salt of the earth (Matt 5:13).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–22 — The Neighbour, the Secret and the Kind Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sayings about neighbours: the sneer and the kept secret, many counsellors and the rash guarantee, kindness and cruelty (vv. 12-22).
verseByVerse.theology: How a person treats the people around him, in speech, trust and kindness, comes back to him.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever belittles his neighbor lacks sense, but a man of understanding remains silent. Whoever goes about slandering reveals secrets, but he who is trustworthy in spirit keeps a thing covered.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Belittling. The sneer, the put-down, the joke at someone's expense feels clever and shows a lack of sense. The man of understanding, when he is tempted to cut someone down, keeps quiet. Do not speak evil against one another, brothers (Jas 4:11).

Slandering. The slanderer goes about, from house to house, from group to group, passing on what he was told in confidence. The law had said, You shall not go around as a slanderer among your people (Lev 19:16). The trustworthy person is a vault. You can tell him your struggle and know it will not be at the church lunch on Sunday.

A test worth putting to yourself: could the people you spoke about this week hear it all and still trust you? Where they could not, the way back is confession, to God and often to them.

verseByVerse.quote: Where there is no guidance, a people falls, but in an abundance of counselors there is safety. Whoever puts up security for a stranger will surely suffer harm, but he who hates striking hands in pledge is secure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where there is no guidance. Nations fall, and companies, churches and families too, when decisions are made by one person who listens to no one. Safety lies in many counsellors. The wise leader surrounds himself with people who can tell him he is wrong. The same applies to personal decisions (15:22).

Security for a stranger. The warning of 6:1-5 again. Striking hands was the handshake that sealed a guarantee. To guarantee a stranger's debt is to hand your financial future to someone you do not know. The one who hates doing it is not stingy; he is wise.

verseByVerse.quote: A gracious woman gets honor, and violent men get riches. A man who is kind benefits himself, but a cruel man hurts himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A gracious woman. Two kinds of gain stand side by side. Violent, ruthless men do get rich; the book is not naive about that. But a gracious woman gets something they cannot take by force: honor. People respect her freely. The violent may have more money; she has more of what money cannot buy.

A man who is kind. Kindness looks like giving something away, but it comes back. The kind person has friends, peace of mind, a good name, a softer heart. The cruel person, who thinks he is winning, is damaging himself: his relationships, his conscience, his soul. Blessed are the merciful, for they shall receive mercy (Matt 5:7).

verseByVerse.quote: The wicked earns deceptive wages, but one who sows righteousness gets a sure reward. Whoever is steadfast in righteousness will live, but he who pursues evil will die. Those of crooked heart are an abomination to the LORD, but those of blameless ways are his delight. Be assured, an evil person will not go unpunished, but the offspring of the righteous will be delivered.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Deceptive wages. The wicked man's pay looks real, but it is deceptive. They promise more than they deliver, and they do not last. The righteous man's reward is sure. And he sows. Righteousness is like planting. The harvest comes later, but it comes.

Steadfast in righteousness. Two words matter: steadfast and pursues. The righteous man keeps going in one direction over years. The wicked man chases evil. Both are committed; both arrive.

Those of crooked heart. The pair from verse 1, abomination and delight, now describes hearts. God weighs the heart the way an honest trader weighs grain, and on that scale no one's ways are blameless but Christ's. His perfect obedience is counted to all who trust him (2 Cor 5:21), and in him they are the LORD's delight.

Be assured. God gives his word on it: evil will be punished. For the victim of injustice who has seen no justice yet, that is a comfort. For the wrongdoer who thinks he got away with it, it is a warning. He will render to each one according to his works (Rom 2:6).

Are the children of believers automatically saved? No. Grace is not inherited (John 1:13). But God does bless the households of those who fear him, and children raised in a godly home are under real promises and means of grace (Acts 2:39). The proverb gives a pattern, not a guarantee for each child.

verseByVerse.quote: Like a gold ring in a pig's snout is a beautiful woman without discretion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The picture is meant to shock. A gold nose ring was a fine piece of jewellery. Put it in a pig's snout, and it is still gold, but it is wasted, rooting through the mud. Beauty without discretion, without good sense and moral judgment, is like that. The beauty is real, but it is attached to something that drags it through the dirt.

The proverb applies to men as well, and to every gift: intelligence without integrity, talent without character. Peter says the lasting beauty is the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which in God's sight is very precious (1 Pet 3:4).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–31 — One Who Waters Will Be Watered
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: One who waters will himself be watered; trust in riches falls, and whoever captures souls is wise (vv. 23-31).
verseByVerse.theology: The open hand is the wealthy one, and the greatest thing a wise person can win is another soul.

verseByVerse.quote: The desire of the righteous ends only in good, the expectation of the wicked in wrath. One gives freely, yet grows all the richer; another withholds what he should give, and only suffers want. Whoever brings blessing will be enriched, and one who waters will himself be watered. The people curse him who holds back grain, but a blessing is on the head of him who sells it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The desire of the righteous. The righteous person's desires, because they are aimed at God and his ways, finish in good. The wicked person's expectations finish in wrath.

One gives freely. By ordinary arithmetic, giving makes you poorer and keeping makes you richer. In God's economy it often runs the other way. The generous person grows all the richer, and the one who clutches what he should give suffers want. Not always in money, though often in that too, but always in joy, friendship and the favour of God. This is not a scheme for getting rich by giving, as some preachers claim. The poor widow who gave her two small coins went home as poor as she came, and Jesus praised her above all the rich givers (Mark 12:41-44). God's repayment is sure, but he chooses its currency.

One who waters. A farmer who waters his neighbour's field in a drought finds that rain falls on his own. Paul put it this way: whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully (2 Cor 9:6). And Jesus: give, and it will be given to you. Good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over, will be put into your lap (Luke 6:38). As the Lord Jesus said, It is more blessed to give than to receive (Acts 20:35). And the open hand begins with God, who gave first: Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift! (2 Cor 9:15).

The people curse him. In a famine, a merchant with a full warehouse can hold his grain back until the price rises. The people curse him, and rightly. Amos condemned those who trample on the needy (Amos 8:4). Modern forms of hoarding are not hard to find: price-gouging in a crisis, exploiting a shortage. The one who sells at a fair price when he could have squeezed people has a blessing on his head.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever diligently seeks good seeks favor, but evil comes to him who searches for it. Whoever trusts in his riches will fall, but the righteous will flourish like a green leaf.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever diligently seeks good. People tend to find what they are looking for. The person who looks for ways to do good finds favour; the ESV notes it may be "acceptance", with God and with people. The person who goes looking for trouble, for a fight, for an opportunity to do wrong, finds it, and it finds him back.

Trusts in his riches. The key word is trusts. Having riches is not condemned; leaning on them is. A person who trusts in money will fall, because money is not strong enough to hold the weight. Jesus said, how difficult it is to enter the kingdom of God!, easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person (Mark 10:24-25), not because God hates wealth, but because wealth is so easy to trust.

The righteous flourish like a green leaf. A leaf is not strong, but it is alive, fed by a root the eye cannot see. The righteous are strong the same way, through the life of God flowing into them.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever troubles his own household will inherit the wind, and the fool will be servant to the wise of heart. The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life, and whoever captures souls is wise. If the righteous is repaid on earth, how much more the wicked and the sinner!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Inherit the wind. A man who brings trouble into his own home, through anger, neglect, drunkenness or financial recklessness, will inherit the wind. At the end he will have nothing to hold. And the fool, who thought himself free and clever, ends up working for the wise man he despised.

A tree of life. The righteous person's fruit is a tree of life, the image from Eden and from 3:18. Other people are nourished and live because of what grows from his life.

To capture a soul is to win a person, to draw him to wisdom and life, and here it is the mark of the wise. The line is hard in Hebrew. The phrase can elsewhere mean taking a life, and the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint) reads it quite differently, so some think a copying slip lies behind it. The King James Version's "he that winneth souls is wise" is the reading most churchgoers know. As it stands, it most likely means winning people over by a good life, and Jesus' call to fish for people is a fair application rather than the proverb's first meaning. He called fishermen and said, Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men (Matt 4:19). Those who turn many to righteousness will shine like the stars forever and ever (Dan 12:3). The wisest investment a person can make is in another person's soul.

Repaid on earth. If God disciplines and repays even his own people in this life, how much more certain is the judgment of the wicked. Peter quotes the verse in the words of the Greek Old Testament, which differ from the Hebrew, to Christians under persecution: If the righteous is scarcely saved, what will become of the ungodly and the sinner? (1 Pet 4:18). The hardships of the righteous are a sign that God is serious about sin. That should drive every reader to the one place where sin has already been fully repaid: the cross, where the righteous One bore what the ungodly deserved, so that the ungodly who trust him are saved after all.

11.theology:
God's standards apply in the marketplace; honest business is his delight (v. 1; Lev 19:35-36). Sin carries its own punishment (vv. 5-6), and God will certainly judge evil (v. 21; Rom 2:6).

Righteousness has public effects on a whole community (vv. 10-11; Jer 29:7). Generosity is enriched in God's economy (vv. 24-25; 2 Cor 9:6; Luke 6:38), and trust in riches fails (v. 28; Mark 10:24-25).

Winning others to wisdom is the mark of the wise (v. 30; Dan 12:3; Matt 4:19). The discipline of the righteous shows the certainty of judgment on the wicked (v. 31; 1 Pet 4:18).
11.examples: Before a major decision, ask who your counsellors are, and whether any of them ever disagrees with you. And when a crisis gives you the chance to squeeze people, a fair price is a small act of righteousness that a whole town notices.

12.title: A Good Word Makes Him Glad
12.text: <sup>1</sup>Whoever loves discipline loves knowledge, but he who hates reproof is stupid.<sup>2</sup>A good man obtains favor from the LORD, but a man of evil devices he condemns.<sup>3</sup>No one is established by wickedness, but the root of the righteous will never be moved.<sup>4</sup>An excellent wife is the crown of her husband, but she who brings shame is like
