but those who plan peace have joy.<sup>21</sup>No ill befalls the righteous, but the wicked are filled with trouble.<sup>22</sup>Lying lips are an abomination to the LORD, but those who act faithfully are his delight.<sup>23</sup>A prudent man conceals knowledge, but the heart of fools proclaims folly.<sup>24</sup>The hand of the diligent will rule, while the slothful will be put to forced labor.<sup>25</sup>Anxiety in a man's heart weighs him down, but a good word makes him glad.<sup>26</sup>One who is righteous is a guide to his neighbor, but the way of the wicked leads them astray.<sup>27</sup>Whoever is slothful will not roast his game, but the diligent man will get precious wealth.<sup>28</sup>In the path of righteousness is life, and in its pathway there is no death.
12.overview: Loving discipline is loving knowledge; the righteous have a root that cannot be moved, and an excellent wife is her husband's crown (vv. 1-12). The fool is right in his own eyes; rash words wound but the tongue of the wise heals, and lies are an abomination to the LORD (vv. 13-23). A good word lifts anxiety, and on the path of righteousness there is no death (vv. 24-28).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Root of the Righteous
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sayings on correction, marriage, honest work and the root of the righteous, which will never be moved (vv. 1-12).
verseByVerse.theology: Stability grows from what cannot be seen: a teachable heart, a good marriage, honest work and a root in God.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever loves discipline loves knowledge, but he who hates reproof is stupid. A good man obtains favor from the LORD, but a man of evil devices he condemns. No one is established by wickedness, but the root of the righteous will never be moved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever loves discipline. Nobody gains knowledge without being corrected, because learning means finding out you were wrong. So a person who loves knowledge must also love the discipline that brings it. A person who hates correction has shut the only door to learning, and that is why Proverbs, which rarely uses so blunt a word, calls him stupid.

Few people love correction naturally. The Spirit teaches it, as a believer sees the peaceful fruit of righteousness it yields (Heb 12:11).

A good man obtains favor. The LORD is not neutral about character. The good man obtains favor; the schemer is condemned. God looks past a person's success to his heart and his plans.

No one is established. Wickedness can build something that looks solid, but it has no foundation. The righteous have a root, and a root is what holds a tree when the wind comes. The picture is of the man in Psalm 1: like a tree planted by streams of water, whose leaf does not wither (Ps 1:3). What keeps a believer standing in a storm is what was growing in secret before it came.

verseByVerse.quote: An excellent wife is the crown of her husband, but she who brings shame is like rottenness in his bones.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A wife of strength and character is her husband's crown. The same phrase opens the great poem at the end of the book: An excellent wife who can find? She is far more precious than jewels (31:10).

And the other side is painful: a wife who brings shame is like rottenness in his bones, a decay no one outside may see, eating away at his strength from inside.

The principle runs both ways: every spouse is a crown or a slow decay to the other, and most are some of each on different days. Where you have been the decay, the way back is confession and the forgiveness of Christ, who loved his bride before she was any crown (Eph 5:25).

verseByVerse.quote: The thoughts of the righteous are just; the counsels of the wicked are deceitful. The words of the wicked lie in wait for blood, but the mouth of the upright delivers them. The wicked are overthrown and are no more, but the house of the righteous will stand. A man is commended according to his good sense, but one of twisted mind is despised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The righteous person's thoughts are already bent toward what is fair. The wicked person's counsels, his plans and advice, are already deceitful before a word is spoken. Character is formed in the mind long before it shows in the hands.

Lie in wait for blood. Words can ambush. A false accusation, a lie in court, a rumour that ruins someone: the wicked use words like an ambush from chapter 1. The upright use their mouths to rescue, both themselves and others.

The wicked are overthrown. A house in Proverbs is a family and its future as well as a building. The wicked may seem powerful, but they are overthrown and are no more. The house of the righteous stands, often for generations.

A man is commended. In the long run, people recognise sense, and a twisted mind too. Reputation is not always fair in the short term, but over years it tends to settle on what a person actually is.

verseByVerse.quote: Better to be lowly and have a servant than to play the great man and lack bread. Whoever is righteous has regard for the life of his beast, but the mercy of the wicked is cruel. Whoever works his land will have plenty of bread, but he who follows worthless pursuits lacks sense. Whoever is wicked covets the spoil of evildoers, but the root of the righteous bears fruit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Better to be lowly. One man lives modestly and is well provided for. Another plays the great man, spends to look important, and has nothing to eat. Think of the car on finance, the house beyond the budget, the credit card paying for the image. Better to be thought ordinary and have bread on the table.

His beast. A righteous person's goodness reaches all the way down to his animals. He has regard for the life of his ox or donkey: he feeds it, rests it, does not beat it. The law said, You shall not muzzle an ox when it is treading out the grain (Deut 25:4). God himself ended the book of Jonah by asking whether he should not pity Nineveh, and also much cattle (Jonah 4:11).

How a person treats creatures that cannot repay him or complain reveals his heart. And the wicked? Even their mercy is cruel. Their best kindness still has an edge of contempt in it.

Whoever works his land. The farmer who works the field in front of him eats. The man who chases worthless pursuits, get-rich schemes, fantasies, endless distractions, lacks sense.

Whoever is wicked covets. The wicked man wants what other crooks have stolen. The righteous man's provision grows from the inside, from what God has planted, while the wicked man's comes from grabbing.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Words can cut like sword thrusts or bring healing, and Truthful lips endure forever (vv. 13-23).
verseByVerse.theology: Words can cut or heal, and truth outlasts every lie.

verseByVerse.quote: An evil man is ensnared by the transgression of his lips, but the righteous escapes from trouble. From the fruit of his mouth a man is satisfied with good, and the work of a man's hand comes back to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ensnared by his lips. The ESV notes that the line may also be read, "In the transgression of the lips, there is an evil snare". Either way, the snare is made of his own words: the lie that needs another lie, the boast that gets checked, the angry email that gets forwarded. The righteous man escapes because he said nothing that needs escaping from.

Words and work. Both come back. A man's words are like seeds, and he eats what grows from them: kind words bring kindness back, harsh ones bring conflict. And the work of his hands comes back to him.

verseByVerse.quote: The way of a fool is right in his own eyes, but a wise man listens to advice. The vexation of a fool is known at once, but the prudent ignores an insult.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Right in his own eyes. The fool's problem is that he is sure. The book of Judges ends with a whole nation in that condition: Everyone did what was right in his own eyes (Judg 21:25), and the result was chaos. There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death (14:12).

The wise man is not the one who is always right. He is the one who listens to advice, who assumes he might be missing something. Before a big decision, who have you asked who might tell you no?

Ignoring an insult. The fool's irritation is on his face and in his voice immediately. He cannot let anything pass. The prudent man ignores an insult. He is not a doormat; he simply does not need to answer every slight. The supreme example is Christ: When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly (1 Pet 2:23).

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever speaks the truth gives honest evidence, but a false witness utters deceit. There is one whose rash words are like sword thrusts, but the tongue of the wise brings healing. Truthful lips endure forever, but a lying tongue is but for a moment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever speaks the truth. The setting is a courtroom, but the principle reaches further. A person who is truthful in everyday speech will be an honest witness when it matters. The ESV notes that speaks is literally "breathes out": truth or lies come out of a person as naturally as breath, because they are what is inside.

Sword thrusts. Rash words, spoken without thinking, go in like a blade. Many people carry scars from a sentence said to them decades ago by a parent, a teacher or a spouse, a sentence the speaker has probably forgotten. James says, no human being can tame the tongue, and From the same mouth come blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so (Jas 3:8, 10).

But the tongue can heal. A word of apology, of encouragement, of blessing, can reach a wound that nothing else touches. If you have wounded someone with words, the healing will very likely also have to come through words.

Truthful lips endure forever. Every lie has a short shelf life. It works for a moment, and then it has to be maintained, defended and eventually exposed. The truth does not need maintaining; it simply stays true. Behind every truthful word stands the God whose faithfulness endures forever (Ps 117:2).

verseByVerse.quote: Deceit is in the heart of those who devise evil, but those who plan peace have joy. No ill befalls the righteous, but the wicked are filled with trouble. Lying lips are an abomination to the LORD, but those who act faithfully are his delight. A prudent man conceals knowledge, but the heart of fools proclaims folly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who plan peace. Both the schemer and the peacemaker are making plans. One carries deceit in his heart as he plans, and there is no joy in that. The other plans peace, and joy comes with it. Planning a reconciliation, a kindness, a way to heal a rift, fills the heart in a way plotting never does.

No ill befalls the righteous. Read on its own, this seems plainly untrue. Righteous people get cancer, lose children and are persecuted. But the proverb is saying something deeper. Nothing that befalls the righteous is finally ill for them, because God turns it to good. For those who love God all things work together for good (Rom 8:28). That does not make the loss less real or the grief wrong; death and pain are still enemies. It means they do not have the last word. The same event can be a disaster to a wicked man and a refining to a righteous one.

Lying lips. Abomination and delight again (11:1, 20). God hates lying because he is the God of truth, and lying is the native language of the enemy. Do not lie to one another, seeing that you have put off the old self (Col 3:9). Therefore, having put away falsehood, let each one of you speak the truth with his neighbor, for we are members one of another (Eph 4:25).

That includes the small lies: the excuse for being late, the exaggerated story, the "I'm fine". God delights in those who act faithfully, people whose words and deeds can be relied upon.

A prudent man conceals knowledge. He does not have to show everything he knows. He waits for the right moment, keeps confidences, and does not need to win every conversation. The fool announces whatever is in his head, and what is in his head is folly.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–28 — The Path Where There Is No Death
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Anxiety in a man's heart weighs him down, but a good word makes him glad, and the path of righteousness is life (vv. 24-28).
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter moves from a weighed-down heart to a path on which death itself does not have the last word.

verseByVerse.quote: The hand of the diligent will rule, while the slothful will be put to forced labor. Anxiety in a man's heart weighs him down, but a good word makes him glad.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hand of the diligent. The irony is sharp. The lazy man avoids work to stay free, and ends up doing forced labor under someone else. The diligent man takes on work willingly, and ends up leading. Avoiding effort does not avoid work; it only decides who will be giving the orders.

Anxiety. This is a tender proverb. Anxiety is a weight. It sits on the heart and presses it down, and anyone who has lived with it knows how physical that feels. The proverb does not tell the anxious man to try harder or pull himself together. It says that a good word lifts him.

That has two applications. First, for the anxious: God has spoken a good word to you. Peter tells believers to humble themselves under God's hand, casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you (1 Pet 5:7). The peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus (Phil 4:7).

Second, for everyone else: you can be the good word to someone carrying a weight you cannot see.

And if anxiety has settled in for months, so that good words do not lift it, that is not a failure of faith. Seeking help from a doctor or counsellor, alongside prayer and the company of the church, is a wise use of God's gifts, not a lack of trust.

verseByVerse.quote: One who is righteous is a guide to his neighbor, but the way of the wicked leads them astray. Whoever is slothful will not roast his game, but the diligent man will get precious wealth. In the path of righteousness is life, and in its pathway there is no death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A guide to his neighbor. The righteous person shows others the way, simply by walking it. The ESV notes that the first line may be read, "The righteous chooses his friends carefully". Both readings belong together: the righteous choose friends wisely and help them, while the wicked lead their companions off the road. Do not be deceived: "Bad company ruins good morals" (1 Cor 15:33).

Will not roast his game. The lazy man goes hunting, catches something, and then cannot be bothered to cook it. The effort is wasted at the last step. Unfinished degrees, half-built projects, good intentions never followed through: the sluggard is often not lazy about starting, only about finishing. The ESV notes that the second line may mean, "but diligence is precious wealth". The habit of finishing is itself a treasure.

No death. The chapter ends on one of the book's most hopeful lines: on the path of righteousness there is life, and no death. The Old Testament does not often speak so directly about what lies beyond the grave, but this proverb reaches toward it. Death is not the end of the righteous man's path. The Hebrew of the second line is difficult, and some early translations read it as a contrast, that the other way leads to death; the ESV follows the Hebrew as it stands. Either way, the path of righteousness is the path of life.

Jesus made the promise explicit: if anyone keeps my word, he will never see death (John 8:51). And at the tomb of Lazarus, I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live, and everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die. Do you believe this? (John 11:25-26). No one walks the path of righteousness perfectly; Christ walked it for us, and his righteousness is counted ours (Rom 5:19). On that path, through him, death has lost its sting.

12.theology:
Stability comes from being rooted in God (vv. 3, 12; Ps 1:3). Teachability is essential to wisdom (vv. 1, 15). Righteousness extends even to care for animals (v. 10; Deut 25:4; Jonah 4:11).

Speech wounds or heals (v. 18; Jas 3:8-10); God hates lies and delights in faithfulness (v. 22; Eph 4:25). The prudent absorb insults, as Christ did (v. 16; 1 Pet 2:23). Nothing is finally ill for the righteous (v. 21; Rom 8:28).

A good word lifts anxiety (v. 25; 1 Pet 5:7). The path of righteousness leads beyond death (v. 28; John 11:25-26).
12.examples: Husbands should read verse 4 and ask whether they honour their wives as the crown they are. And somebody you will see today is carrying a weight you cannot see; a sentence of encouragement from you may be exactly what lifts it.

13.title: Hope Deferred Makes the Heart Sick
13.text: <sup>1</sup>A wise son hears his father's instruction, but a scoffer does not listen to rebuke.<sup>2</sup>From the fruit of his mouth a man eats what is good, but the desire of the treacherous is for violence.<sup>3</sup>Whoever guards his mouth preserves his life; he who opens wide his lips comes to ruin.<sup>4</sup>The soul of the sluggard craves and gets nothing, while the soul of the diligent is richly supplied.<sup>5</sup>The righteous hates falsehood, but the wicked brings shame and disgrace.<sup>6</sup>Righteousness guards him whose way is blameless, but sin overthrows the wicked.<sup>7</sup>One pretends to be rich, yet has nothing; another pretends to be poor, yet has great wealth.<sup>8</sup>The ransom of a man's life is his wealth, but a poor man hears no threat.<sup>9</sup>The light of the righteous rejoices, but the lamp of the wicked will be put out.<sup>10</sup>By insolence comes nothing but strife, but with those who take advice is wisdom.<sup>11</sup>Wealth gained hastily will dwindle, but whoever gathers little by little will increase it.<sup>12</sup>Hope deferred makes the heart sick, but a desire fulfilled is a tree of life.<sup>13</sup>Whoever despises the word brings destruction on himself, but he who reveres the commandment will be rewarded.<sup>14</sup>The teaching of the wise is a fountain of life, that one may turn away from the snares of death.<sup>15</sup>Good sense wins favor, but the way of the treacherous is their ruin.<sup>16</sup>Every prudent man acts with knowledge, but a fool flaunts his folly.<sup>17</sup>A wicked messenger falls into trouble, but a faithful envoy brings healing.<sup>18</sup>Poverty and disgrace come to him who ignores instruction, but whoever heeds reproof is honored.<sup>19</sup>A desire fulfilled is sweet to the soul, but to turn away from evil is an abomination to fools.<sup>20</sup>Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise, but the companion of fools will suffer harm.<sup>21</sup>Disaster pursues sinners, but the righteous are rewarded with good.<sup>22</sup>A good man leaves an inheritance to his children's children, but the sinner's wealth is laid up for the righteous.<sup>23</sup>The fallow ground of the poor would yield much food, but it is swept away through injustice.<sup>24</sup>Whoever spares the rod hates his son, but he who loves him is diligent to discipline him.<sup>25</sup>The righteous has enough to satisfy his appetite, but the belly of the wicked suffers want.
13.overview: A wise son listens; guarding the mouth preserves life, and wealth gathered little by little grows (vv. 1-11). Hope deferred makes the heart sick, but a desire fulfilled is a tree of life, and wise teaching is a fountain of life (vv. 12-19). Walking with the wise makes a person wise; injustice sweeps away the harvest of the poor; the loving parent disciplines his child (vv. 20-25).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Guarded Mouth and the Honest Purse
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A son who listens, a guarded mouth, and money gathered patiently: Whoever guards his mouth preserves his life, and whoever gathers little by little will increase it (vv. 1-11).
verseByVerse.theology: Mouth and money are both kept by restraint and patience, and both are ruined by haste.

verseByVerse.quote: A wise son hears his father's instruction, but a scoffer does not listen to rebuke. From the fruit of his mouth a man eats what is good, but the desire of the treacherous is for violence. Whoever guards his mouth preserves his life; he who opens wide his lips comes to ruin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A wise son hears. The chapter opens where the book began, with a son and a father. The scoffer has made up his mind in advance that nothing his father says is worth his attention. Rebuke bounces off him because he has already dismissed the speaker.

The fruit of his mouth. A good man's words produce fruit he himself gets to eat: friendships, trust, peace. The treacherous man's appetite is for something else, violence, and that is what he feeds on.

Whoever guards his mouth. Opens wide his lips pictures a mouth with no gate at all. The man who guards his mouth has a gatekeeper, and the Spirit, whose fruit is self-control (Gal 5:23), keeps that gate. A single unguarded sentence has ended careers, friendships and marriages. James goes further: If anyone thinks he is religious and does not bridle his tongue but deceives his heart, this person's religion is worthless (Jas 1:26).

verseByVerse.quote: The soul of the sluggard craves and gets nothing, while the soul of the diligent is richly supplied. The righteous hates falsehood, but the wicked brings shame and disgrace. Righteousness guards him whose way is blameless, but sin overthrows the wicked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sluggard craves. He is not a man without desires. He craves, often intensely. He wants the house, the qualifications, the fit body, the good marriage. He simply does not do what gets them. Laziness does not kill desire; it only guarantees frustration.

The righteous hates falsehood. The righteous person does not merely avoid lies; he hates them, in himself and in others. The ESV notes that brings shame may be rendered "stench". The wicked man's life gives off a bad smell, and the people around him notice.

Righteousness guards. Righteousness is pictured as a bodyguard, and sin as an enemy that knocks a man flat. A blameless life does not make a person invulnerable, but it removes a great many dangers that sin would have brought with it.

verseByVerse.quote: One pretends to be rich, yet has nothing; another pretends to be poor, yet has great wealth. The ransom of a man's life is his wealth, but a poor man hears no threat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One pretends to be rich. Appearances deceive both ways. One man drives the expensive car and is drowning in debt. Another lives quietly and has saved for decades. The ESV notes the lines may be read, "One makes himself rich", "another makes himself poor". Wealth is not always where it looks.

The deepest form of the proverb is spiritual. The church at Laodicea said, I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing, not realizing that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked (Rev 3:17). And Paul described the apostles as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, yet possessing everything (2 Cor 6:10).

The ransom of a man's life. Wealth is a mixed blessing. It can pay a ransom when a rich man is kidnapped or sued. But it is also why he is a target. The poor man hears no threat; nobody bothers to rob a man with nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: The light of the righteous rejoices, but the lamp of the wicked will be put out. By insolence comes nothing but strife, but with those who take advice is wisdom. Wealth gained hastily will dwindle, but whoever gathers little by little will increase it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The light of the righteous. A righteous life is like a bright light that seems to shine gladly. The wicked man has a lamp, a smaller thing, and it will be put out. In the ancient world a lamp burning in a house meant the family was alive and present; a lamp going out meant the house was empty. The light of the wicked is put out, and the flame of his fire does not shine (Job 18:5).

Insolence. Pride produces only one crop. The proud person will not take advice, will not back down, will not admit fault, so every disagreement becomes a war. James asks, What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you? Is it not this, that your passions are at war within you? (Jas 4:1). Where there is constant conflict, look for pride first, and look for it in the mirror.

Wealth gained hastily. The ESV notes that hastily may be "by fraud". Quick money, whether from a scam, a gamble, an inheritance squandered or a get-rich-quick scheme, tends to disappear as fast as it came. Gathering little by little, through honest work and patient saving, increases it. Whoever hastens to be rich will not go unpunished (28:20).

The same principle holds far beyond money. Character, knowledge, a marriage, a knowledge of Scripture: they are built little by little, and the person who wants them instantly rarely gets them at all.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hope deferred makes the heart sick, but a desire fulfilled is a tree of life, and the teaching of the wise is a fountain of life (vv. 12-19).
verseByVerse.theology: The heart can sicken while it waits, and God's word is what keeps it alive until the desire is met.

verseByVerse.quote: Hope deferred makes the heart sick, but a desire fulfilled is a tree of life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is one of the most honest sentences in the Bible about what waiting does to a person. Hope deferred, hope postponed and postponed again, makes the heart sick. Think of the infertile couple who hoped each month, the single person who hoped for marriage year after year, the parent praying for a child who has walked away, the medical result or the reconciliation that does not come. The heart grows sick. The proverb does not tell such a person to feel differently. It simply says: this is what happens, and God knows it.

The disciples on the road to Emmaus spoke with sick hearts: But we had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel (Luke 24:21). They said it to the risen Jesus himself, walking beside them unrecognised. Their hope had not failed; it had been fulfilled beyond anything they imagined. The psalmist talked to his own heart in the same condition: Why are you cast down, O my soul, Hope in God; for I shall again praise him (Ps 42:5).

And then the second line: a desire fulfilled is a tree of life. When hope finally comes true, it is like the tree of Eden, life-giving and full. The Christian's hope is sometimes deferred for a whole lifetime, and not every earthly desire is granted in this life. The saints of Hebrews 11 all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar (Heb 11:13). But the tree of life stands at the end of the Bible, beside the river, and no hope placed in Christ will be disappointed there. If we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience (Rom 8:25).

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever despises the word brings destruction on himself, but he who reveres the commandment will be rewarded. The teaching of the wise is a fountain of life, that one may turn away from the snares of death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever despises the word. The ESV notes that this may be "a word" and "a commandment", any piece of good instruction. But in the whole Bible the supreme word is God's. The one who despises it destroys himself. God says, this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word (Isa 66:2).

A fountain of life. Wise teaching has a practical purpose: to help a person turn away from the snares of death. Good teaching shows where the traps are before you step in them. Think of the teachers, parents or pastors whose words kept you out of a snare you did not even see at the time.

verseByVerse.quote: Good sense wins favor, but the way of the treacherous is their ruin. Every prudent man acts with knowledge, but a fool flaunts his folly. A wicked messenger falls into trouble, but a faithful envoy brings healing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Good sense wins favor. People trust good sense. The ESV notes that the second line is a probable reading, and that the Hebrew says the way of the treacherous "is rugged" or "is an enduring rut". Either picture works: a rocky road, or a rut worn so deep a person cannot climb out.

Every prudent man acts. He thinks before he acts. The fool flaunts his folly, spreading it out for display like a merchant with his goods.

A wicked messenger falls. A messenger who distorts his message causes disaster. A faithful envoy brings healing, because he delivers the message as it was given. Paul described the ministry of the gospel this way: we are ambassadors for Christ, God making his appeal through us. We implore you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God (2 Cor 5:20). Every Christian who speaks of Christ is an envoy, and the healing comes when the message is told faithfully, without additions or subtractions.

verseByVerse.quote: Poverty and disgrace come to him who ignores instruction, but whoever heeds reproof is honored. A desire fulfilled is sweet to the soul, but to turn away from evil is an abomination to fools.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Poverty and disgrace come. Ignoring instruction has a cost that shows up in two places: the bank account and the reputation. Heeding reproof leads to honour. The irony is that accepting correction feels humiliating at the time, and refusing it feels dignified. In the long run it is the other way round.

Sweet to the soul. The first line echoes verse 12; the second explains why fools never taste that sweetness. They want the fulfilment, but they will not turn away from the evil that blocks it. The fool wants the good life and hates the very idea of giving up what ruins it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Companions shape a life, a good man blesses his grandchildren, and the loving parent disciplines (vv. 20-25).
verseByVerse.theology: A life is shaped by the company it keeps, and it shapes the generations that come after it.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise, but the companion of fools will suffer harm. Disaster pursues sinners, but the righteous are rewarded with good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Walks with the wise. People become like the people they spend time with. Not immediately, but surely. Walk with the wise and you absorb their habits, their way of thinking, their instincts. Walk with fools and you will not merely be influenced; you will suffer harm, because fools bring their consequences on everyone near them.

Psalm 1 opens by describing the slide: Blessed is the man who walks not in the counsel of the wicked, nor stands in the way of sinners, nor sits in the seat of scoffers (Ps 1:1).

A test worth running: are the five people you spend most time with making you wiser? God has given his people one another in the church, so that no one need walk alone.

Disaster pursues sinners. The ESV notes that Disaster may be "Evil". The picture is of something chasing a man. The sinner may outrun his consequences for a while, but they follow him. Moses warned, be sure your sin will find you out (Num 32:23).

verseByVerse.quote: A good man leaves an inheritance to his children's children, but the sinner's wealth is laid up for the righteous. The fallow ground of the poor would yield much food, but it is swept away through injustice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An inheritance. A good man thinks two generations ahead. He leaves an inheritance to his grandchildren. That can be money, and planning well for a family's future is a godly thing to do. But the best inheritance is not financial: a name, a faith, a pattern of prayer and honesty that grandchildren remember. Timothy inherited a faith that dwelt first in his grandmother (2 Tim 1:5).

The sinner, meanwhile, is storing up wealth that will pass out of his hands, often to the very people he despised.

Swept away through injustice. This proverb refuses to blame all poverty on laziness. The poor man's field would yield much food. He has the land and he has worked it. But injustice sweeps his harvest away: unjust taxes, stolen land, corrupt officials, withheld wages. The book that praises diligence is honest that diligence is not always enough in a crooked world. James thunders against rich men whose laborers' wages were kept back by fraud and are crying out against you (Jas 5:4).

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever spares the rod hates his son, but he who loves him is diligent to discipline him. The righteous has enough to satisfy his appetite, but the belly of the wicked suffers want.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever spares the rod. This proverb is often misunderstood, in both directions.

First, the point is love. The parent who never disciplines a child is not being kind; the proverb says he hates his son, because he is leaving him to grow up without the correction he needs. A child who is never told no, never faces consequences, never learns that his actions matter, is being set up for a painful life. The loving parent is diligent to discipline him, and the ESV notes that it may be read, "disciplines him early", before patterns harden.

Second, the rod stands for discipline as a whole: correction, consequences, including physical correction. Whatever form discipline takes, the Bible never licenses cruelty, rage or abuse. The same Scriptures that say discipline your children also say, Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger (Eph 6:4), and Fathers, do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged (Col 3:21). Discipline given in anger serves the parent. Discipline given in love serves the child.

And behind every parent stands the Father who disciplines his children: God is treating you as sons. For what son is there whom his father does not discipline? (Heb 12:7).

And no discipline, however faithful, guarantees the outcome. Parents are responsible for faithfulness, not for their child's heart, which only God can change. And no parent is perfectly faithful: the Father who disciplines also forgives, and Christ's obedience covers failing parents who come to him in confession (1 John 1:9).

Enough. The righteous man does not necessarily have a feast, but he has enough to be satisfied. That is a gift. Paul had learned, in whatever situation I am, to be content (Phil 4:11). The wicked man's belly suffers want, sometimes because he is poor, and often because nothing is ever enough for him.

Does this mean physical punishment today? Many Christians read the rod as a figure for discipline of every kind and hold that physical correction now does more harm than good. Others, including most of the Reformed tradition, take the rod at its word: measured physical correction, alongside instruction, is one God-given means for young children. The proverbs do speak of a real rod. But what Scripture requires of every parent is loving, consistent discipline; whether to use measured physical correction is left to wise parents. Where it is used, it is never given in anger, never to injure or humiliate, always with explanation and restored affection, and parents must also keep the law of the land they live in. Any discipline that frightens or harms a child is abuse, not the rod of Proverbs, and a child or parent caught in it should seek help and safety at once. Faithful Christian parents differ on this question, and neither side should despise the other.

13.theology:
Restraint in speech and patience with money are marks of wisdom (vv. 3, 11). True wealth and poverty are not always as they appear (v. 7; 2 Cor 6:10; Rev 3:17).

God knows the sickness of deferred hope, and the believer's hope, though sometimes deferred for a lifetime, ends at the tree of life (v. 12; Heb 11:13; Rom 8:25). God's word is to be revered (v. 13; Isa 66:2), and gospel messengers bring healing by faithfulness (v. 17; 2 Cor 5:20).

Companions shape character (v. 20; Ps 1:1). Poverty can be caused by injustice as well as laziness (v. 23; Jas 5:4). Loving discipline is essential to parenting, and never licenses harshness (v. 24; Eph 6:4; Heb 12:7).
13.examples: Parents might ask whether they know who their children walk with (v. 20). And everyone might ask what their grandchildren will inherit from them that cannot be spent (v. 22).

14.title: Whoever Oppresses a Poor Man Insults His Maker
14.text: <sup>1</sup>The wisest of women builds her house, but folly with her own hands tears it down.<sup>2</sup>Whoever walks in uprightness fears the LORD, but he who is devious in his ways 14.overview: A wise woman builds her house; fruitful work is messy; the heart knows its own bitterness; a way that seems right may end in death (vv. 1-14). The prudent think before they believe, and generosity to the poor is blessed (vv. 15-24). The fear of the LORD is a fountain of life; oppressing the poor insults their Maker; the righteous find refuge in death, and righteousness exalts a nation (vv. 25-35).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — Houses Built and Torn Down
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A household built or torn down, a messy manger, the private heart, and a road that misleads: The wisest of women builds her house, and a way can seem right and end in death (vv. 1-14).
verseByVerse.theology: Homes and lives are built or torn down by choices made from the inside, often out of sight of everyone else.

verseByVerse.quote: The wisest of women builds her house, but folly with her own hands tears it down. Whoever walks in uprightness fears the LORD, but he who is devious in his ways despises him. By the mouth of a fool comes a rod for his back, but the lips of the wise will preserve them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wisest of women. As Wisdom built her house (9:1), so does a real woman. A house in Proverbs means a household: a family, its atmosphere, its future. A wise woman builds it, day after day, through countless small acts of care, patience, prayer and good sense.

And folly tears it down with her own hands. No enemy is needed. Bitterness, a sharp tongue, contempt, neglect, the refusal to forgive: a person can dismantle her own home brick by brick without ever intending to. The proverb applies equally to husbands. Every day each person adds a brick or pulls one out, and where we have pulled them out, the God who forgives can rebuild (Ps 127:1).

Whoever walks in uprightness. How can anyone tell whether a person fears God? Uprightness is the visible evidence. And the devious man, whatever he says in church, despises God. Crooked conduct is a statement about what someone thinks of the God who sees it.

A rod for his back. The fool's mouth makes the stick he will be beaten with. The ESV notes the line may read, "In the mouth of a fool is a rod of pride": his proud speech is itself the rod. Either way, his words turn on him, while the wise are protected by theirs.

verseByVerse.quote: Where there are no oxen, the manger is clean, but abundant crops come by the strength of the ox.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A farmer who wants a spotless barn can have one: get rid of the oxen. But then there is no ploughing and no harvest.

Anything fruitful is messy. Children bring noise, broken things and sleepless nights. A church full of new believers brings problems a tidy, empty church never has. A growing business has complications a failing one does not. A person who wants a life with no mess must accept a life with no harvest.

Is there a mess in your life you resent, which is really the manger of something God is using to feed you and others?

verseByVerse.quote: A faithful witness does not lie, but a false witness breathes out lies. A scoffer seeks wisdom in vain, but knowledge is easy for a man of understanding. Leave the presence of a fool, for there you do not meet words of knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A false witness. The false witness breathes out lies: they come as easily as breath because falsehood has become his nature.

A scoffer seeks wisdom. He does seek wisdom, and does not find it. Why? Because he seeks it while mocking the very things that would teach him. He wants the benefits of wisdom without bowing to its source. For the man of understanding, who has begun with the fear of the LORD, knowledge comes easily, because he is humble enough to receive it.

Leave the presence of a fool. Sometimes the wise thing is simply to leave. Some conversations produce nothing but folly, and staying in them only lets it rub off.

verseByVerse.quote: The wisdom of the prudent is to discern his way, but the folly of fools is deceiving. Fools mock at the guilt offering, but the upright enjoy acceptance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Discerning his way. The prudent man's wisdom is practical: he knows where he is going and why. The fool's folly is deceiving, and chiefly it deceives the fool himself. He does not merely lie to others; he believes his own story about where his road leads.

The guilt offering. It was the sacrifice by which an Israelite acknowledged wrongdoing and made it right. Fools find the idea laughable. The ESV notes that the second line is literally "but among the upright is acceptance": among people who take guilt seriously, there is reconciliation, with God and with each other.

Modern people mock guilt in their own ways, calling it repression or old-fashioned religion. But the person who cannot take his own guilt seriously can never know the joy of having it taken away. The whole Old Testament sacrificial system pointed to the final guilt offering, Christ himself, the Servant of whom Isaiah said, when his soul makes an offering for guilt, he shall see his offspring (Isaiah 53:10). In him, who bore our guilt and obeyed in our place, the upright find their acceptance.

verseByVerse.quote: The heart knows its own bitterness, and no stranger shares its joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is a lonely sentence, and a true one. Every human heart has depths no one else can reach. Friends can sit with you, and should, weep with those who weep (Rom 12:15). But there is a place inside each person where he is alone. Who knows a person's thoughts except the spirit of that person, which is in him? (1 Cor 2:11).

It should make us slow to say "I know exactly how you feel" to a grieving person.

And it points to the one who does. The LORD looks on the heart (1 Sam 16:7). There is no bitterness so private that God does not see it, and no joy so personal that he does not share it. And Christ, who took on a human heart, is a high priest who is not unable to sympathize with our weaknesses (Heb 4:15). The place where no stranger can come is exactly where he comes.

verseByVerse.quote: The house of the wicked will be destroyed, but the tent of the upright will flourish. There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
House and tent. The wicked have a house, solid and impressive. The upright have a tent, flimsy and temporary. And yet the house is destroyed and the tent flourishes. What lasts is not determined by how strong it looks, but by who lives in it and whom they serve.

There is a way. The road that leads to death does not look like it. It seems right. It feels reasonable, even good.

The ESV notes that the Hebrew says "ways of death", plural. There are many such roads: the respectable career that pushes God to the edge, the religion of good deeds that never needs a Saviour, the relationship everyone says is fine. Jesus said, what is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God (Luke 16:15).

So feelings cannot be the final judge of a way. The only safe test of a road is God's word, not how it seems.
verseByVerse.note: Repeated word for word in 16:25.

verseByVerse.quote: Even in laughter the heart may ache, and the end of joy may be grief. The backslider in heart will be filled with the fruit of his ways, and a good man will be filled with the fruit of his ways.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even in laughter. Behind many laughing faces is an aching heart. The life of the party may be the loneliest person in the room. The proverb is a call to look past appearances, and to be gentle. It is also honest about life in a fallen world: every earthly joy has an end, and many end in grief; even the happiest marriage on earth ends one day in a parting.

Jesus said, Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted (Matt 5:4). The proverb says earthly joy may end in grief. The gospel promises that for believers, grief ends in joy.

The backslider in heart. The same phrase is used of both men: each is filled with the fruit of his ways. Everyone eats what he grows.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–24 — The Simple, the Prudent and the Poor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The simple believes everything; the poor are avoided, yet blessed is he who is generous to the poor (vv. 15-24).
verseByVerse.theology: The prudent person tests what he hears, does not follow the crowd in despising the poor, and works rather than talks.

verseByVerse.quote: The simple believes everything, but the prudent gives thought to his steps. One who is wise is cautious and turns away from evil, but a fool is reckless and careless. A man of quick temper acts foolishly, and a man of evil devices is hated. The simple inherit folly, but the prudent are crowned with knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The simple believes everything. This proverb speaks straight to an age of viral rumour. The simple believe every forwarded message, every health scare, every conspiracy, every flattering salesman. The prudent person gives thought. He checks, weighs, waits.

The same applies to spiritual claims. Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God (1 John 4:1). The Bereans were praised because they received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so (Acts 17:11). They even tested what an apostle told them.

Cautious. The ESV notes that is cautious may be "fears", meaning fears the LORD. The wise man is careful because he takes God and consequences seriously. The fool is reckless and careless, and often proud of it, calling his recklessness courage.

Quick temper. Verse 17 names two kinds of trouble-maker: the hot-headed man who blows up, and the cold schemer who plots. Both damage everyone around them.

The simple inherit folly. The simple person does not need to work to become a fool; he inherits folly by drifting. Knowledge is a crown, and it is never had by drifting.

verseByVerse.quote: The evil bow down before the good, the wicked at the gates of the righteous. The poor is disliked even by his neighbor, but the rich has many friends. Whoever despises his neighbor is a sinner, but blessed is he who is generous to the poor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The evil bow down. For now, the wicked often seem to be in charge. The proverb looks to the end, when the order is reversed and evil bows before good. The last day will show it fully.

The poor is disliked. The poor man is avoided even by his neighbours, because he may ask for something. The rich man is surrounded by friends, many of whom are friends of his money. Proverbs shows it so that we recognise it in ourselves.

Whoever despises his neighbor. Despising a neighbour, including the poor neighbour everyone avoids, is sin. James rebuked a church that gave the rich visitor a good seat and told the poor man, You stand over there, and asked, have you not then made distinctions among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts? (Jas 2:3-4). The blessing is on the one who is generous to the poor.

verseByVerse.quote: Do they not go astray who devise evil? Those who devise good meet steadfast love and faithfulness. In all toil there is profit, but mere talk tends only to poverty. The crown of the wise is their wealth, but the folly of fools brings folly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Devise good. Both kinds of people devise, make plans. Those who plan evil go astray. Those who plan good meet steadfast love and faithfulness, the two great covenant words from 3:3. The ESV notes that meet may be "show". Both are true: the one who plans good both receives and gives God's loyal love.

Mere talk. Every workplace and every church knows the person who has endless ideas and opinions and does nothing. All toil, even the dull and unnoticed kind, produces something.

The crown of the wise. For the wise, wealth can be a crown, an honour that they use well. For fools, whatever they have only produces more foolishness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–35 — The Fear of the LORD Is a Fountain of Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The fear of the LORD is a fountain of life; Whoever oppresses a poor man insults his Maker, and Righteousness exalts a nation (vv. 25-35).
verseByVerse.theology: Reverence for God reaches into a person's temper, his view of the poor, his death, and the life of his nation.

verseByVerse.quote: A truthful witness saves lives, but one who breathes out lies is deceitful. In the fear of the LORD one has strong confidence, and his children will have a refuge. The fear of the LORD is a fountain of life, that one may turn away from the snares of death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A truthful witness saves lives. In a courtroom one honest witness can save an innocent man. A lie in the wrong place can destroy a person; the truth told at cost can rescue one.

Strong confidence. Reverence for God produces strong confidence. The person who fears God fears nothing else in the same way. And the benefit reaches his children. A parent's fear of the LORD becomes a refuge for the next generation: a home where God is honoured, a model of faith, prayers offered for them for decades. It is a refuge, not a guarantee: children still make their own choices, and a parent's faithfulness is never wasted, even when a child wanders.

A fountain of life. This is nearly identical to 13:14, with the fear of the LORD in place of the teaching of the wise. The two belong together: wise teaching is only a fountain because it flows from reverence for God.

verseByVerse.quote: In a multitude of people is the glory of a king, but without people a prince is ruined. Whoever is slow to anger has great understanding, but he who has a hasty temper exalts folly. A tranquil heart gives life to the flesh, but envy makes the bones rot.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A multitude of people. A king's greatness is measured by his people, not merely by his palace. That is a word for anyone who leads: your glory is the flourishing of the people entrusted to you. And the King of kings will be glorified by a people no one can number.

Slow to anger. This is how God describes himself: a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger (Exod 34:6). The person who is slow to anger reflects God, and shows great understanding, because he takes time to see the whole situation. The hot-tempered man exalts folly. Patience is the Spirit's fruit (Gal 5:22), grown in those who have first known God's patience with them.

A tranquil heart. Body and soul are closely bound. A tranquil heart, at peace with God and content, gives life to the flesh; the ESV notes it may be "healing". Envy, or "jealousy", makes the bones rot. It eats a person from inside. The envious man thinks he is damaging the reputation of the one he envies. He is rotting his own bones. Where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there will be disorder and every vile practice (Jas 3:16).

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever oppresses a poor man insults his Maker, but he who is generous to the needy honors him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why does oppressing a poor man "insult his Maker"? Because the poor man was made by God, in God's image: So God created man in his own image (Gen 1:27). To crush him is to show contempt for the one whose image he bears. The same truth appears in 17:5, Whoever mocks the poor insults his Maker.

Generosity to the needy honors God. Every act of kindness to a poor person is an act of worship. Whoever is generous to the poor lends to the LORD (19:17).

Jesus went further, identifying himself with his needy brothers (many think he means his disciples, others the needy in general; either way the point about him stands). As you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me (Matt 25:40). And John will not let anyone separate love for God from love for people: he who does not love his brother whom he has seen cannot love God whom he has not seen (1 John 4:20).

How we treat the cleaner, the refugee or the employee who cannot complain is how we treat God. And the open hand has its ground in grace: though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor (2 Cor 8:9).

verseByVerse.quote: The wicked is overthrown through his evildoing, but the righteous finds refuge in his death. Wisdom rests in the heart of a man of understanding, but it makes itself known even in the midst of fools.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wicked is overthrown. Death, the thing every human being dreads, becomes for the righteous a place of refuge. Death is still an enemy, the last one Christ will destroy (1 Cor 15:26), and believers grieve it; but the righteous man is not destroyed by death. He is sheltered in it. The Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint) reads in his integrity instead of in his death, from very similar Hebrew letters, and some modern versions follow it; the ESV keeps the Hebrew.

The New Testament fills in the picture. For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain (Phil 1:21). We would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord (2 Cor 5:8). The wicked is overthrown by his own evil; the believer walks through death into the arms of God.

Wisdom rests. Wisdom is at home, at rest, in the heart of a wise man. The ESV notes the line may mean that wisdom "rests quietly" there. It does not need to show off. And yet even among fools, wisdom makes itself known. A truly wise person cannot be completely hidden, even in a foolish crowd.

verseByVerse.quote: Righteousness exalts a nation, but sin is a reproach to any people. A servant who deals wisely has the king's favor, but his wrath falls on one who acts shamefully.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Righteousness exalts a nation. Here Proverbs speaks to nations. A nation is lifted up not by military power or economic strength alone, but by righteousness: justice in its courts, honesty in its business, care for its weakest. And sin is a reproach to any people, any nation, whatever its size or history. Blessed is the nation whose God is the LORD (Ps 33:12).

That gives Christians a reason to care about the moral life of their nation, to pray for it and to live righteously in it, not in order to make it the kingdom of God, but because righteousness is good for every people.

A servant who deals wisely. A servant who acts wisely wins his king's favour; the one who acts shamefully faces his anger. Every Christian serves a King who has already shown him favour, and serves best as one secure in it.

14.theology:
Homes are built or destroyed by the character of those in them (v. 1). Human perception is unreliable: a way can seem right and lead to death (v. 12; 16:25), so every claim must be tested (v. 15; 1 John 4:1). The heart has depths only God fully knows (v. 10; 1 Sam 16:7; Heb 4:15).

Every human being bears God's image, so treatment of the poor is treatment of God (v. 31; Gen 1:27; Matt 25:40). The fear of the LORD is a fountain of life (v. 27) and a refuge for the next generation (v. 26). The righteous have hope in death (v. 32; Phil 1:21). Righteousness exalts nations (v. 34).
14.examples: Before you forward the next alarming message, give it the thought verse 15 asks for. And ask who the person is that you tend to avoid because he might need something (v. 20); he bears his Maker's image.

15.overview: A soft answer turns away wrath; the eyes of the LORD are everywhere, and he accepts the prayer of the upright (vv. 1-12). A glad heart is a continual feast; a little with the fear of the LORD, and a dinner of herbs with love, are better than riches with trouble; a word in season is good (vv. 13-23). The LORD tears down the proud and protects the widow; the fear of the LORD is instruction in wisdom, and humility comes before honour (vv. 24-33).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Tongue and the Eyes of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A soft answer turns away wrath; the LORD sees every place and every heart, and the prayer of the upright is acceptable to him (vv. 1-12).
verseByVerse.theology: The LORD who sees everything, down to the hidden heart, hears every word and every prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger. The tongue of the wise commends knowledge, but the mouths of fools pour out folly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A soft answer. Someone comes at you angry: a customer, a teenager, a spouse, a colleague. You have a choice. Answer in kind, and the anger doubles. Answer softly, and very often it drains away.

A soft answer is not a weak answer. It may say something hard. It simply refuses to add heat. It lowers the voice, acknowledges the other person's frustration, and does not reach for the sharpest word available. A harsh word is petrol on a small fire.

Peter tells Christians who are challenged about their faith to answer with gentleness and respect (1 Pet 3:15). Gentleness is the Spirit's fruit (Gal 5:23): when a sharp reply rises, ask for it, lower your voice and see what happens.

Commends knowledge. The wise man makes knowledge attractive; people want to hear more. The fool pours out folly, like water from an overturned jar, with no control and no end.

verseByVerse.quote: The eyes of the LORD are in every place, keeping watch on the evil and the good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is nowhere God does not see: not the locked office, the hotel room on a business trip, the browser in private mode, or the thought no one will ever hear. Where shall I go from your Spirit? Or where shall I flee from your presence? (Ps 139:7).

The verse is a warning and a comfort at once. For the evil, it means nothing is hidden and nothing will be forgotten. No creature is hidden from his sight (Heb 4:13). For the good, it means no act of faithfulness goes unnoticed: the prayer said alone, the kindness nobody thanked you for, the temptation resisted with no one watching. God was watching.

How would today change if you lived it knowing, really knowing, that the LORD's eyes are on this room?

verseByVerse.quote: A gentle tongue is a tree of life, but perverseness in it breaks the spirit. A fool despises his father's instruction, but whoever heeds reproof is prudent. In the house of the righteous there is much treasure, but trouble befalls the income of the wicked. The lips of the wise spread knowledge; not so the hearts of fools.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A gentle tongue. The ESV notes it may be a "healing" tongue; it gives life to the people around it. And a twisted tongue breaks the spirit. Some people have been broken inside by years of harsh, mocking or manipulative words from someone close to them.

His father's instruction. The fool's contempt starts at home. The prudent man, whatever his age, heeds reproof.

Much treasure. The righteous man's house holds treasure, not necessarily money, but everything that makes a home rich: peace, love, faith, stability. The wicked man has income, perhaps a large one, and trouble comes with it: legal battles, family conflict, anxiety, the constant need for more.

Spread knowledge. Wise people scatter knowledge like seed. The ESV notes the second line may be read, "the hearts of fools are not steadfast". A fool's heart is unstable, so his words are too.

verseByVerse.quote: The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination to the LORD, but the prayer of the upright is acceptable to him. The way of the wicked is an abomination to the LORD, but he loves him who pursues righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sacrifice of the wicked. A wicked man comes to worship and brings a costly sacrifice. God calls it an abomination. An upright man simply prays, with nothing in his hands, and God finds it acceptable. God is not impressed by religious activity that is cut off from a changed life. He said through Isaiah, What to me is the multitude of your sacrifices? (Isa 1:11), and through Samuel, Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice (1 Sam 15:22).

That is a warning for anyone who uses church attendance, giving or religious duty as a cover for a life he has no intention of changing. And it is an encouragement to the person who feels he has nothing to offer God but a simple prayer. The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise (Ps 51:17). The prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working (Jas 5:16). And the upright are not heard because their prayers are good enough. The New Testament says believers draw near to God by the blood of Jesus (Hebrews 10:19), the one sacrifice that never needs repeating.

Pursues righteousness. From worship the proverb turns to the whole way of life. Notice the verb: he loves the one who pursues righteousness. Not the one who has fully arrived, but the one who is chasing it. His love comes first, and the pursuit is its fruit, not its price (1 John 4:19).

verseByVerse.quote: There is severe discipline for him who forsakes the way; whoever hates reproof will die. Sheol and Abaddon lie open before the LORD; how much more the hearts of the children of man! A scoffer does not like to be reproved; he will not go to the wise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is severe discipline. A person who leaves God's way does not escape discipline; the discipline gets severe. God corrects gently at first, and more firmly if gentle correction is ignored. And a person who hates reproof altogether cuts himself off from the correction that could save him. The end is death.

Sheol and Abaddon. Sheol is the realm of the dead; Abaddon is a word for destruction, the deepest place of ruin. Even these lie open before the LORD, like a book on a table. If God sees the depths of death, how much more does he see the human heart?

No motive is hidden from him, no secret resentment, no self-deception. That is terrifying for anyone trying to hide from God. It is freeing for anyone who has stopped trying. There is no point pretending to the one who already knows everything, and no need to, because he loved us knowing it.

A scoffer. The scoffer avoids the very people who could help him. He will not seek out a wise friend, a pastor, a counsellor, because they might tell him something he does not want to hear. So he surrounds himself with people who agree with him, and stays a scoffer.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–23 — Better a Dinner of Herbs
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A glad heart, a mind well fed, a quiet temper and a word in season: Better is a dinner of herbs where love is than a fattened ox and hatred with it (vv. 13-23).
verseByVerse.theology: What makes a table or a life rich is not what is on it, but reverence for God and love around it.

verseByVerse.quote: A glad heart makes a cheerful face, but by sorrow of heart the spirit is crushed. The heart of him who has understanding seeks knowledge, but the mouths of fools feed on folly. All the days of the afflicted are evil, but the cheerful of heart has a continual feast.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A glad heart. The face shows the heart. Proverbs does not pretend the believer is never crushed. A joyful heart is good medicine, but a crushed spirit dries up the bones (17:22).

Feed on folly. Everyone is hungry for something. The man of understanding goes looking for knowledge. The fool "feeds on folly": gossip, trivia, scandal, entertainment that empties the mind. What a person feeds on, he becomes.

A continual feast. Two people can live through similar circumstances very differently. The difference is not always what happens to them, but what is in their hearts. A cheerful heart is not the same as denial. It is a heart that has found something to rejoice in that circumstances cannot take. Rejoice in the Lord always; again I will say, rejoice (Phil 4:4). Paul wrote that from prison.

But this is no rebuke to a believer living with depression. Sorrow of heart that crushes the spirit (v. 13) is named here as a real affliction, not a sin, and The LORD is near to the brokenhearted (Psalm 34:18).

verseByVerse.quote: Better is a little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure and trouble with it. Better is a dinner of herbs where love is than a fattened ox and hatred with it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Better is a little. A small income with the fear of the LORD beats a fortune with trouble attached. The trouble may be anxiety, family fights, a guilty conscience, the constant fear of losing it. Keep your life free from love of money, and be content with what you have, for he has said, "I will never leave you nor forsake you." (Heb 13:5).

A dinner of herbs. On one table there is a bowl of vegetables and a family that loves each other. On the other is a roast from the fattened ox, the most expensive meal there was, eaten in cold silence or open hostility. Which table would you rather sit at?

It is a word to anyone chasing a bigger house, a better car or a more impressive holiday at the cost of the relationships inside the home. The children will not remember what was on the table. They will remember whether there was love around it.

verseByVerse.quote: A hot-tempered man stirs up strife, but he who is slow to anger quiets contention. The way of a sluggard is like a hedge of thorns, but the path of the upright is a level highway.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A hot-tempered man. Some people bring conflict into every room; others bring calm. The hot-tempered man does not merely react to strife; he "stirs it up". The person slow to anger actively quiets it. That reflects God, who is slow to anger (Exod 34:6).

A hedge of thorns. The sluggard's road is blocked with thorns. Everything is hard, everything is an obstacle, every task has a reason it cannot be done today. Part of this is excuse: the thorns are in his imagination. Part of it is real: tasks put off grow into tangles. The upright person's path is a level highway, not because life is easy, but because he deals with things as they come, and so they do not grow into thickets.

verseByVerse.quote: A wise son makes a glad father, but a foolish man despises his mother. Folly is a joy to him who lacks sense, but a man of understanding walks straight ahead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Despises his mother. The first line repeats 10:1; the second has sharpened: in chapter 10 a foolish son was a sorrow to his mother; here a foolish man despises her. It is one thing to cause a mother grief; it is worse to hold her in contempt. And the fool here is a grown man, not a boy, still treating the woman who raised him with scorn.

Folly is a joy. The man of understanding does not get distracted by what is merely entertaining; he walks straight ahead, keeping to the road.

verseByVerse.quote: Without counsel plans fail, but with many advisers they succeed. To make an apt answer is a joy to a man, and a word in season, how good it is!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without counsel plans fail. A plan made alone is a plan made with one set of blind spots. Many advisers bring many angles. The person who is too proud to ask for advice will watch his plans fail, and the person who seeks it will often find problems before they happen (compare 11:14).

A word in season. Almost everyone has known the right word at the right moment: a friend who knew exactly what to say at the funeral, or a teacher's sentence that changed a direction. The same words at the wrong time do nothing, or harm.

Isaiah's Servant, whom the New Testament finds in Jesus, says, The Lord GOD has given me the tongue of those who are taught, that I may know how to sustain with a word him who is weary (Isa 50:4). Jesus spoke exactly that word: Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matthew 11:28). The word in season comes from a person who has first been listening, to God and to the one in front of him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–33 — The Path That Leads Upward
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The path of life leads upward; the LORD defends the widow and hears the righteous, and humility comes before honor (vv. 24-33).
verseByVerse.theology: The road of wisdom climbs, and the way up is always by the way down: humility before honour.

verseByVerse.quote: The path of life leads upward for the prudent, that he may turn away from Sheol beneath. The LORD tears down the house of the proud but maintains the widow's boundaries.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The path of life. The path of the wise climbs, toward life and toward God. The other direction goes down to Sheol. Paul puts it this way: If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is (Col 3:1).

The widow's boundaries. In the ancient world a widow was among the most vulnerable people there were. A powerful neighbour could simply move her boundary stones, a few feet each year, and take her land. She had no husband to defend her. But she has the LORD. He maintains her boundaries himself. He executes justice for the fatherless and the widow (Deut 10:18). And the proud man's house, built partly on what he took, God tears down.

Mary sang the same reversal: he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate (Luke 1:52). That is both a comfort to the vulnerable and a summons to everyone who has power over them.

verseByVerse.quote: The thoughts of the wicked are an abomination to the LORD, but gracious words are pure. Whoever is greedy for unjust gain troubles his own household, but he who hates bribes will live. The heart of the righteous ponders how to answer, but the mouth of the wicked pours out evil things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God judges not only deeds but thoughts. The schemes of the wicked are an abomination to him before they are ever carried out. And gracious words are pure in his sight: clean, like refined metal.

Unjust gain. The greedy man thinks he is providing for his family. He is actually troubling it: bringing stress, danger, shame and eventually ruin into his home. The man who hates bribes, who will not take the under-the-table payment or the corrupt deal, will live. Integrity at work protects the family at home.

Ponders how to answer. The wicked person's mouth pours out, again the image of an overturned jar. In an age of instant replies, the discipline of pausing to consider how to answer is rare and precious.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD is far from the wicked, but he hears the prayer of the righteous. The light of the eyes rejoices the heart, and good news refreshes the bones.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Far from the wicked. God is everywhere (v. 3), and yet he is far from the wicked. The distance is not in space but in relationship. He is near to hear the righteous. The difference is not that the righteous are sinless, but that they have turned toward him. A heart that holds on to its wickedness and prays anyway is praying into a wall. A heart that turns to God in repentance finds him close enough to hear a whisper. Your Father who sees in secret will reward you (Matt 6:6).

Good news. The light of the eyes may be the bright face of a friend, or simply the joy of seeing clearly. And good news refreshes the bones; the ESV notes that the Hebrew is "makes fat", the ancient picture of health and strength.

And there is no better news than the gospel. How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news (Isa 52:7). The angel said to the shepherds, Fear not, for behold, I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people (Luke 2:10). That is the news that refreshes the bones.

verseByVerse.quote: The ear that listens to life-giving reproof will dwell among the wise. Whoever ignores instruction despises himself, but he who listens to reproof gains intelligence. The fear of the LORD is instruction in wisdom, and humility comes before honor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Life-giving reproof. That is not how reproof usually feels. But the person whose ear accepts correction ends up living among the wise, one of them.

Despises himself. A person who ignores instruction thinks he is defending himself. The proverb says he despises himself: he is treating his own life as worthless by refusing what would improve it. Real self-respect listens.

Humility before honor. The fear of the LORD is not just the beginning of wisdom; it is the whole school. And humility comes before honor, always in that order. The way up is down.

No one showed this more than Christ. He humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross. Therefore God has highly exalted him (Phil 2:8-9). That obedience is counted to all who trust him (Rom 5:19), and the same path is open to everyone who follows him: Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God so that at the proper time he may exalt you (1 Pet 5:6).

15.theology:
God sees everything, including the hidden heart (vv. 3, 11; Ps 139:7-8; Heb 4:13). Worship is acceptable only from a life turned toward God; simple prayer from the upright pleases him more than costly sacrifice from the wicked (vv. 8-9, 29; 1 Sam 15:22; Ps 51:17).

Speech can defuse anger, give life or crush the spirit (vv. 1, 4, 23). Contentment and love are better than wealth (vv. 16-17; Heb 13:5). God defends the vulnerable against the proud (v. 25; Deut 10:18; Luke 1:52).

The good news refreshes the whole person (v. 30; Isa 52:7). Humility precedes honour, supremely in Christ (v. 33; Phil 2:8-9; 1 Pet 5:6).
15.examples: Ask what your mind has been feeding on this week (v. 14). Notice the person at work or church who quietly settles strife, and thank God for him. And the next time a sharp reply rises, try the soft answer and see what happens to the anger in the room.

16.title: The Heart of Man Plans His Way
16.text: <sup>1</sup>The plans of the heart belong to man, but the answer of the tongue is from the LORD.<sup>2</sup>All the ways of a man are pure in his own eyes, but the LORD weighs the spirit.<sup>3</sup>Commit your work to the LORD, and your plans will be established.<sup>4</sup>The LORD has made everything for its purpose, even the wicked for the day of trouble.<sup>5</sup>Everyone who is arrogant in heart is an abomination to the LORD; be assured, he will not go unpunished.<sup>6</sup>By steadfast love and faithfulness iniquity is atoned for, and by the fear of the LORD one turns away from evil.<sup>7</sup>When a man's ways please the LORD, he makes even his enemies to be at peace with him.<sup>8</sup>Better is a little with righteousness than great revenues with injustice.<sup>9</sup>The heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps.<sup>10</sup>An oracle is on the lips of a king; his mouth does not sin in judgment.<sup>11</sup>A just balance and scales are the LORD's; all the weights in the bag are his work.<sup>12</sup>It is an abomination to kings to do evil, for the throne is established by righteousness.<sup>13</sup>Righteous lips are the delight of a king, and he loves him who speaks what is right.<sup>14</sup>A king's wrath is a messenger of death, and a wise man will appease it.<sup>15</sup>In the light of a king's face there is life, and his favor is like the clouds that bring the spring rain.<sup>16</sup>How much better to get wisdom than gold! To get understanding is to be chosen rather than silver.<sup>17</sup>The highway of the upright turns aside from evil; whoever guards his way preserves his life.<sup>18</sup>Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall.<sup>19</sup>It is better to be of a lowly spirit with the poor than to divide the spoil with the proud.<sup>20</sup>Whoever gives thought to the word will discover good, and blessed is he who trusts in the LORD.<sup>21</sup>The wise of heart is called discerning, and sweetness of speech increases persuasiveness.<sup>22</sup>Good sense is a fountain of life to him who has it, but the instruction of fools is folly.<sup>23</sup>The heart of the wise makes his speech judicious and adds persuasiveness to his lips.<sup>24</sup>Gracious words are like a honeycomb, sweetness to the soul and health to the body.<sup>25</sup>There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death.<sup>26</sup>A worker's appetite works for him; his mouth urges him on.<sup>27</sup>A worthless man plots evil, and his speech is like a scorching fire.<sup>28</sup>A dishonest man spreads strife, and a whisperer separates close friends.<sup>29</sup>A man of violence entices his neighbor and leads him in a way that is not good.<sup>30</sup>Whoever winks his eyes plans dishonest things; he who purses his lips brings evil to pass.<sup>31</sup>Gray hair is a crown of glory; it is gained in a righteous life.<sup>32</sup>Whoever is slow to anger is better than the mighty, and he who rules his spirit than he who takes a city.<sup>33</sup>The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD.
16.overview: People plan, but the LORD weighs motives, establishes the plans committed to him and directs the steps; iniquity is atoned for by steadfast love and faithfulness (vv. 1-9). The ideal king judges rightly and his favour is life (vv. 10-15). Wisdom is better than gold, pride goes before a fall, and gracious words are like honey (vv. 16-24). The whisperer separates friends, self-control is better than conquest, and every decision of the lot is from the LORD (vv. 25-33).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Man Plans, the LORD Establishes
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nine sayings on our plans and the LORD's purpose: The heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps (vv. 1-9).
verseByVerse.theology: Human planning is real and responsible, but it always happens inside the purpose of a sovereign God.

verseByVerse.quote: The plans of the heart belong to man, but the answer of the tongue is from the LORD. All the ways of a man are pure in his own eyes, but the LORD weighs the spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The plans of the heart. The first nine verses are one of the Bible's richest meditations on how human choice and God's sovereignty fit together. A man plans. He prepares what he will say. But what actually comes out when the moment arrives, the answer of the tongue, is in God's hands.

Anyone who has prepared for a hard conversation and said something quite different knows this. Jesus gave his disciples a promise built on it: do not be anxious how you are to speak or what you are to say, for what you are to say will be given to you in that hour (Matt 10:19).

This does not make planning pointless. The proverb assumes people plan, and later verses commend it. It makes planning humble. Prepare, and then pray.

The LORD weighs the spirit. Nearly everyone thinks his own motives are good; we give ourselves the benefit of every doubt. But the LORD weighs the spirit, and the ESV notes this may be "spirits", every one of them. He puts motives on the scale, and the reading is often different from ours.

Paul knew this. For I am not aware of anything against myself, but I am not thereby acquitted. It is the Lord who judges me (1 Cor 4:4). A clear conscience is good, but it is not the final verdict. That is a reason for humility about ourselves, and for leaving other people's motives to God.
