verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–19 — The Seeing Eye and the Mouth Full of Gravel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD who made eye and ear watches the market and the mouth: honest dealing, wise counsel, and the babbler to avoid.
verseByVerse.theology: The God who made eyes and ears sees the haggler's lie and the cheat's sweet bread turning to gravel.

verseByVerse.quote: The hearing ear and the seeing eye, the LORD has made them both. Love not sleep, lest you come to poverty; open your eyes, and you will have plenty of bread.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hearing ear. It is a simple and wonderful statement. Every eye that sees and every ear that hears was made by God. That is a reason for gratitude: sight and hearing are gifts, not rights. And it is a reason for sober thought. The God who made the eye sees; the God who made the ear hears. And he intends the ears and eyes he made to be used for what he made them for. When Moses complained that he could not speak, the LORD answered, Who has made man's mouth? Who makes him mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Is it not I, the LORD? (Exod 4:11).

Love not sleep. Sleep is good; loving it is dangerous. The sleepy man is poor. Open your eyes, get up, face the day, and there will be bread. The eyes God made are for opening.

verseByVerse.quote: "Bad, bad," says the buyer, but when he goes away, then he boasts. There is gold and abundance of costly stones, but the lips of knowledge are a precious jewel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Bad, bad," says the buyer. A scene from any market. The buyer picks up the item and frowns. "Poor quality. Far too expensive. I could get it cheaper elsewhere." The seller lowers the price. And the buyer walks away and tells his friends what a bargain he got.

The proverb does not condemn bargaining. It exposes the lie. Many people who would never tell an outright lie think nothing of misrepresenting a car they are selling or running down a house they want to buy. The God who hates unequal weights (v. 10) also hears the buyer's "Bad, bad".

The lips of knowledge. Gold and gems are plentiful enough in the market. What is truly rare is a mouth that speaks knowledge.

verseByVerse.quote: Take a man's garment when he has put up security for a stranger, and hold it in pledge when he puts up security for foreigners. Bread gained by deceit is sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth will be full of gravel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take a man's garment. A piece of hard-headed financial advice, repeated at 27:13. If a man is foolish enough to guarantee a stranger's debts, do not lend to him without collateral. Take his cloak as security. The ESV notes that the last phrase may be "for an adulteress". Either way, a man with such poor judgment is a bad risk.

Bread gained by deceit. Imagine biting into a loaf of fresh bread and finding your mouth full of grit and stones. That is what dishonest gain becomes. At first it is sweet: the money from the fraud, the promotion won by lying, the grade from cheating. Afterward, it turns to gravel: guilt, exposure, broken trust, a conscience that grinds.

Moses chose rather to be mistreated with the people of God than to enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin (Heb 11:25). Sin's pleasure is real, but it is fleeting, and it leaves gravel.

verseByVerse.quote: Plans are established by counsel; by wise guidance wage war. Whoever goes about slandering reveals secrets; therefore do not associate with a simple babbler.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Plans are established by counsel. No sensible king goes to war on a whim, and the same is true of the battles of ordinary life: starting a business, confronting a problem, making a big move. Plans are established by counsel (compare 24:6).

A simple babbler. The first line is from 11:13. The second draws the practical conclusion: do not keep company with a person who cannot keep his mouth shut. The ESV notes that the Hebrew is "with one who is simple in his lips". If he is telling you other people's secrets, he is telling other people yours.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Honour for parents and patience over an inheritance; no revenge, but waiting for the LORD (v. 22); steps directed by God and vows made with thought; and the blows that cleanse the heart.
verseByVerse.theology: Leave vengeance and direction to God, and let him search the heart with the lamp he has put inside it.

verseByVerse.quote: If one curses his father or his mother, his lamp will be put out in utter darkness. An inheritance gained hastily in the beginning will not be blessed in the end.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If one curses. Under the law, cursing a parent was a capital crime: Whoever curses his father or his mother shall be put to death (Exod 21:17). God takes the honour of parents that seriously. The proverb uses the image of a lamp going out: the life of the one who curses his parents ends in darkness.

An inheritance gained hastily. Think of the prodigal son demanding his inheritance before his father was dead. Wealth grabbed early, before it is rightly due, or wealth acquired too quickly, rarely brings blessing. What comes fast often goes fast, and brings ruin with it.

The death penalty for cursing parents ended with Israel’s civil law, but the duty to honour them stands (Eph 6:2). Honouring does not mean obeying sin or tolerating abuse.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not say, "I will repay evil"; wait for the LORD, and he will deliver you. Unequal weights are an abomination to the LORD, and false scales are not good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wait for the LORD. When someone wrongs us, the instinct is immediate: I will get him back. The proverb forbids even saying it. Instead: wait for the LORD. That is not passivity. It is trust that God sees the wrong, cares about justice, and will act. And it is freedom: you do not have to carry the weight of evening the score.

Paul quotes the principle in Romans: Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, "Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord." (Rom 12:19). Is there a wrong you have been planning to repay? Hand it over to the God who has forgiven you, and ask his Spirit for the patience to wait.

False scales. The repetition of verse 10, placed right after the call not to take revenge, may be deliberate. Revenge is a kind of false scale: we weigh the other person's offence heavily and our own lightly. God's scales are true.

Does “wait for the LORD” forbid going to the police or the courts? It forbids private revenge. The magistrate is God’s servant to punish evil (Rom 13:4), so seeking justice lawfully is not revenge.

verseByVerse.quote: A man's steps are from the LORD; how then can man understand his way? It is a snare to say rashly, "It is holy," and to reflect only after making vows.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man's steps. If God directs every step, no human being can fully understand his own path. We see a few steps ahead at best. Jeremiah prayed, I know, O LORD, that the way of man is not in himself, that it is not in man who walks to direct his steps (Jer 10:23).

That is a relief rather than a burden. You do not have to understand your whole life to walk it faithfully. The confusing season, the closed door, the unexpected turn: you may not understand your way, but the one directing your steps does.

It is a snare. Some people make promises to God in a moment of emotion, "I dedicate this to you", "If you get me through this, I will...", and only think about what they have promised afterward. It becomes a trap. Jephthah vowed that whatever comes out from the doors of my house to meet me would be offered up, and his daughter came out (Judg 11:31). It is better that you should not vow than that you should vow and not pay (Eccl 5:5). Think first. Then promise.

verseByVerse.quote: A wise king winnows the wicked and drives the wheel over them. The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD, searching all his innermost parts. Steadfast love and faithfulness preserve the king, and by steadfast love his throne is upheld.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A wise king winnows. The picture comes from the threshing floor, where a heavy wheel was rolled over the grain to separate it from the husk. A wise ruler separates out the wicked in the same way and deals with them firmly: justice is not soft on evil.

The lamp of the LORD. God has placed a lamp inside every human being. The ESV notes the Hebrew word is "breath", the breath of life God breathed into man. With it he searches all his innermost parts. That is the conscience, and more than the conscience: the human capacity to know oneself, which God uses to shine light into the corners we would rather keep dark.

When you feel that inner discomfort about something you have done, that may be the lamp of the LORD. Do not blow it out. Who knows a person's thoughts except the spirit of that person, which is in him? (1 Cor 2:11). And God searches deeper than we can ever search ourselves.

Steadfast love and faithfulness. A king is not ultimately kept on his throne by armies but by steadfast love and faithfulness, the two great covenant words. Steadfast love and faithfulness meet (Ps 85:10). And the one King whose throne is upheld forever is the one who came full of grace and truth (John 1:14).

verseByVerse.quote: The glory of young men is their strength, but the splendor of old men is their gray hair. Blows that wound cleanse away evil; strokes make clean the innermost parts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The glory of young men. Every age has its own glory. The young have strength, energy and courage. The old have gray hair, the sign of experience, wisdom and a long life (16:31). Neither should despise the other; a church or family that honours both is strong.

Blows that wound. The chapter ends on a hard truth. Pain can cleanse. Discipline that hurts, the wound of correction, the painful consequence, can reach the innermost parts and make them clean in a way that gentle words sometimes do not. No one enjoys it at the time. For the moment all discipline seems painful rather than pleasant, but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness (Heb 12:11).

A believer going through a painful season may be in exactly this place: the strokes of a loving Father, cleansing something deep. But not every pain is correction for a particular sin, as Jesus said of the man born blind (John 9:3). And the verse never excuses anyone who wounds another in the name of discipline: abuse is not God's refining, and anyone suffering it should seek safety at once.

20.theology: No one can make his own heart pure (v. 9), but God cleanses all who confess (1 John 1:9). He sees the deep motives no one else can (vv. 5, 27), hates double standards (vv. 10, 23), and directs our steps beyond our understanding (v. 24). So his people leave vengeance to him (v. 22), make vows with thought (v. 25), and receive even painful discipline as his cleansing (v. 30).
20.examples:
The chapter's pictures stay in the mind: Noah uncovered in his tent, the sluggard who would not plow in the cold autumn rain, the bucket lowered into the deep water of a heart, the buyer's "Bad, bad" and his boast afterward, the mouthful of gravel, and Jephthah's rash vow.

Two of them are for this week. Hand over to God a wrong you have been planning to repay. And when the lamp of conscience shows you something you would rather not see, do not blow it out.

21.title: The Victory Belongs to the LORD

his neighbor finds no mercy in his eyes.<sup>11</sup>When a scoffer is punished, the simple becomes wise; when a wise man is instructed, he gains knowledge.<sup>12</sup>The Righteous One observes the house of the wicked; how much more when he brings it with evil intent.<sup>28</sup>A false witness will perish, but the word of a man who hears will endure.<sup>29</sup>A wicked man puts on a bold face, but the upright gives thought to his ways.<sup>30</sup>No wisdom, no understanding, no counsel can avail against the LORD.<sup>31</sup>The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but the victory belongs to the LORD.
21.overview: God turns the king's heart, weighs every heart, and wants justice more than sacrifice (vv. 1-8). Mercy to the poor, joy in justice, and the misery of a quarrelsome home (vv. 9-19). The wise save, the righteous give, and however well the horse is prepared, the victory belongs to the LORD (vv. 20-31).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The King's Heart in the LORD's Hand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God directs even a king's heart, weighs every heart, and wants justice more than sacrifice. Hasty and dishonest gain vanishes (vv. 4-8).
verseByVerse.theology: No heart, not even a king's, is outside God's direction, and no religious act replaces a just life.

verseByVerse.quote: The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will. Every way of a man is right in his own eyes, but the LORD weighs the heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king's heart. Picture a farmer sending irrigation water this way or that with a movement of his hoe. The king's heart is like that water in God's hand. The most powerful person in the land, whose decisions seem to shape history, is himself being directed.

Scripture shows it again and again. God put it into the heart of a Persian king to beautify the temple: Blessed be the LORD, the God of our fathers, who put such a thing as this into the heart of the king (Ezra 7:27). Nebuchadnezzar, the proudest king on earth, was humbled until you know that the Most High rules the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will (Dan 4:32).

That is enormous comfort in a world of frightening leaders and elections. No president, dictator or board of directors is outside God's hand. And it is why Paul urges prayer for kings and all who are in high positions, that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life (1 Tim 2:2). Pray for the leaders who worry you.

The LORD weighs the heart. Almost the same as 16:2, and placed after the king's heart it applies the same truth to everyone: God weighs what is actually inside. The scales we use on ourselves are always flattering.

If God turns the king’s heart, is the king still responsible for evil? Yes. God directed Assyria’s king to his purpose, and then punished him for his arrogant heart (Isa 10:5–15); Herod and Pilate did what God had planned, and were guilty (Acts 4:27–28). God steers without forcing, and is never the author of sin.

verseByVerse.quote: To do righteousness and justice is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice. Haughty eyes and a proud heart, the lamp of the wicked, are sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Righteousness and justice. God commanded sacrifices in the law. But he never wanted them as a substitute for a righteous life. A worshipper who cheats his workers on Monday and brings an offering on Saturday has misunderstood God completely. Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice (1 Sam 15:22). For I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice (Hos 6:6). Micah asked what the LORD really wants, and answered: to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God (Mic 6:8).

The modern form of sacrifice is religious activity: attendance, giving, serving on committees. All good. None of it can cover for a life of injustice. God looks first at how we treat people. And where we have failed here, as all have, the cover is not more ritual but Christ, who did justice and loved kindness perfectly in our place.

Haughty eyes. Pride shows in the eyes and lives in the heart. It is the lamp the wicked walk by, the light they steer their lives with. The ESV notes that lamp may be "the plowing": pride is what the wicked cultivate, the work of their fields. Either way, the verdict is simple: it is sin.

verseByVerse.quote: The plans of the diligent lead surely to abundance, but everyone who is hasty comes only to poverty. The getting of treasures by a lying tongue is a fleeting vapor and a snare of death. The violence of the wicked will sweep them away, because they refuse to do what is just. The way of the guilty is crooked, but the conduct of the pure is upright.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The plans of the diligent. Two paths to wealth, and only one works. The diligent plan carefully and work steadily, and it leads surely to abundance. The hasty want it now: the shortcut, the gamble, the scheme. Everyone who goes that way ends poor. Patience is not only a virtue; it is a financial strategy.

A lying tongue. Money made by lies is like breath on a cold morning: visible for a second and gone. The ESV notes that most Hebrew manuscripts read "a vapor for those who seek death", while some, with the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), read a snare of death; the sense is much the same. The liar thinks he is seeking treasure; he is seeking death. What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes (Jas 4:14). If life itself is a vapor, riches gained by lying are a vapor within a vapor.

The violence of the wicked. The violence the wicked use against others becomes the flood that carries them off. And the root cause is named: they refuse. Their problem is not that they do not know what is just; they will not do it.

The way of the guilty. Guilt bends a person's path. The guilty must twist and turn to avoid being found out. The pure can walk in a straight line because they have nothing to hide.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–19 — The Cry of the Poor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A quarrelsome home, the wicked who show no mercy, and the ear closed to the poor (v. 13); then justice that brings joy to some and terror to others, the love of pleasure, and the wicked caught in their own plans (vv. 14-19).
verseByVerse.theology: A person who will not hear the poor will one day find that he is not heard.

verseByVerse.quote: It is better to live in a corner of the housetop than in a house shared with a quarrelsome wife. The soul of the wicked desires evil; his neighbor finds no mercy in his eyes. When a scoffer is punished, the simple becomes wise; when a wise man is instructed, he gains knowledge. The Righteous One observes the house of the wicked; he throws the wicked down to ruin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A corner of the housetop. Israel's houses had flat roofs, and a cramped shelter up there, exposed to the weather, is better than a spacious house full of conflict. It appears again word for word at 25:24, and in a different form at verse 19.

The proverb is written for young men, and it is honest about a real misery. But the point applies to husbands as much as wives. A home can be large and comfortable and unbearable because of the atmosphere in it. What kind of atmosphere do you create at home: the kind people want to come in from the roof to, or escape to it from?

The soul of the wicked. Wickedness is ultimately a matter of desire. The wicked man does not merely do evil; he wants it. And people who live near him get no mercy.

When a scoffer is punished. A near repeat of 19:25. The simple learn by watching consequences land on others. The wise learn by being taught. Better to be the second kind of learner.

The Righteous One observes. The ESV prints The Righteous One with capitals: this is God himself. He observes the house of the wicked, watches closely, and in his time brings it down. The wicked man thinks no one is watching his house. Someone is.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever closes his ear to the cry of the poor will himself call out and not be answered. A gift in secret averts anger, and a concealed bribe, strong wrath. When justice is done, it is a joy to the righteous but terror to evildoers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The cry of the poor. A person hears the cry of someone in need and deliberately closes his ear. Shutting out need is a choice, and God answers it in kind: the day will come when he is the one crying out, and no one will answer.

Jesus told the story of a rich man who feasted sumptuously every day, while at his gate lay a poor man named Lazarus who desired to be fed with what fell from the rich man's table (Luke 16:19-21). After death the rich man cried out for mercy, and none came. For judgment is without mercy to one who has shown no mercy (Jas 2:13). And John asks, if anyone has the world's goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does God's love abide in him? (1 John 3:17).

The poor are not always at the gate. Sometimes they are in an email appeal, a news story, a colleague whose family is struggling. Is there a cry you have closed your ear to?

A gift in secret. This is an observation, not a recommendation. The ESV notes the Hebrew is "a bribe in the bosom". A quiet gift can calm an angry person, and a bribe can buy off wrath. There is a legitimate form of this: Jacob sending gifts ahead to Esau. And a corrupt form, which Proverbs condemns elsewhere (17:23). The proverb describes how people work, and leaves the reader to use it rightly.

When justice is done. The same event, a just verdict, a crime exposed, a corrupt official jailed, produces joy in one group and terror in another. How a person reacts when justice is done shows which group he belongs to. And the final day of justice will be exactly this: joy for those who belong to the Judge, terror for those who do not.

verseByVerse.quote: One who wanders from the way of good sense will rest in the assembly of the dead. Whoever loves pleasure will be a poor man; he who loves wine and oil will not be rich. The wicked is a ransom for the righteous, and the traitor for the upright. It is better to live in a desert land than with a quarrelsome and fretful woman.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One who wanders. He wandered: not a dramatic rebellion, just a drift off the path. And he ends up resting, but among the dead. Folly offers rest and delivers death.

Whoever loves pleasure. Wine and oil were the luxuries of the ancient world. God gave them as good gifts: wine to gladden the heart of man, oil to make his face shine (Ps 104:15). The problem is not enjoying them but loving them. A person who lives for pleasure, spending on every comfort and experience, will be poor, and often poor in more than money.

A ransom for the righteous. This does not describe atonement. It describes God's justice reversing the plans of the wicked, so that the trouble they planned for the righteous falls on them instead, as Haman hanged on the gallows he built for Mordecai. God said to Israel, I give Egypt as your ransom (Isa 43:3).

And the gospel reverses even this proverb in the most astonishing way. There, the Righteous One became the ransom for the wicked. Christ, who was not a traitor, took the place of traitors, so that traitors could be brought home.

A desert land. Verse 9 said a corner of the roof; now the picture escalates to the desert, with its heat and loneliness. Constant complaint makes any home a wilderness.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saving and devouring, craving and giving, the scoffer named, and the chapter's climax in the battle that belongs to the LORD (vv. 30-31).
verseByVerse.theology: Prepare the horse, and trust the LORD for the victory, for no plan can succeed against him.

verseByVerse.quote: Precious treasure and oil are in a wise man's dwelling, but a foolish man devours it. Whoever pursues righteousness and kindness will find life, righteousness, and honor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Precious treasure and oil. The wise man's house has reserves; the fool devours everything as soon as it comes in. The difference between them is not how much they earn, but what they do with it.

Righteousness and kindness. The person who pursues righteousness and kindness finds three things: life, honour, and righteousness itself. The pursuit is rewarded with more of what was pursued. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied (Matt 5:6). Most people chase honour and miss it. Those who chase righteousness find honour as well.

verseByVerse.quote: A wise man scales the city of the mighty and brings down the stronghold in which they trust. Whoever keeps his mouth and his tongue keeps himself out of trouble. "Scoffer" is the name of the arrogant, haughty man who acts with arrogant pride.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The city of the mighty. Wisdom beats brute power, in war, in business and in life. The strong trust their strongholds; the wise find a way over.

Whoever keeps his mouth. A near repeat of 13:3. Most of the trouble a person gets into could have been avoided by keeping quiet.

"Scoffer" is the name. The proverb gives a definition, piling up words for pride: arrogant, haughty, arrogant pride. That is what a scoffer is. His mockery is not wit; it is pride wearing a smile.

verseByVerse.quote: The desire of the sluggard kills him, for his hands refuse to labor. All day long he craves and craves, but the righteous gives and does not hold back.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The desire of the sluggard. The sluggard is not killed by lack of desire. He is killed by desire itself, desire that never gets turned into work. The unfulfilled craving eats him alive.

He craves and craves. One spends his day craving, the other giving. The craver never has enough. The giver, who seems to have less because he gives it away, is the one who is full. Jesus said, It is more blessed to give than to receive (Acts 20:35).

Which describes your average day: craving or giving? An open hand is the Spirit's work in those who have been given everything in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination; how much more when he brings it with evil intent. A false witness will perish, but the word of a man who hears will endure. A wicked man puts on a bold face, but the upright gives thought to his ways.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sacrifice of the wicked. Verse 3 said justice is better than sacrifice. This goes further. A wicked man's sacrifice is already an abomination (15:8). It is worse still when he brings it with evil intent: using religion to cover a crime, buy favour, or look respectable.

A false witness. The liar perishes (compare 19:5, 9). The man who hears, who listens carefully before he speaks, gives testimony that lasts. Careful listening makes for truthful speaking.

A bold face. The wicked man bluffs and brazens it out. The upright man does something harder: he gives thought to his ways. The ESV notes it may be "establishes" his ways. Bluster hides; reflection builds.

verseByVerse.quote: No wisdom, no understanding, no counsel can avail against the LORD. The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but the victory belongs to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No wisdom. Three nouns, three denials: no human wisdom can succeed against the LORD. When the rulers gathered against Jesus, they thought they were in control, and the church prayed that they had only done whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place (Acts 4:28). The greatest crime in history accomplished God's plan of salvation.

The horse is made ready. The war horse was the tank of the ancient world. The proverb does not say, do not prepare it. It says, prepare it, and know that the victory belongs to the LORD. Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God (Ps 20:7). David said to Goliath, the battle is the LORD's (1 Sam 17:47).

Here is the balance of the whole book. Work hard, plan well, study, prepare, get advice, saddle the horse. Then trust God with the outcome, because it is his. The farmer plows and waits for rain. What is the horse you need to make ready this week, and have you handed its victory to the LORD?

21.theology:
God is sovereign over the hearts of rulers (v. 1) and over every plan against him (v. 30). Human preparation is right, but the outcome belongs to God (v. 31; Ps 20:7).

A just life matters more to God than religious ritual (vv. 3, 27; Mic 6:8; Hos 6:6). Refusing mercy to the poor brings judgment without mercy (v. 13; Luke 16:19-25; Jas 2:13). Righteousness and generosity are pursued and rewarded (vv. 21, 26; Matt 5:6).

The chapter's last verse finds its fullest answer at the cross. The rulers took counsel against the LORD and his Anointed (Ps 2:2; Acts 4:25–28), and what looked like their victory and his defeat was the reverse: through the cross Christ disarmed the powers and triumphed over them (Col 2:15). The horse must still be made ready, but the believer works knowing that the decisive battle is already won.
21.examples:
The pictures to remember are the farmer turning irrigation water with his hoe, breath on a cold morning, the corner of the roof and the desert, and the rich man with Lazarus at his gate.

The practice is simpler: pray for the leaders who worry you, do not cheat on Monday and give on Saturday, ask whether your day is spent craving or giving, and saddle the horse while trusting the LORD for the victory.

22.title: Train Up a Child in the Way He Should Go
22.text: <sup>1</sup>A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches, and favor is better than silver or gold.<sup>2</sup>The rich and the poor meet together; the LORD is the Maker of them all.<sup>3</sup>The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and suffer for it.<sup>4</sup>The reward for humility and fear of the LORD is riches and honor and life.<sup>5</sup>Thorns and snares are in the way of the crooked; whoever guards his soul will keep far from them.<sup>6</sup>Train up a child in the way he should go; even when he is old he will not depart from it.<sup>7</sup>The rich rules over the poor, and the borrower is the slave of the lender.<sup>8</sup>Whoever sows injustice will reap calamity, and the rod of his fury will fail.<sup>9</sup>Whoever has a bountiful eye will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor.<sup>10</sup>Drive out a scoffer, and strife will go out, and quarreling and abuse will cease.<sup>11</sup>He who loves purity of heart, and whose speech is gracious, will have the king as his friend.<sup>12</sup>The eyes of the LORD keep watch over knowledge, but he overthrows the words of the traitor.<sup>13</sup>The sluggard says, "There is a lion outside! I shall be killed in the streets!"<sup>14</sup>The mouth of forbidden women is a deep pit; he with whom the LORD is angry will fall into it.<sup>15</sup>Folly is bound up in the heart of a child, but the rod of discipline drives it far from him.<sup>16</sup>Whoever oppresses the poor to increase his own wealth, or gives to the rich, will only come to poverty.<sup>17</sup>Incline your ear, and hear the words of the wise, and apply your heart to my knowledge,<sup>18</sup>for it will be pleasant if you keep them within you, if all of them are ready on your lips.<sup>19</sup>That your trust may be in the LORD, I have made them known to you today, even to you.<sup>20</sup>Have I not written for you thirty sayings of counsel and knowledge,<sup>21</sup>to make you know what is right and true, that you may give a true answer to those who sent you?<sup>22</sup>Do not rob the poor, because he is poor, or crush the afflicted at the gate,<sup>23</sup>for the LORD will plead their cause and rob of life those who rob them.<sup>24</sup>Make no friendship with a man given to anger, nor go with a wrathful man,<sup>25</sup>lest you learn his ways and entangle yourself in a snare.<sup>26</sup>Be not one of those who give pledges, who put up security for debts.<sup>27</sup>If you have nothing with which to pay, why should your bed be taken from under you?<sup>28</sup>Do not move the ancient landmark that your fathers have set.<sup>29</sup>Do you see a man skillful in his work? He will stand before kings; he will not stand before obscure men.
22.overview: A good name, one Maker of rich and poor, the training of a child, and the slavery of debt (vv. 1-9). Folly bound up in a child's heart, and the sluggard's lion (vv. 10-16). The words of the wise begin, written so that the reader's trust may be in the LORD, who pleads the cause of the poor (vv. 17-29).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — A Good Name, Rich and Poor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Character outweighs wealth, and the LORD is the Maker of them all (v. 2). Humility, the training of a child, debt and generosity (vv. 3-9).
verseByVerse.theology: Character, reputation and the shaping of a child are worth more than money, and every rich and poor person was made by the same God.

verseByVerse.quote: A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches, and favor is better than silver or gold. The rich and the poor meet together; the LORD is the Maker of them all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A good name. The verb matters: to be chosen. Life presents the choice again and again. Sign the misleading contract and make money, or refuse and keep your name. Cut the corner that no one will notice, or do the job right. A good name is built slowly by thousands of such choices, and it can be destroyed by one.

A name means a reputation for integrity, the trust people place in your word. When the early church needed men to handle money, they looked for seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom (Acts 6:3). A good name is better than precious ointment (Eccl 7:1). Money can be lost and regained. A name, once lost, is very hard to recover, though the Lord who restored Peter still restores those who return to him.

The rich and the poor. Rich and poor live in the same town and sit (or should sit) in the same church. Beneath all the differences of income is the deepest equality: the LORD is the Maker of them all. Job said of his servant, Did not he who made me in the womb make him? (Job 31:15).

That truth humbles the rich, who owe their existence to the same Maker as the beggar. And it lifts the poor, who bear the same image as the millionaire. In God's presence there is no first class.

verseByVerse.quote: The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and suffer for it. The reward for humility and fear of the LORD is riches and honor and life. Thorns and snares are in the way of the crooked; whoever guards his soul will keep far from them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prudent sees danger. The prudent person sees the storm clouds and takes shelter. The simple person keeps walking and gets soaked. Prudence is not paranoia; it is simply paying attention to warning signs: the debt rising, the relationship getting too close, the health symptom that keeps coming back. The same proverb appears again at 27:12.

The reward for humility. Humility and the fear of the LORD go together, and they lead to riches, honour and life. The ESV notes that the verse may be read, "The reward for humility is the fear of the LORD", which is perhaps even more beautiful: the reward of humility is a deeper reverence for God, and with it everything else.

Thorns and snares. The crooked path is full of hazards that snag and trap. The person who cares about his soul keeps far not only from the trap but from the road it lies on.

Does humility guarantee riches? This is the usual fruit of wise living under God’s favour, not a formula; Proverbs itself says Better is a little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure and trouble with it (15:16).

verseByVerse.quote: Train up a child in the way he should go; even when he is old he will not depart from it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is one of the most quoted verses in Proverbs, and often the most painful, because many faithful parents have watched a child walk away from the faith they tried to teach. So it needs to be read carefully and honestly.

First, what it says. Train up pictures shaping a young life from the start, when it is most pliable, in the way he should go. Early training goes deep. Habits, convictions, instincts, a love of Scripture and prayer planted in childhood very often last a lifetime. Timothy had known from childhood the sacred writings, which are able to make you wise for salvation (2 Tim 3:15). That is a strong encouragement for parents to invest in the early years.

Second, it is a proverb. Proverbs describe how God's world generally runs, not a guarantee in every case. The book itself says elsewhere that a wise father can have a foolish son (17:21). Children are not machines; each one makes his own choices before God (9:12). The proverb is not a promise that parents can control the outcome, and it is not a verdict that parents of a wandering child must have failed.

Third, a word to the parent whose child has left. The seed planted is not lost. Many who wander come back, often much later, to what they were taught. The proverb says even when he is old, and that may be a long time coming. Keep praying. And the God who is a Father has prodigal children too, and waits at the end of the road for them.

Parents plant and water, but only God gives new birth (John 3:8; 1 Cor 3:6), so a child's wandering is not proof that you failed, and a child's faith is not your achievement. And where a parent did fail, as every parent does in some way, there is forgiveness in Christ for that too, and freedom to keep loving a wayward child without carrying his choices as your own.
verseByVerse.note: The Hebrew reads literally "according to his way", which most take as the way he ought to go; some also hear in it training suited to each child's age and nature.

verseByVerse.quote: The rich rules over the poor, and the borrower is the slave of the lender. Whoever sows injustice will reap calamity, and the rod of his fury will fail. Whoever has a bountiful eye will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The borrower is the slave. A blunt statement of how debt works. The one who owes is not free. His decisions, his time and his future belong partly to the one he owes. Many people today live as slaves to consumer debt without calling it that. The proverb does.

Debt is not always sin; a mortgage can be wise. But the verse is a reason to borrow rarely and carefully, and to get free when you can. Owe no one anything, except to love each other (Rom 13:8).

Whoever sows injustice. What you plant, you harvest. Plant injustice, and calamity grows. Hosea said of Israel, they sow the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind (Hos 8:7). And the rod of his fury, the power the unjust man used to beat others down, breaks in his hand.

A bountiful eye. The ESV notes that bountiful is literally "good": a good eye. A generous person looks at others with kindness, sees their need, and shares his bread. Generosity begins with how we see people.
verseByVerse.note: After v. 8 the Greek Old Testament adds a line about God blessing a cheerful giver, which Paul echoes (2 Cor 9:7).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–16 — Folly Bound Up in a Child
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The scoffer, the pure heart, the sluggard's excuse, the pit of forbidden women, and Folly is bound up in the heart of a child (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: No child is born wise, and no excuse is too absurd for a lazy man.

verseByVerse.quote: Drive out a scoffer, and strife will go out, and quarreling and abuse will cease. He who loves purity of heart, and whose speech is gracious, will have the king as his friend. The eyes of the LORD keep watch over knowledge, but he overthrows the words of the traitor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Drive out a scoffer. Sometimes one person is the source of all the conflict in a group. Remove him, and the quarrelling stops. A church, a team or a friendship group that tolerates a persistent scoffer will never have peace. There is a time when love requires removing someone who will not stop sowing strife.

Purity of heart. A pure heart and gracious speech, the inner and the outer, win the friendship of those in high places. People in power are surrounded by flatterers and schemers; they value someone pure and gracious. And the King of kings says, Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God (Matt 5:8).

The eyes of the LORD. God guards true knowledge, keeping it from being lost, and he overturns the words of the treacherous. Lies may seem to win for a while. God is watching over the truth.

verseByVerse.quote: The sluggard says, "There is a lion outside! I shall be killed in the streets!" The mouth of forbidden women is a deep pit; he with whom the LORD is angry will fall into it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"There is a lion outside!" Why won't the sluggard go to work? There might be a lion in the middle of town! It is absurd, and that is the point. The lazy man's excuses are often ridiculous, but he states them with complete seriousness. A similar line appears at 26:13.

We all have lions. "The weather is bad." "I'm not in the right frame of mind." "It won't work anyway." "Someone else would do it better." What is the lion you have been using to avoid something you know you should do? Name it to the Lord, whose Spirit gives the strength to walk past it.

The mouth of forbidden women. The ESV notes that the Hebrew is "strange" women, as in chapters 2, 5 and 7. Their mouth, their flattery, is a deep pit, easy to fall into and almost impossible to climb out of. And the second line is sobering: falling into it can itself be a mark of God's judgment. Sometimes God's anger against a person's persistent sin takes the form of giving him over to it.

verseByVerse.quote: Folly is bound up in the heart of a child, but the rod of discipline drives it far from him. Whoever oppresses the poor to increase his own wealth, or gives to the rich, will only come to poverty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Folly is bound up. Children are not born innocent and wise, needing only to be left alone to flourish. Folly is bound up in their hearts, tied in tight. Anyone who has watched a two-year-old knows this. David confessed, Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity (Ps 51:5). Selfishness, rebellion and foolishness do not need to be taught; they come naturally.

So children need discipline, loving correction that loosens what is tied in their hearts and drives it away, with the same balance as at 13:24. Its aim is to free the child from folly, not to vent the parent's frustration.

Whoever oppresses the poor. Two ways of getting ahead by injustice: squeezing the poor, and buying favour with the rich. Both end in poverty. God is not mocked.

Is the rod literal? It stands for discipline of every kind, and the words speak of a real rod. Scripture requires loving, consistent discipline; whether to use measured physical correction with young children is left to wise parents. Where it is used, it comes with explanation, never in anger or to injure (Eph 6:4). Anything that frightens or harms a child is abuse.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–29 — The Words of the Wise
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A new collection, the words of the wise (v. 17), given so that the reader will trust the LORD (v. 19). Its first saying is for the poor, whose cause the LORD pleads (v. 23); then come angry friends, pledges, landmarks and skilful work.
verseByVerse.theology: The sayings of the wise are given so that the reader's trust will rest in the LORD, and they begin with the poor.

verseByVerse.quote: Incline your ear, and hear the words of the wise, and apply your heart to my knowledge, for it will be pleasant if you keep them within you, if all of them are ready on your lips. That your trust may be in the LORD, I have made them known to you today, even to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Incline your ear. A new section of the book begins here and runs to 24:22: the words of the wise. The style changes. The sayings become longer, often two or three verses, and they return to direct commands, like the father's speeches of chapters 1 to 9. The introduction calls for ear and heart together, hearing and applying.

Ready on your lips. Wisdom is to be stored within and kept ready on your lips. The picture is of someone who has memorised these sayings so well that they come out when needed. The Christian who has Scripture ready on his lips in a moment of temptation, grief or counsel knows how pleasant that is.

That your trust. Here is the purpose of all the practical advice that follows: that your trust may be in the LORD. The sayings about money, anger, food and work are not a self-help programme. They are meant to lead a person to trust God. Every wise habit is an act of faith in the God who designed life to work this way. And the teacher says, even to you. This is personal.

Did the Bible copy an Egyptian book? Parts of this section resemble the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope. Wisdom was shared across the ancient world, and the author may have used and reshaped such sayings. But inspiration does not mean the writer used no sources (Luke 1:1–4); the Spirit guided what he wrote, and verse 19 gives the purpose no Egyptian text had: That your trust may be in the LORD.
verseByVerse.note: A new collection, “the words of the wise” (22:17–24:22). Parts of its opening section are similar to an Egyptian wisdom text, the Instruction of Amenemope.

verseByVerse.quote: Have I not written for you thirty sayings of counsel and knowledge, to make you know what is right and true, that you may give a true answer to those who sent you?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thirty sayings. The teacher has put these sayings into writing, and there are thirty of them, a collection designed to be learned and passed on. The Hebrew word here is uncertain. The KJV reads "excellent things"; most modern translations read thirty, partly because the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope, which this section resembles, has thirty chapters.

A true answer. The purpose is not only personal. The student learns what is right and true so that he can bring back a reliable answer to those who sent him, like a messenger who returns with an accurate report. Wisdom makes a person trustworthy to others, someone whose word can be relied on.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not rob the poor, because he is poor, or crush the afflicted at the gate, for the LORD will plead their cause and rob of life those who rob them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not rob the poor. The first of the thirty sayings is about the poor, and that is surely deliberate. Why would anyone rob the poor? Because he is poor, because he cannot fight back. He has no lawyer, no influence, no voice. The gate was where courts sat. Crushing the afflicted at the gate means using the legal system against people who cannot defend themselves.

The LORD will plead. But the poor man does have a lawyer: the LORD will plead their cause. God becomes their advocate. The law said of widows and orphans, If you do mistreat them, and they cry out to me, I will surely hear their cry (Exod 22:23). God is Father of the fatherless and protector of widows (Ps 68:5). The man who robs the poor has made the most dangerous enemy in the universe. The saying returns at 23:10-11: their Redeemer is strong; he will plead their cause against you.

verseByVerse.quote: Make no friendship with a man given to anger, nor go with a wrathful man, lest you learn his ways and entangle yourself in a snare.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Make no friendship. Choose friends carefully, and do not choose a hot-tempered one. Angry people are not beyond love, but close friendship with them is dangerous.

Lest you learn his ways. Anger is contagious. Spend enough time with an angry man and you will learn his ways. You start reacting as he reacts, seeing slights where he sees them, raising your voice as he does. Bad company ruins good morals (1 Cor 15:33). And you become entangled in his quarrels and their consequences. Who are you learning your ways from?

verseByVerse.quote: Be not one of those who give pledges, who put up security for debts. If you have nothing with which to pay, why should your bed be taken from under you?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who give pledges. The warning against guaranteeing debts returns, now as one of the thirty sayings (compare 6:1-5; 11:15; 17:18).

Why should your bed be taken? When the borrower defaults, the creditor comes for you, and you have nothing, so he takes your bed. You end up sleeping on the floor for someone else's debt. Count the cost before you sign.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not move the ancient landmark that your fathers have set. Do you see a man skillful in his work? He will stand before kings; he will not stand before obscure men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ancient landmark. Boundary stones marked each family's land, set when the land was first divided. Moving one a few feet was an easy, secret way to steal a neighbour's inheritance, often from someone too weak to object. The law forbade it: You shall not move your neighbor's landmark, which the men of old have set (Deut 19:14). The saying is repeated and applied to the fatherless at 23:10.

The principle reaches further: respect what has been rightly established by those before you. Not every old boundary is sacred, but some are, and moving them for personal gain is theft.

A man skillful in his work. A man who is truly skillful at what he does, whether a craftsman, a scribe, a builder or a nurse, will be noticed and promoted. Daniel and his friends were found ten times better than all the magicians and enchanters, and they stood before the king (Dan 1:19-20).

Christian work should be skilful work, done as for the Lord. Whether or not a king ever notices, the King of kings always does.

22.theology:
All human beings share one Maker, which grounds the dignity of the poor (v. 2; Job 31:15). Reputation and character outweigh wealth (v. 1). Children are born with folly bound in their hearts and need loving discipline (v. 15; Ps 51:5). Early training shapes a life, though proverbs describe patterns rather than guarantees (v. 6; 17:21).

The purpose of practical wisdom is trust in the LORD (v. 19). God is the advocate of the poor against their oppressors (vv. 22-23; Exod 22:22-24; Ps 68:5). Debt enslaves (v. 7), character is shaped by companions (vv. 24-25), and excellent work honours God (v. 29).

The LORD who pleads the poor man's cause (v. 23) is seen most fully in Christ, who preached good news to the poor (Luke 4:18) and is his people's advocate (1 John 2:1). The one Maker of rich and poor (v. 2) became poor himself, so that you by his poverty might become rich (2 Cor 8:9).
22.examples:
Think of a reputation built by thousands of small choices, or of the millionaire and the beggar who have one Maker. Think of a credit card that has quietly become a master, or of the sluggard's lion in the street, or of a two-year-old's heart.

Above all, remember that the poor man has a lawyer, and that the parent of a child who has walked away is praying to a Father who waits for his own prodigals.

23.title: My Son, Give Me Your Heart
23.text: <sup>1</sup>When you sit down to eat with a ruler, observe carefully what is before you,<sup>2</sup>and put a knife to your throat if you are given to appetite.<sup>3</sup>Do not desire his delicacies, for they are deceptive food.<sup>4</sup>Do not toil to acquire wealth; be discerning enough to desist.<sup>5</sup>When your eyes light on it, it is gone, for suddenly it sprouts wings, flying like an eagle toward heaven.<sup>6</sup>Do not eat the bread of a man who is stingy; do not desire his delicacies,<sup>7</sup>for he is like one who is inwardly calculating. "Eat and drink!" he says to you, but his heart is not with you.<sup>8</sup>You will vomit up the morsels that you have eaten, and waste your pleasant words.<sup>9</sup>Do not speak in the hearing of a fool, for he will despise the good sense of your words.<sup>10</sup>Do not move an ancient landmark or enter the fields of the fatherless,<sup>11</sup>for their Redeemer is strong; he will plead their cause against you.<sup>12</sup>Apply your heart to instruction and your ear to words of knowledge.<sup>13</sup>Do not withhold discipline from a child; if you strike him with a rod, he will not die.<sup>14</sup>If you strike him with the rod, you will save his soul from Sheol.<sup>15</sup>My son, if your heart is wise, my heart too will be glad.<sup>16</sup>My inmost being will exult when your lips speak what is right.<sup>17</sup>Let not your heart envy sinners, but continue in the fear of the LORD all the day.<sup>18</sup>Surely there is a future, and your hope will not be cut off.<sup>19</sup>Hear, my son, and be wise, and direct your heart in the way.<sup>20</sup>Be not among drunkards or among gluttonous eaters of meat,<sup>21</sup>for the drunkard and the glutton will come to poverty, and slumber will clothe them with rags.<sup>22</sup>Listen to your father who gave you life, and do not despise your mother when she is old.<sup>23</sup>Buy truth, and do not sell it; buy wisdom, instruction, and understanding.<sup>24</sup>The father of the righteous will greatly rejoice; he who fathers a wise son will be glad in him.<sup>25</sup>Let your father and mother be glad; let her who bore you rejoice.<sup>26</sup>My son, give me your heart, and let your eyes observe my ways.<sup>27</sup>For a prostitute is a deep pit; an adulteress is a narrow well.<sup>28</sup>She lies in wait like a robber and increases the traitors among mankind.<sup>29</sup>Who has woe? Who has sorrow? Who has strife? Who has complaining? Who has wounds without cause? Who has redness of eyes?<sup>30</sup>Those who tarry long over wine; those who go to try mixed wine.<sup>31</sup>Do not look at wine when it is red, when it sparkles in the cup and goes down smoothly.<sup>32</sup>In the end it bites like a serpent and stings like an adder.<sup>33</sup>Your eyes will see strange things, and your heart utter perverse things.<sup>34</sup>You will be like one who lies down in the midst of the sea, like one who lies on the top of a mast.<sup>35</sup>"They struck me," you will say, "but I was not hurt; they beat me, but I did not feel it. When shall I awake? I must have another drink."
23.overview: Self-control at a ruler's table, wealth that flies away, the false host, and the fatherless whose Redeemer is strong (vv. 1-12). Loving discipline, a father's joy, and a future hope that envy cannot see (vv. 13-25). The father asks for the heart, and paints the misery of drink (vv. 26-35).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Appetite, Wealth and the Fatherless
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Traps of appetite, greed and false hospitality, and the fatherless, for their Redeemer is strong (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: Appetite, greed and false hospitality are traps, and the fatherless have a Redeemer strong enough to defend them.

verseByVerse.quote: When you sit down to eat with a ruler, observe carefully what is before you, and put a knife to your throat if you are given to appetite. Do not desire his delicacies, for they are deceptive food.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Observe carefully. The scene is a young man invited to dine with someone powerful: a king, an official, a wealthy patron. Today it might be the chief executive's dinner, the influential donor's table, the invitation that could open doors. Be alert. The ESV notes it may be "who" is before you. Watch the food, and watch the man.

A knife to your throat. It is a startling image: if you cannot resist good food and drink, treat it as seriously as a knife at your throat. Self-control at a powerful man's table is not a matter of manners. A man who overindulges, drinks too much, talks too freely or looks too eager has put himself in the host's power. And self-control is the Spirit's fruit (Gal 5:22-23), which he supplies to those who ask.

Deceptive food. Why deceptive? Because rich hospitality often has a purpose. The meal may be a way to gain influence, extract information or create an obligation. Daniel, at the table of Babylon's king, resolved that he would not defile himself with the king's food (Dan 1:8). There are tables where the food is a hook.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not toil to acquire wealth; be discerning enough to desist. When your eyes light on it, it is gone, for suddenly it sprouts wings, flying like an eagle toward heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not toil to acquire wealth. This is not a command against working hard; Proverbs praises diligence constantly. It is a command against making wealth the goal that you wear yourself out for. There is a point where a wise person says: enough.

Many people never find that point. The next promotion, the bigger house, the larger pension: always one more. They sacrifice health, marriage and children on the altar of acquiring more than they will ever need.

It sprouts wings. You look at your money, and in the moment you look, it grows wings and flies off like an eagle. A market crash, a lawsuit, an illness, inflation, a thief: wealth is not a possession you hold; it is a bird that happens to be perched near you for now.

Jesus told of the rich fool: Fool! This night your soul is required of you, and the things you have prepared, whose will they be? (Luke 12:20). Paul tells the rich not to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy (1 Tim 6:17), and to be rich in good works, so that they may take hold of that which is truly life (1 Tim 6:18-19).

verseByVerse.quote: Do not eat the bread of a man who is stingy; do not desire his delicacies, for he is like one who is inwardly calculating. "Eat and drink!" he says to you, but his heart is not with you. You will vomit up the morsels that you have eaten, and waste your pleasant words.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man who is stingy. The ESV notes that stingy is literally "whose eye is evil", the opposite of the "good eye" of the generous man (22:9). He offers you food, but he begrudges every mouthful.

His heart is not with you. His words say "Help yourself!" while inside he counts the cost. The ESV notes an alternative reading: for "as he calculates in his soul, so is he". What a man truly is, is what goes on inside him, not what he says. Everyone has sat at a table like that and felt the chill beneath the welcome.

You will vomit up. When you realise what was really going on, the meal turns your stomach, and all your polite compliments were wasted.

The old rendering “as he thinketh in his heart, so is he” (v. 7) is often taken to mean that our thoughts create our reality. In context it describes a stingy host who counts the cost of every bite while urging you to eat. It is a warning about hypocrisy, not a principle of positive thinking.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not speak in the hearing of a fool, for he will despise the good sense of your words. Do not move an ancient landmark or enter the fields of the fatherless, for their Redeemer is strong; he will plead their cause against you. Apply your heart to instruction and your ear to words of knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the hearing of a fool. Some people cannot be helped by good advice, because they will only despise it. Wisdom is knowing when speaking is useful and when it is only casting pearls.

The fields of the fatherless. The warning of 22:28 returns, applied to orphans, whose fields no father will defend. But they do have someone: their Redeemer.

The word is go'el, the kinsman-redeemer, the close relative whose duty was to buy back family land and defend family members, as Boaz did in the book of Ruth: If you will redeem it, redeem it (Ruth 4:4). Here God himself is the Redeemer of those who have no one. And he is strong. Job, in his darkest hour, said, For I know that my Redeemer lives (Job 19:25). The person who takes advantage of an orphan has made the Redeemer his opponent. The kinsman-redeemer pattern reaches its height in Christ, who shared our flesh and blood to become our near kinsman (Heb 2:14–17) and bought back those who could not free themselves (Gal 4:4–5).

Apply your heart. A fresh call to attention, heart and ear together, introduces the next sayings: this is hearing that goes all the way in.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–25 — A Glad Father and a Future Hope
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Loving discipline, a father's gladness, and the cure for envy: Surely there is a future, and your hope will not be cut off (v. 18). Avoid drunkards, buy truth, and gladden your parents (vv. 19-25).
verseByVerse.theology: The fear of the LORD looks to a future the envied sinner does not have, and a wise child is a parent's joy.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not withhold discipline from a child; if you strike him with a rod, he will not die. If you strike him with the rod, you will save his soul from Sheol.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not withhold discipline. Parents sometimes hold back discipline because they fear it will harm the child. The proverb reassures them: loving correction will not destroy him. What will harm him is growing up without it.

The same balance as 13:24 and 22:15 must be kept: discipline is for the child's good, always.

Save his soul from Sheol. And here is what is at stake: not only the child's behaviour, but his soul. A child who never learns that wrong has consequences, never learns to submit to authority, never hears no, is being prepared for a life that runs toward destruction.

How does discipline “save his soul from Sheol”? Sheol here is death, a life ruined and cut short by folly. Discipline cannot give a child a new heart; only God does that. But it is a means God uses to restrain folly and point a child toward life.

Does this mean physical punishment today? Many Christians read the rod as a figure for discipline of every kind and hold that physical correction now does more harm than good. Others, including most of the Reformed tradition, take the rod at its word: measured physical correction, alongside instruction, is one God-given means for young children. The proverbs do speak of a real rod. But what Scripture requires of every parent is loving, consistent discipline; whether to use measured physical correction is left to wise parents. Where it is used, it is never given in anger, never to injure or humiliate, always with explanation and restored affection, and parents must also keep the law of the land they live in. Any discipline that frightens or harms a child is abuse, not the rod of Proverbs.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, if your heart is wise, my heart too will be glad. My inmost being will exult when your lips speak what is right.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My heart too will be glad. The father's heart is bound to his son's. It is not merely that the son has done well; the father feels it inside.

My inmost being. The ESV notes that My inmost being is literally "My kidneys", the Hebrew way of speaking of the deepest feelings. When the son speaks rightly, his father's joy goes all the way down. There are few joys like hearing your child say something wise and true. And the heavenly Father delights in his children in the same way: he will rejoice over you with gladness (Zeph 3:17).

verseByVerse.quote: Let not your heart envy sinners, but continue in the fear of the LORD all the day. Surely there is a future, and your hope will not be cut off.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let not your heart envy. Envy of sinners is a real temptation. They seem freer, richer, happier; they seem to get away with things. The psalmist almost slipped because of it. The cure is not to study the sinner's life more closely but to keep going in the fear of the LORD, all the day, steadily, every hour.

Surely there is a future. The envied sinner's success is short-sighted. The person who fears God has a future. The psalmist found it when I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end (Ps 73:17). And he could say, My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever (Ps 73:26).

For the Christian, the future is guaranteed by the resurrection of Christ. Whatever the sinner has now, the believer's hope will not be cut off. Which is better: a good present with no future, or a hard present with a certain one?

verseByVerse.quote: Hear, my son, and be wise, and direct your heart in the way. Be not among drunkards or among gluttonous eaters of meat, for the drunkard and the glutton will come to poverty, and slumber will clothe them with rags.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Direct your heart. The heart does not naturally steer toward wisdom; it must be turned in the way.

Be not among drunkards. Excess in food and drink is not merely unhealthy; it leads to poverty and a lethargy that ends in rags. And the warning is about company: do not be among them. The crowd you eat and drink with shapes your habits. Jesus warned, watch yourselves lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness and cares of this life (Luke 21:34).

verseByVerse.quote: Listen to your father who gave you life, and do not despise your mother when she is old. Buy truth, and do not sell it; buy wisdom, instruction, and understanding.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Listen to your father. A word for grown children. Your father gave you life; keep listening to him. And your mother, when she is old, when she repeats herself, moves slowly, needs help, forgets things: do not despise her. The temptation to treat aged parents with impatience or contempt is real. The fifth commandment has no age limit.

Buy truth. Truth is something to buy, to pay for, whatever it costs: time, effort, pride, popularity. And once you have it, do not sell it. There will be offers. Compromise the truth for a promotion, for acceptance, for peace in the family, for an easier life.

What would you not sell the truth for? And what have you, perhaps, already sold a little of? If so, the God of truth forgives those who confess, and his Spirit makes them faithful again.

verseByVerse.quote: The father of the righteous will greatly rejoice; he who fathers a wise son will be glad in him. Let your father and mother be glad; let her who bore you rejoice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The father of the righteous. A parent's purest joy is not in a child's success but in his character.

Let your father and mother be glad. Give your parents that gladness. That is a beautiful motive for a young person: not only obeying God for himself, but bringing joy to the people who gave him life.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–35 — The Heart and the Cup
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: My son, give me your heart (v. 26). The prostitute's pit (vv. 27-28), and the drunkard's misery down to his last line: I must have another drink (v. 35).
verseByVerse.theology: The father asks for the heart, because the heart that is given to God is kept from the pit and the cup.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, give me your heart, and let your eyes observe my ways. For a prostitute is a deep pit; an adulteress is a narrow well. She lies in wait like a robber and increases the traitors among mankind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Give me your heart. Here is the centre of the whole chapter, and in a sense of the whole book. The father does not ask first for obedience, or effort, or good behaviour. He asks for the heart. Everything else will follow. A son who has given his heart to his father will want to watch his ways and walk in them. The ESV notes that observe may be "delight in".

Read it as God's voice, and it is the invitation of the gospel. God does not want our rule-keeping without our hearts. He wants us. For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also (Matt 6:21). What would it mean today to give him your heart, not just your time or your duty? No one gives it wholly; Christ alone gave the Father an undivided heart, and he gave it in our place.

A deep pit. And the reason the father asks for the heart immediately appears. A heart not given to him will be given to someone else. The prostitute is a deep pit; the adulteress, literally "a foreign woman" as the ESV notes, is a narrow well, easy to fall into and almost impossible to get out of.

She lies in wait. She is a hunter, lying in wait. And she increases the traitors: every man who falls to her has betrayed a wife, a family, a vow, a God. Sexual sin multiplies betrayal.

verseByVerse.quote: Who has woe? Who has sorrow? Who has strife? Who has complaining? Who has wounds without cause? Who has redness of eyes? Those who tarry long over wine; those who go to try mixed wine. Do not look at wine when it is red, when it sparkles in the cup and goes down smoothly. In the end it bites like a serpent and stings like an adder.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who has woe? Perhaps the fullest portrait of drunkenness in the Bible opens with six questions, like a riddle. Anyone who has lived with an alcoholic, or been one, recognises every line.

Those who tarry long. The answer: those who tarry long, who stay and keep drinking. Not the person who has a glass with dinner, but the one who lingers, and the one who goes looking for new kinds of drink to try. Isaiah pronounced woe on those who tarry late into the evening as wine inflames them (Isa 5:11).

Do not look at wine. The warning starts with the eyes, and the attraction is described honestly. The father does not pretend it is not appealing. He says: for some people, the only safe thing is not to look.

Does the Bible forbid all alcohol? No. Wine is among God's gifts (Ps 104:15), and Jesus made it at a wedding (John 2:1–11). What Scripture condemns is drunkenness (Eph 5:18) and lingering over drink. For some, especially those who have struggled with it, not drinking at all is the wise and free choice, and no one should press a drink on them (Rom 14:21).

In the end. These are the same words as 5:4, where the forbidden woman, sweet at first, turns bitter in the end. The sparkle hides fangs. What goes down smoothly bites like a snake: liver disease, lost jobs, broken families, violence, death on the roads.

verseByVerse.quote: Your eyes will see strange things, and your heart utter perverse things. You will be like one who lies down in the midst of the sea, like one who lies on the top of a mast. "They struck me," you will say, "but I was not hurt; they beat me, but I did not feel it. When shall I awake? I must have another drink."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Strange things. Drunkenness distorts perception and loosens the tongue. Many a person has said something drunk that destroyed a relationship he spent years building.

On the top of a mast. The room is spinning, like a ship's mast (the ESV notes "of the rigging") swaying in a storm. He cannot find anything steady.

"I must have another drink." The saddest line: he wakes with bruises he cannot remember, and his first thought on waking is not "I must stop" but I must have another drink. That is addiction, described thousands of years ago with perfect accuracy: the substance that has hurt him is the thing he reaches for first.

Scripture takes this seriously. Paul said, I will not be dominated by anything (1 Cor 6:12). But the gospel also meets the addict where he is. Jesus said, Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick (Mark 2:17). The cry of the enslaved person is Paul's: Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord! (Rom 7:24-25).

If this verse describes you, or someone you love, it is not a hopeless verdict. It is a diagnosis, and diagnosis is where help begins. Tell someone, get help, and bring it to Christ, who sets captives free.

23.theology:
Wealth is uncertain and must not become the goal of life (vv. 4-5; 1 Tim 6:17-19). God is the strong Redeemer of the fatherless (vv. 10-11; Job 19:25). The fear of the LORD has a future hope that cannot be cut off (vv. 17-18; Ps 73:17, 26).

God asks first for the heart (v. 26). Drunkenness enslaves and distorts (vv. 29-35; Eph 5:18; 1 Cor 6:12), yet Christ came as a physician for the sick and delivers those enslaved (Mark 2:17; Rom 7:24-25).
23.examples:
The chapter moves from the chief executive's dinner and the host who says "Eat and drink!" while counting the cost, to money growing wings, to Boaz the redeemer standing behind the orphan's field.

At home it asks for patience with a mother who repeats herself in old age, and for truth bought and never sold. And at its centre is the call to give God the heart, set against the drunkard in his spinning room whose first waking thought is another drink.

24.title: The Righteous Falls Seven Times and Rises Again
24.text: <sup>1</sup>Be not envious of evil men, nor desire to be with them,<sup>2</sup>for their hearts devise violence, and their lips talk of trouble.<sup>3</sup>By wisdom a house is built, and by understanding it is established;<sup>4</sup>by knowledge the rooms are filled with all precious and pleasant riches.<sup>5</sup>A wise man is full of strength, and a man of knowledge enhances his might,<sup>6</sup>for by wise guidance you can wage your war, and in abundance of counselors there is victory.<sup>7</sup>Wisdom is too high for a fool; in the gate he does not open his mouth.<sup>8</sup>Whoever plans to do evil will be called a schemer.<sup>9</sup>The devising of folly is sin, and the scoffer is an abomination to mankind.<sup>10</sup>If you faint in the day of adversity, your strength is small.<sup>11</sup>Rescue those who are being taken away to death; hold back those who are stumbling to the slaughter.<sup>12</sup>If you say, "Behold, we did not know this," does not he who weighs the heart perceive it? Does not he who keeps watch over your soul know it, and will he not repay man according to his work?<sup>13</sup>My son, eat honey, for it is good, and the drippings of the honeycomb are sweet to your taste.<sup>14</sup>Know that wisdom is such to your soul; if you find it, there will be a future, and your hope will not be cut off.<sup>15</sup>Lie not in wait as a wicked man against the dwelling of the righteous; do no violence to his home;<sup>16</sup>for the righteous falls seven times and rises again, but the wicked stumble in times of calamity.<sup>17</sup>Do not rejoice when your enemy falls, and let not your heart be glad when he stumbles,<sup>18</sup>lest the LORD see it and be displeased, and turn away his anger from him.<sup>19</sup>Fret not yourself because of evildoers, and be not envious of the wicked,<sup>20</sup>for the evil man has no future; the lamp of the wicked will be put out.<sup>21</sup>My son, fear the LORD and the king, and do not join with those who do otherwise,<sup>22</sup>for disaster will arise suddenly from them, and who knows the ruin that will come from them both?<sup>23</sup>These also are sayings of the wise. Partiality in judging is not good.<sup>24</sup>Whoever says to the wicked, "You are in the right," will be cursed by peoples, abhorred by nations,<sup>25</sup>but those who rebuke the wicked will have delight, and a good blessing will come upon them.<sup>26</sup>Whoever gives an honest answer kisses the lips.<sup>27</sup>Prepare your work outside; get everything ready for yourself in the field, and after that build your house.<sup>28</sup>Be not a witness against your neighbor without cause, and do not deceive with your lips.<sup>29</sup>Do not say, "I will do to him as he has done to me; I will pay the man back for what he has done."<sup>30</sup>I passed by the field of a sluggard, by the vineyard of a man lacking sense,<sup>31</sup>and behold, it was all overgrown with thorns; the ground was covered with nettles, and its stone wall was broken down.<sup>32</sup>Then I saw and considered it; I looked and received instruction.<sup>33</sup>A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest,<sup>34</sup>and poverty will come upon you like a robber, and want like an armed man.
24.overview: Wisdom builds, strengthens, and does not look away from those being led to death (vv. 1-12). Wisdom is sweet, the righteous fall seven times and rise again, and no one should gloat or fret over the wicked (vv. 13-22). Further sayings of the wise, ending at the sluggard's ruined vineyard (vv. 23-34).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Do not envy evil men. Wisdom builds a house and gives strength, adversity tests it, and the one who weighs the heart calls the wise to rescue those being led to death (vv. 11-12).
verseByVerse.theology: Wisdom builds, strengthens and refuses to look away from those being led to death.

verseByVerse.quote: Be not envious of evil men, nor desire to be with them, for their hearts devise violence, and their lips talk of trouble.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be not envious of evil men. The warning of 23:17 comes back, and it adds something: nor desire to be with them. Envy of the wicked does not stay envy. It becomes a longing to belong to their circle, to share their freedom and their success. It is the same pull the gang exerted in chapter 1.

Their hearts devise violence. Look past the success to the heart, and the topics are violence and trouble. The life that looked enviable from outside is poison from inside.

verseByVerse.quote: By wisdom a house is built, and by understanding it is established; by knowledge the rooms are filled with all precious and pleasant riches.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By wisdom a house is built. A house, a family, a business, a church: all built by wisdom and made firm by understanding. Not by money first, or cleverness, or luck.

The rooms are filled. The riches here are precious and pleasant: not only valuable but lovely to live with. Think of a home where wisdom lives: laughter, peace, stored-up memories, faith, good conversation, hospitality. Those are the treasures that fill rooms built by wisdom. A large house built by folly can be empty in every room.

verseByVerse.quote: A wise man is full of strength, and a man of knowledge enhances his might, for by wise guidance you can wage your war, and in abundance of counselors there is victory. Wisdom is too high for a fool; in the gate he does not open his mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Full of strength. The wise man may not be physically powerful, but he knows what to do, how to do it, and when. Knowledge multiplies whatever might he has.

Wise guidance. Battles are won by good planning and good advice (compare 11:14; 20:18). A general who listens to his advisers beats one who trusts only himself. The same is true of every struggle a person faces: an illness, a financial crisis, a troubled child. Get counsel.

Wisdom is too high for a fool. In the city gate, where the elders gathered to decide matters, the fool has nothing to contribute. Wisdom is out of his reach, like fruit on a high branch.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever plans to do evil will be called a schemer. The devising of folly is sin, and the scoffer is an abomination to mankind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A schemer. The man who keeps planning evil soon has a name for it. Reputation follows intention.

The devising of folly. Even planning folly is sin; the ESV notes that devising may be "scheming". Sin does not begin when the act is done; it begins in the plotting. And the scoffer, the mocker of everything good, is not merely disliked; he is an abomination to mankind.

verseByVerse.quote: If you faint in the day of adversity, your strength is small.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Adversity reveals strength. Anyone can look strong when life is easy. If you collapse the moment trouble comes, your strength was small all along.

That can sound harsh, but it is an honest mirror, and it drives a believer to the right source. Human strength is small. God's is not. He gives power to the faint, and to him who has no might he increases strength, and they who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength (Isa 40:29, 31). Paul discovered that the Lord's power is made perfect in weakness, so that he could say, For when I am weak, then I am strong (2 Cor 12:9-10).

So the proverb is not a command to grit your teeth and be tough. It is an invitation to find strength larger than your own before the day of adversity comes. Let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up (Gal 6:9).
