verseByVerse.quote: Rescue those who are being taken away to death; hold back those who are stumbling to the slaughter. If you say, "Behold, we did not know this," does not he who weighs the heart perceive it? Does not he who keeps watch over your soul know it, and will he not repay man according to his work?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rescue those. There are people being led toward death, whether through injustice, violence, addiction, despair or their own folly, and the wise are commanded to act: rescue, hold back. Not to observe, not to feel sorry, but to intervene.

The applications are wide: the vulnerable unborn, the trafficked, the persecuted, the neighbour sinking into suicidal despair, the friend drinking himself to death, and above all the person without Christ walking toward eternal death. Which of them is within your reach?

We did not know this. The proverb refuses the excuse. God weighs the heart. He knows whether we truly did not know, or chose not to know, or knew and looked away. The priest and the Levite in Jesus' parable saw the wounded man and passed by on the other side (Luke 10:31). So whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, for him it is sin (Jas 4:17).

That is uncomfortable, and meant to be. Deliberate ignorance is not innocence in God's eyes. Yet the God who weighs the heart forgives those who confess, and Christ, who did not pass by on the other side, sends them out again in his Spirit's strength.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wisdom is sweet as honey, for the righteous falls seven times and rises again (v. 16). Do not gloat over an enemy or fret over evildoers; fear the LORD and the king (vv. 17-22).
verseByVerse.theology: The righteous are not those who never fall but those who keep getting up, and they do not gloat when others fall.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, eat honey, for it is good, and the drippings of the honeycomb are sweet to your taste. Know that wisdom is such to your soul; if you find it, there will be a future, and your hope will not be cut off.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eat honey. After a heavy warning, a sweet invitation. Honey is good; enjoy it. God gave good things to be tasted.

Wisdom is such to your soul. Wisdom is like honey to the soul: sweet, nourishing, delightful. The psalmist said of God's words, How sweet are your words to my taste, sweeter than honey to my mouth! (Ps 119:103). Many people think of God's wisdom as bitter medicine. The proverb says: taste it, it is honey.

And it brings a future. The second half repeats the promise of 23:18 word for word: your hope will not be cut off. Wisdom is sweet now and secure later.

verseByVerse.quote: Lie not in wait as a wicked man against the dwelling of the righteous; do no violence to his home; for the righteous falls seven times and rises again, but the wicked stumble in times of calamity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seven times. Here is why plots against the righteous fail, and it must be read carefully. It does not say the righteous never fall. They fall seven times, a number meaning again and again. They fall into hardship, into failure, into sin. What makes them righteous is not that they never go down, but that they rise again.

The wicked stumble once and stay down. The righteous keep getting up, because God keeps lifting them. Rejoice not over me, O my enemy; when I fall, I shall rise (Mic 7:8).

Peter fell as badly as a disciple can fall, denying Jesus three times. But Jesus had said to him beforehand, I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers (Luke 22:32). He rose. If you have fallen, perhaps for the seventh time, the question is not whether you fell. It is whether you will rise. And the one who prays for Peter prays for you.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not rejoice when your enemy falls, and let not your heart be glad when he stumbles, lest the LORD see it and be displeased, and turn away his anger from him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not rejoice. The natural response when an enemy comes to disaster is satisfaction: he got what he deserved. The proverb forbids even the inner gladness: let not your heart be glad. It is a remarkable command for the Old Testament, and it points straight to Jesus: Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you (Matt 5:44).

Lest the LORD see it. The second line is surprising. If you gloat, God may be so displeased with your gloating that he turns his anger away from your enemy, and perhaps toward you. The point is not that we should hide our gladness in order to make sure the enemy suffers. It is that gloating over someone's fall is itself an ugly sin, one God will not reward. God himself says, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezek 33:11). Neither should we.

verseByVerse.quote: Fret not yourself because of evildoers, and be not envious of the wicked, for the evil man has no future; the lamp of the wicked will be put out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fret not yourself. This echoes Psalm 37, which begins, Fret not yourself because of evildoers; be not envious of wrongdoers! (Ps 37:1). To fret is to get heated and anxious, to lie awake angry that the wicked are doing well. It burns the fretter, not the wicked.

No future. Whatever the evil man has now, it ends (compare 13:9). The righteous have a future that will not be cut off (v. 14). The wicked have only a present. There is nothing there to envy.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, fear the LORD and the king, and do not join with those who do otherwise, for disaster will arise suddenly from them, and who knows the ruin that will come from them both?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fear the LORD and the king. The fear of the LORD comes first, and then respect for rightful authority. Peter says the same, in the same order: Fear God. Honor the emperor (1 Pet 2:17). And do not join rebels, people who despise both God and those in authority. Pay to all what is owed to them, respect to whom respect is owed (Rom 13:7).

Disaster will arise suddenly. Those who rebel against God and rightful authority bring sudden disaster on themselves, and on those who join them. Keep away from the revolt.

Must we obey every government? We honour and obey rulers (Rom 13:1–7; 1 Pet 2:17), but the LORD comes first: when a ruler commands sin, We must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29; cf. Dan 3). The verse warns against rebellion, not against refusing to sin.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Further sayings of the wise (v. 23): impartial judgment, honest answers, order in work, no revenge, and the lesson of the sluggard's vineyard: A little sleep, a little slumber (v. 33).
verseByVerse.theology: Honest words and ordered work build a life; neglect lets thorns take it over quietly.

verseByVerse.quote: These also are sayings of the wise. Partiality in judging is not good. Whoever says to the wicked, "You are in the right," will be cursed by peoples, abhorred by nations, but those who rebuke the wicked will have delight, and a good blessing will come upon them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Partiality in judging. A new heading introduces a short appendix of further sayings. The first is about justice: a judge must not play favourites. The law said, You shall not be partial in judgment. You shall hear the small and the great alike (Deut 1:17). That applies wherever anyone makes judgments about others: the parent between children, the teacher grading work, the church leader settling a dispute.

"You are in the right". A judge who acquits the guilty is not merely wrong; he is cursed by peoples. Calling evil good destroys public trust.

Those who rebuke the wicked. And the one with the courage to say "You are in the wrong" to the guilty is blessed. Honest judgment takes courage, and God honours it.
verseByVerse.note: Another short collection of “sayings of the wise” (24:23–34).

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever gives an honest answer kisses the lips. Prepare your work outside; get everything ready for yourself in the field, and after that build your house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An honest answer. An honest answer is a kiss, a sign of true friendship: honesty is a form of love. The friend who tells you the truth, gently, is kissing you.

Prepare your work outside. First the field, which provides a living; then the house. Do not build the beautiful home before you have the income to support it. A young couple who get the foundations of work and finances right before taking on large commitments are following this proverb. Jesus asked, which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost (Luke 14:28)?

verseByVerse.quote: Be not a witness against your neighbor without cause, and do not deceive with your lips. Do not say, "I will do to him as he has done to me; I will pay the man back for what he has done."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be not a witness. This is the ninth commandment in proverb form: do not testify against a neighbour without cause, or deceive with your lips.

As he has done to me. The voice of revenge sounds reasonable, even like justice. The proverb forbids saying it. Personal revenge is not ours to take (compare 20:22).

Jesus turned this completely around. Not "do to him as he has done to me", but whatever you wish that others would do to you, do also to them (Matt 7:12). The Golden Rule is the opposite of revenge. Repay no one evil for evil (Rom 12:17).

verseByVerse.quote: I passed by the field of a sluggard, by the vineyard of a man lacking sense, and behold, it was all overgrown with thorns; the ground was covered with nettles, and its stone wall was broken down. Then I saw and considered it; I looked and received instruction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The field of a sluggard. The chapter ends with an eyewitness story, like the father's in chapter 7.

Overgrown with thorns. With the wall down, animals and thieves could get in. No enemy had attacked the vineyard. No drought had struck. It had simply been left alone.

That is the terrifying thing about neglect. It does not require any action at all. Thorns grow by themselves. Walls fall by themselves. A marriage left untended, a prayer life abandoned, a child not taught, a body not cared for, a faith not fed: none needs to be attacked to be ruined. It only needs to be left.

I saw and considered it. He did not just see a mess and walk on. He considered it and received instruction. Wise people learn from what they see in other people's lives. Is there a neglected vineyard you have watched fall apart, and what did it teach you about your own?

verseByVerse.quote: A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest, and poverty will come upon you like a robber, and want like an armed man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A little sleep. The ruin of the vineyard did not come from one big decision to let it go. It came from a little sleep, a little slumber, a little rest. Every day, a small postponement. Every season, the work put off a bit longer.

Like a robber. And one day it arrives, sudden and unstoppable. The sluggard is surprised. No one who walked past his vineyard is.

What is the vineyard in your life where the wall is starting to crumble? Today, with the Lord's help, is a better day than tomorrow to pull the first thorn and lay the first stone back in place.
verseByVerse.note: Repeats 6:10–11.

24.theology:
Wisdom builds lasting homes (vv. 3-4). Human strength fails in adversity, but God gives strength to the faint (v. 10; Isa 40:29-31; 2 Cor 12:9-10). God holds people responsible for rescuing those in mortal danger and sees through deliberate ignorance (vv. 11-12; Jas 4:17).

The righteous are marked not by never falling but by rising again through God's grace (v. 16; Mic 7:8; Luke 22:32). Gloating over an enemy's fall displeases God (vv. 17-18; Ezek 33:11; Matt 5:44). Revenge is forbidden (v. 29; Matt 7:12). Neglect alone brings ruin (vv. 30-34).

The rising of the righteous (v. 16) rests on more than resilience. The Righteous One himself went down into death for the unrighteous and was raised (Acts 3:14–15; 1 Pet 3:18), and because he rose, those who are his will rise too, from every fall and at last from the grave (1 Cor 15:20–22). He is also the one who did what verse 11 commands: he came to rescue those being led away to death.
24.examples:
Picture rooms filled with riches that are precious and pleasant, and strength found out on the day of adversity. Hear the excuse "We didn't know," and notice the quiet gladness that rises when an enemy stumbles.

Then remember Peter, who fell and rose; an honest answer given like a kiss; the field prepared before the house; and the vineyard ruined without any enemy at all.

25.title: A Word Fitly Spoken
25.text: <sup>1</sup>These also are proverbs of Solomon which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied.<sup>2</sup>It is the glory of God to conceal things, but the glory of kings is to search things out.<sup>3</sup>As the heavens for height, and the earth for depth, so the heart of kings is unsearchable.<sup>4</sup>Take away the dross from the silver, and the smith has material for a vessel;<sup>5</sup>take away the wicked from the presence of the king, and his throne will be established in righteousness.<sup>6</sup>Do not put yourself forward in the king's presence or stand in the place of the great,<sup>7</sup>for it is better to be told, "Come up here," than to be put lower in the presence of a noble. What your eyes have seen<sup>8</sup>do not hastily bring into court, for what will you do in the end, when your neighbor puts you to shame?<sup>9</sup>Argue your case with your neighbor himself, and do not reveal another's secret,<sup>10</sup>lest he who hears you bring shame upon you, and your ill repute have no end.<sup>11</sup>A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in a setting of silver.<sup>12</sup>Like a gold ring or an ornament of gold is a wise reprover to a listening ear.<sup>13</sup>Like the cold of snow in the time of harvest is a faithful messenger to those who send him; he refreshes the soul of his masters.<sup>14</sup>Like clouds and wind without rain is a man who boasts of a gift he does not give.<sup>15</sup>With patience a ruler may be persuaded, and a soft tongue will break a bone.<sup>16</sup>If you have found honey, eat only enough for you, lest you have your fill of it and vomit it.<sup>17</sup>Let your foot be seldom in your neighbor's house, lest he have his fill of you and hate you.<sup>18</sup>A man who bears false witness against his neighbor is like a war club, or a sword, or a sharp arrow.<sup>19</sup>Trusting in a treacherous man in time of trouble is like a bad tooth or a foot that slips.<sup>20</sup>Whoever sings songs to a heavy heart is like one who takes off a garment on a cold day, and like vinegar on soda.<sup>21</sup>If your enemy is hungry, give him bread to eat, and if he is thirsty, give him water to drink,<sup>22</sup>for you will heap burning coals on his head, and the LORD will reward you.<sup>23</sup>The north wind brings forth rain, and a backbiting tongue, angry looks.<sup>24</sup>It is better to live in a corner of the housetop than in a house shared with a quarrelsome wife.<sup>25</sup>Like cold water to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country.<sup>26</sup>Like a muddied spring or a polluted fountain is a righteous man who gives way before the wicked.<sup>27</sup>It is not good to eat much honey, nor is it glorious to seek one's own glory.<sup>28</sup>A man without self-control is like a city broken into and left without walls.
25.overview: The men of Hezekiah copied these proverbs. God's glory conceals and a king's glory searches out; humility waits to be called up, and disputes are settled privately (vv. 1-10). Words fitly spoken, faithful messengers, gentle persuasion, and the wounds of false friends (vv. 11-20). Kindness to an enemy, good news from afar, and the broken wall of a life without self-control (vv. 21-28).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Glory of Kings and the Wisdom of Restraint
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A new collection, copied by the men of Hezekiah (v. 1). It is the glory of God to conceal things (v. 2); the wise wait to be honoured and settle disputes privately (vv. 6-10).
verseByVerse.theology: God's glory hides what is too deep for us; human wisdom searches, waits to be honoured, and settles disputes privately.

verseByVerse.quote: These also are proverbs of Solomon which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A new collection begins, and the heading tells us something moving about how the Bible came to us. King Hezekiah of Judah had scholars at his court gather and copy out further proverbs of Solomon. Hezekiah was one of Judah's most faithful kings: He trusted in the LORD, the God of Israel, and held fast to the LORD (2 Kgs 18:5-6). Part of his reformation was preserving God's word for the next generation.

Chapters 25 to 29 are the fruit of that work. The men of Hezekiah are unnamed, but every reader of these chapters owes them a debt. Faithful copying, preserving and passing on of Scripture is an act of love for people not yet born.
verseByVerse.note: Hezekiah reigned about 715–686 BC, more than two centuries after Solomon.

verseByVerse.quote: It is the glory of God to conceal things, but the glory of kings is to search things out. As the heavens for height, and the earth for depth, so the heart of kings is unsearchable. Take away the dross from the silver, and the smith has material for a vessel; take away the wicked from the presence of the king, and his throne will be established in righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The glory of God to conceal. God is glorious in what he hides: the depths of his purposes, the reasons for suffering, the workings of providence that we cannot trace. The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us (Deut 29:29). How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways! (Rom 11:33).

A human ruler, by contrast, is glorious in searching things out: investigating a case, discovering the truth, understanding his realm. God does not need to search; he knows. Kings must search, because they do not.

That gives a believer permission to be humble about what God has not revealed, and energy to investigate everything he has given us to understand. Science, scholarship, justice and study of Scripture are all royal work: searching out what God has placed within our reach.

As the heavens for height. And yet even a king's heart is too deep for his subjects to read: people cannot fully know what a ruler is thinking or planning. How much less can anyone fathom the heart of God.

Take away the dross. A silversmith cannot make a beautiful vessel until the impurities are removed. A king cannot rule justly while surrounded by wicked advisers. Remove them, and the throne rests on righteousness. Every leader should look at the people closest to him and ask whether they are silver or dross.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not put yourself forward in the king's presence or stand in the place of the great, for it is better to be told, "Come up here," than to be put lower in the presence of a noble. What your eyes have seen do not hastily bring into court, for what will you do in the end, when your neighbor puts you to shame?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not put yourself forward. In the royal court it is foolish to push yourself into a place of honour that is not yours.

"Come up here". Jesus built a parable on exactly this proverb: go and sit in the lowest place, so that when your host comes he may say to you, 'Friend, move up higher.' And he drew the conclusion: For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted (Luke 14:10-11).

In the office, the church, the family: the person who promotes himself is often embarrassed, and the one who waits to be recognised is often honoured.

Do not hastily bring into court. The last words of verse 7 run into verse 8: What your eyes have seen, do not hastily bring into court. The ESV notes a different way of dividing the lines is possible, but the counsel is the same. You saw something, and you are sure. Do not rush to sue or accuse. What if you misunderstood? What if your neighbour has a side you did not see? You may end up the one put to shame.

Jesus urged, Come to terms quickly with your accuser while you are going with him to court (Matt 5:25). And Paul told the Corinthians, To have lawsuits at all with one another is already a defeat for you. Why not rather suffer wrong? (1 Cor 6:7).
verseByVerse.note: Jesus told a parable along these lines.

verseByVerse.quote: Argue your case with your neighbor himself, and do not reveal another's secret, lest he who hears you bring shame upon you, and your ill repute have no end.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Argue your case. Take a dispute to the person directly, not to the court of public opinion, and never use another's private information as ammunition. Jesus gave the same order: go to your brother first, between you and him alone (Matt 18:15).

Lest he who hears you. A person who reveals secrets to win an argument may win it, and lose his reputation for good. Everyone who hears him learns that he cannot be trusted. That kind of name does not wash off.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in a setting of silver (v. 11). Faithful messengers, empty boasters, a soft tongue, moderation, and the wounds of false witnesses and false friends (vv. 13-20).
verseByVerse.theology: Words and presence can refresh or wound, and the difference is timing, truth and restraint.

verseByVerse.quote: A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in a setting of silver. Like a gold ring or an ornament of gold is a wise reprover to a listening ear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A word fitly spoken. Picture golden fruit set in silver filigree. A word fitly spoken fits the moment, the person, the need.

The same sentence can be gold in one setting and lead in another. Comfort offered too soon to the grieving, correction given in public, a joke at the wrong moment: the words may be true and still not fit. Wisdom is knowing not only what to say but when and how.

A wise reprover. A rebuke can be jewellery, on two conditions: a wise reprover, and a listening ear. Then it makes the listener more beautiful, not less.

verseByVerse.quote: Like the cold of snow in the time of harvest is a faithful messenger to those who send him; he refreshes the soul of his masters. Like clouds and wind without rain is a man who boasts of a gift he does not give.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The cold of snow. Imagine labouring in the fields at harvest in the heat, and being handed a drink cooled with snow brought down from the mountains. That is what a faithful messenger is to the one who sent him: pure refreshment.

Christians are messengers of Christ. A faithful one refreshes the heart of his Master.

Clouds and wind without rain. In a dry land, clouds raise hope of rain, and when none falls the disappointment is bitter. So with the man who talks of the gift he will give and never gives it. Jude uses the same picture for false teachers: waterless clouds, swept along by winds (Jude 12). Is there a promise of help you made and have not kept? Keep it if you still can; the God who keeps every promise to you forgives the ones you have broken.

verseByVerse.quote: With patience a ruler may be persuaded, and a soft tongue will break a bone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gentleness is stronger than force. The person who shouts at a stubborn authority usually hardens it. The person who is patient and speaks gently can wear down resistance that seemed unbreakable. Water softly dripping cuts through rock.

Patience and gentleness are not weakness. They break bones.

verseByVerse.quote: If you have found honey, eat only enough for you, lest you have your fill of it and vomit it. Let your foot be seldom in your neighbor's house, lest he have his fill of you and hate you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eat only enough. Even good things become bad in excess. Honey is sweet and good (24:13), but eat too much and you will be sick. Good gifts need to be enjoyed with moderation: food, pleasure, entertainment, even rest.

Let your foot be seldom. Friendship is sweet too, but the friend who is always at your door, who overstays, who never gives you space, becomes wearying. Wise friends leave before they are too much.

verseByVerse.quote: A man who bears false witness against his neighbor is like a war club, or a sword, or a sharp arrow. Trusting in a treacherous man in time of trouble is like a bad tooth or a foot that slips. Whoever sings songs to a heavy heart is like one who takes off a garment on a cold day, and like vinegar on soda.
verseByVerse.commentary:
False witness. Three weapons: one crushes, one cuts, one pierces from a distance. False testimony does all three. It crushes a reputation, cuts relationships, and can wound from far away, spoken where the victim cannot answer.

A treacherous man. A bad tooth fails you exactly when you bite down. A foot slips exactly when you put weight on it. A treacherous friend fails you exactly when you lean on him. It is not merely that he does not help; relying on him makes the pain worse. Choose friends you can put weight on.

Songs to a heavy heart. Cheerful songs sung to someone in grief are like taking away his coat in the cold, or pouring vinegar on soda so that it fizzes and foams: well meant, perhaps, but they make things worse.

That is a sensitive word for Christians, who sometimes rush to say "Everything happens for a reason" or "Just rejoice" to people in deep pain. Weep with those who weep (Rom 12:15). Sometimes the best thing is to sit quietly with them and say little. The songs can come later.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–28 — Burning Coals and Broken Walls
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: If your enemy is hungry, give him bread to eat (v. 21). Backbiting, good news, a muddied spring, and A man without self-control is like a city broken into and left without walls (v. 28).
verseByVerse.theology: Kindness to an enemy is the strongest answer to evil, and self-control is the wall around a life.

verseByVerse.quote: If your enemy is hungry, give him bread to eat, and if he is thirsty, give him water to drink, for you will heap burning coals on his head, and the LORD will reward you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Give him bread. Here the Old Testament anticipates the Sermon on the Mount. The answer to an enemy is not revenge, and not even neutrality, but kindness.

Burning coals. What does it mean to heap burning coals on his head? Not to hurt him more cleverly. The image is of the burning shame and conviction that kindness produces in an enemy. He expected retaliation and got bread, and it sears his conscience. Kindness may melt his hostility and bring him to repentance.

Paul quotes these verses in Romans 12 and adds his own conclusion: Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good (Rom 12:21). And God himself did exactly this. While we were his enemies, he gave us his Son: while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son (Rom 5:10). The hungry enemy he fed was us. Is there an enemy you could feed this week?

Some read the coals as judgment: if the enemy will not repent, kindness increases his guilt before God. Others point to an Egyptian ritual in which a penitent carried coals on his head as a sign of shame. The best reading is that kindness burns the conscience, bringing shame that may lead to repentance; Paul uses the verse to say overcome evil with good (Rom 12:20–21).

verseByVerse.quote: The north wind brings forth rain, and a backbiting tongue, angry looks. It is better to live in a corner of the housetop than in a house shared with a quarrelsome wife.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The north wind. As surely as a certain wind brings rain, a tongue that talks behind people's backs brings angry faces. The people talked about find out, and the storm comes.

A corner of the housetop. Word for word the same as 21:9: some truths about home life deserve saying twice.

verseByVerse.quote: Like cold water to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country. Like a muddied spring or a polluted fountain is a righteous man who gives way before the wicked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cold water to a thirsty soul. In a world without phones, a family might wait months for news of a son who had travelled far away. When the messenger finally came and said, "He is well", it was like cold water to a parched throat.

There is no better news from a far country than the gospel: news from heaven that God has sent his Son, that sins are forgiven, that death is defeated. How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news (Isa 52:7).

A muddied spring. A spring is where people come for clean water. If it is muddied, everyone who depends on it suffers. A righteous person who caves in to the wicked, who compromises his integrity under pressure, muddies the spring. That is a heavy responsibility for anyone whose example others follow.

verseByVerse.quote: It is not good to eat much honey, nor is it glorious to seek one's own glory. A man without self-control is like a city broken into and left without walls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is not good. Honey again (compare v. 16), now compared with glory. The ESV notes that the meaning of this line is uncertain, but the sense is clear enough. Glory, like honey, is sweet in its place and sickening when a person gorges on it. Chasing your own glory is not glorious. Jesus asked, How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God? (John 5:44).

A man without self-control. An unwalled city was helpless before any raiding band. So is a person without self-control. Anger walks in. Lust walks in. Greed, gluttony, laziness and every passing impulse walk in and take what they want. There is nothing to stop them.

Self-control is the wall around a life. And it is a gift of the Spirit: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control (Gal 5:22-23). Peter tells believers to add to their faith knowledge with self-control (2 Pet 1:6). Where is your wall broken down? That is where the enemy is walking in.

25.theology:
God's glory includes what he conceals (v. 2; Deut 29:29; Rom 11:33). The preservation of Scripture is a work of faithful people (v. 1). Humility waits to be exalted (vv. 6-7; Luke 14:8-11). Disputes are to be settled privately and quickly (vv. 8-10; Matt 5:25; 18:15).

Fitting speech is precious (v. 11), and compassion must be sensitive to the grieving (v. 20; Rom 12:15). Kindness to enemies overcomes evil (vv. 21-22; Rom 12:20-21). The counsel to take the lower seat (vv. 6-7) was lived out by Christ himself, who humbled himself to the cross and was given the name above every name (Phil 2:5–11). And the glory of God in concealing (v. 2) has its counterpart in the gospel: the mystery hidden for ages is now revealed in Christ (Col 1:26–27). Self-control is a life's wall and a fruit of the Spirit (v. 28; Gal 5:23).
25.examples: Hezekiah's scribes copy for readers not yet born; the humble guest takes the lowest seat; a fitting word is apples of gold in silver, and an empty promise a cloud with no rain. Then come the hard cases: cheerful clichés said too soon to the grieving, bread for a hungry enemy, and a life as open as a city with no walls.

26.title: Answer Not a Fool According to His Folly
26.text: <sup>1</sup>Like snow in summer or rain in harvest, so honor is not fitting for a fool.<sup>2</sup>Like a sparrow in its flitting, like a swallow in its flying, a curse that is causeless does not alight.<sup>3</sup>A whip for the horse, a bridle for the donkey, and a rod for the back of fools.<sup>4</sup>Answer not a fool according to his folly, lest you be like him yourself.<sup>5</sup>Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own eyes.<sup>6</sup>Whoever sends a message by the hand of a fool cuts off his own feet and drinks violence.<sup>7</sup>Like a lame man's legs, which hang useless, is a proverb in the mouth of fools.<sup>8</sup>Like one who binds the stone in the sling is one who gives honor to a fool.<sup>9</sup>Like a thorn that goes up into the hand of a drunkard is a proverb in the mouth of fools.<sup>10</sup>Like an archer who wounds everyone is one who hires a passing fool or drunkard.<sup>11</sup>Like a dog that returns to his vomit is a fool who repeats his folly.<sup>12</sup>Do you see a man who is wise in his own eyes? There is more hope for a fool than for him.<sup>13</sup>The sluggard says, "There is a lion in the road! There is a lion in the streets!"<sup>14</sup>As a door turns on its hinges, so does a sluggard on his bed.<sup>15</sup>The sluggard buries his hand in the dish; it wears him out to bring it back to his mouth.<sup>16</sup>The sluggard is wiser in his own eyes than seven men who can answer sensibly.<sup>17</sup>Whoever meddles in a quarrel not his own is like one who takes a passing dog by the ears.<sup>18</sup>Like a madman who throws firebrands, arrows, and death<sup>19</sup>is the man who deceives his neighbor and says, "I am only joking!"<sup>20</sup>For lack of wood the fire goes out, and where there is no whisperer, quarreling ceases.<sup>21</sup>As charcoal to hot embers and wood to fire, so is a quarrelsome man for kindling strife.<sup>22</sup>The words of a whisperer are like delicious morsels; they go down into the inner parts of the body.<sup>23</sup>Like the glaze covering an earthen vessel are fervent lips with an evil heart.<sup>24</sup>Whoever hates disguises himself with his lips and harbors deceit in his heart;<sup>25</sup>when he speaks graciously, believe him not, for there are seven abominations in his heart;<sup>26</sup>though his hatred be covered with deception, his wickedness will be exposed in the assembly.<sup>27</sup>Whoever digs a pit will fall into it, and a stone will come back on him who starts it rolling.<sup>28</sup>A lying tongue hates its victims, and a flattering mouth works ruin.
26.overview: A portrait of the fool, who does not fit honour and keeps returning to his folly, yet has more hope than the man wise in his own eyes (vv. 1-12); a portrait of the sluggard (vv. 13-16); and portraits of troublemakers: the meddler, the joker, the whisperer, the hater with warm lips, and the flatterer (vv. 17-28).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — A Portrait of the Fool
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Honour does not fit the fool; answer him, or do not, as wisdom sees fit (vv. 4-5); and There is more hope for a fool than for the man wise in his own eyes (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: The fool is out of place in honour, useless with wisdom, and bound to repeat himself; only the self-satisfied man is worse.

verseByVerse.quote: Like snow in summer or rain in harvest, so honor is not fitting for a fool. Like a sparrow in its flitting, like a swallow in its flying, a curse that is causeless does not alight. A whip for the horse, a bridle for the donkey, and a rod for the back of fools.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Snow in summer. Verses 1-12 are a gallery of portraits of the fool. Snow in summer is strange; rain at harvest ruins the crop. Honour given to a fool is like that. It does not belong, and it does damage. Promoting someone who lacks character, celebrating a foolish celebrity, giving authority to a person who will misuse it: it spoils the harvest for everyone.

Like a sparrow in its flitting. A lovely word of comfort in the middle of the fools. A curse spoken without cause is like a small bird darting about: it never lands. If someone curses you unjustly, slanders you, wishes you harm, or claims some spiritual power over you, it has no power to settle on you. When Balak hired Balaam to curse Israel, Balaam could only say, How can I curse whom God has not cursed? (Num 23:8). The believer under God's blessing does not need to fear the causeless curse.

A rod for the back of fools. Animals that will not respond to reason must be directed by force. The fool has made himself like them. He will not listen to words, so pain has to teach him.

verseByVerse.quote: Answer not a fool according to his folly, lest you be like him yourself. Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Answer not a fool. One of the book's most famous pairs. Do not answer a fool on his own terms: if he shouts or mocks, do not do the same, or you sink to his level.

Answer a fool. And verse 5 says the opposite: do answer him, in a way that exposes his folly, or he will go away thinking he was right.

Is the Bible contradicting itself? No. It is teaching how proverbs work. They are not rules to be applied mechanically. Both of these statements are true, and wisdom is knowing which one fits this fool, on this day, in this situation. Sometimes silence is right, because an answer would only drag you down. Sometimes an answer is right, because silence would leave a lie standing and let the fool mislead others.

Jesus did both. When the chief priests demanded to know his authority, he answered with a question that exposed their dishonesty, The baptism of John, from where did it come? From heaven or from man?, and when they refused to answer, he said, Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things (Matt 21:25, 27). The next time someone foolish provokes you, the question is not only "What is true?" but "Will answering help, or will it only make me like him?"
verseByVerse.note: The pairing was noticed early: the rabbis of the Talmud debated these two verses and settled the matter by applying them to different situations.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever sends a message by the hand of a fool cuts off his own feet and drinks violence. Like a lame man's legs, which hang useless, is a proverb in the mouth of fools. Like one who binds the stone in the sling is one who gives honor to a fool.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By the hand of a fool. Sending a fool as your messenger is like cutting off your own feet: the message will not arrive, or will arrive garbled, and you will suffer for it. Compare the faithful messenger of 25:13, like cold snow at harvest.

A lame man's legs. A proverb in a fool's mouth is like a lame man's legs: it is there, but it does nothing. A fool can quote wise sayings, even Bible verses, but he cannot use them. They hang limp, because wisdom requires a wise heart to apply it.

Binds the stone in the sling. A sling is meant to release a stone. If you tie the stone into the sling, the whole thing becomes useless, or the stone flies back and hits you. Honouring a fool is that absurd and that self-defeating.

verseByVerse.quote: Like a thorn that goes up into the hand of a drunkard is a proverb in the mouth of fools. Like an archer who wounds everyone is one who hires a passing fool or drunkard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like a thorn. Verse 7 said a proverb in a fool's mouth is useless. This says it can be dangerous. A drunkard waving a thorn branch around hurts himself and everyone near him. A fool who wields a wise saying or a verse of Scripture, out of context and without understanding, can do real damage: condemning people who need comfort, excusing sins, justifying cruelty. Scripture in the wrong hands becomes a weapon.

Like an archer. Hiring a fool or a drunk you know nothing about is like an archer shooting at random: someone is going to get hurt. The ESV notes that the line may be read, "hires a fool or passersby".

verseByVerse.quote: Like a dog that returns to his vomit is a fool who repeats his folly. Do you see a man who is wise in his own eyes? There is more hope for a fool than for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A dog that returns. A disgusting image, and meant to be: the fool suffers for his folly and goes back to it. The same bad relationship, the same addiction, the same financial disaster, the same explosive temper, again and again.

Peter quotes this proverb about people who had known the way of righteousness and turned back from it: What the true proverb says has happened to them: "The dog returns to its own vomit" (2 Pet 2:22). What is the vomit you keep going back to? Naming it honestly to God is the first step; the Spirit Christ gives is the power to leave it.

Wise in his own eyes? After eleven verses of fools, someone worse: the man wise in his own eyes. The fool, at least, might one day realise he is a fool. The self-satisfied man never will. He cannot be taught, because he already knows. He cannot be corrected, because he is never wrong. And while he sees no need, he will not look for a Saviour.

That is why Jesus said the tax collectors and prostitutes were entering the kingdom ahead of the religious experts. Never be wise in your own sight (Rom 12:16). The most dangerous place to stand is certainty that you do not need to change.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–16 — A Portrait of the Sluggard
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Four sketches of the sluggard, ending: The sluggard is wiser in his own eyes than seven men who can answer sensibly (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: The lazy man has excuses, turns without moving, tires of feeding himself, and is sure he is right.

verseByVerse.quote: The sluggard says, "There is a lion in the road! There is a lion in the streets!" As a door turns on its hinges, so does a sluggard on his bed. The sluggard buries his hand in the dish; it wears him out to bring it back to his mouth. The sluggard is wiser in his own eyes than seven men who can answer sensibly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"There is a lion in the road!" Four quick sketches of the sluggard. The first is the excuse already met at 22:13.

A door turns on its hinges. The second sketch is pure comedy: the sluggard turns over in bed, with plenty of motion and no progress. He is fixed to his bed as a door is fixed to its frame.

Buries his hand in the dish. The third sketch sharpens 19:24. There the sluggard would not bring his hand back to his mouth; here it wears him out to do it. Laziness grows until even eating seems like too much effort.

Than seven men. The fourth sketch matters most. He has a theory for why work is pointless, why effort does not pay, why the people who get up early are fools. And he will not be argued out of it. Laziness nearly always comes with a philosophy to justify it. And it links him with verse 12: wise in his own eyes, and so beyond help.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–28 — Firebrands, Whispers and a Glazed Pot
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The meddler, the "joker", the whisperer and the hater, and Whoever digs a pit will fall into it (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: Destructive speech hides behind jokes, whispers and warm words, and it ends by burying the one who uses it.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever meddles in a quarrel not his own is like one who takes a passing dog by the ears. Like a madman who throws firebrands, arrows, and death is the man who deceives his neighbor and says, "I am only joking!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meddles in a quarrel. A last gallery: troublemakers. Grab a passing dog by the ears and you will be bitten, and cannot safely let go. So with quarrels that are none of your business. Peter lists the meddler alongside the murderer and the thief (1 Pet 4:15).

That does not forbid peacemaking when it is invited and fitting. It forbids the busybody who wades in uninvited and makes things worse.

Like a madman. Such is the man who hurts someone with a lie, a prank or a cruel remark, and then, when he sees the damage, says I am only joking!

Everyone has heard it: the humiliating prank, the cutting "joke" in front of friends, the deceit laughed off when discovered. The joker claims innocence, but the arrows still land. Paul says there should be no crude joking, but instead let there be thanksgiving (Eph 5:4). If you have said "only joking" after hurting someone, the words did not pull the arrow out. An apology might.

verseByVerse.quote: For lack of wood the fire goes out, and where there is no whisperer, quarreling ceases. As charcoal to hot embers and wood to fire, so is a quarrelsome man for kindling strife. The words of a whisperer are like delicious morsels; they go down into the inner parts of the body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For lack of wood. A quarrel with no gossip feeding it dies down. Many conflicts in families and churches would end on their own if people simply stopped carrying the stories back and forth. You may not be able to put out a quarrel, but you can refuse to be its fuel.

Charcoal to hot embers. And some people are fuel: a quarrelsome man keeps strife burning as charcoal keeps embers glowing. Are you the charcoal or the lack of wood in the conflicts around you?

Delicious morsels. Repeated word for word from 18:8. Placed here, it explains why the whisperer keeps finding listeners: gossip tastes good. And what goes down lodges deep. That is why the fire keeps having wood.

verseByVerse.quote: Like the glaze covering an earthen vessel are fervent lips with an evil heart. Whoever hates disguises himself with his lips and harbors deceit in his heart; when he speaks graciously, believe him not, for there are seven abominations in his heart; though his hatred be covered with deception, his wickedness will be exposed in the assembly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Glaze. A cheap clay pot can be coated with a shiny glaze so that it looks like fine ware. The ESV notes that by a change of vowels the Hebrew gives glaze, and otherwise reads "silver of dross", a thin silvery coating over worthless clay. Either way, fervent lips, warm and enthusiastic words, can be a glaze over an evil heart. The warmth is on the surface only.

Jesus said to religious hypocrites, you are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful, but within are full of dead people's bones (Matt 23:27).

Whoever hates disguises himself. A secret hater may speak very graciously. Believe him not. There are seven abominations, a whole heart full of them, behind the pleasant words. The psalmist knew such a man: His speech was smooth as butter, yet war was in his heart (Ps 55:21). Wisdom does not judge by tone alone.

Exposed in the assembly. But the disguise will not last. His wickedness will be exposed in the assembly, in public. Nothing is covered up that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not be known (Luke 12:2). The glaze eventually cracks.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever digs a pit will fall into it, and a stone will come back on him who starts it rolling. A lying tongue hates its victims, and a flattering mouth works ruin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever digs a pit. Two pictures of evil boomeranging. He makes a pit, digging it out, and falls into the hole that he has made. His mischief returns upon his own head (Ps 7:15-16). Haman, hanged on the gallows he had built for Mordecai, is the classic case.

A flattering mouth. The liar may seem friendly, but lying is a form of hatred: you do not lie to people you truly love. And flattery is worse than it looks. It feels pleasant, but it works ruin, because it inflates people, blinds them to their faults, and leads them into disaster. Paul warns of those who by smooth talk and flattery deceive the hearts of the naive (Rom 16:18), and says of his own ministry, we never came with words of flattery (1 Thess 2:5).

Who in your life tells you only what you want to hear? And to whom are you doing that? Real love tells the truth, even when flattery would be easier.

26.theology:
Proverbs must be applied with discernment, not mechanically, as the paired sayings of vv. 4-5 show (Matt 21:24-27). Self-righteous certainty is more hopeless than folly itself (v. 12; Rom 12:16). A causeless curse has no power over those God blesses (v. 2; Num 23:8).

Repeated sin is like a dog returning to its vomit (v. 11; 2 Pet 2:22). Hypocrisy, deceptive joking, gossip and flattery are forms of hatred that will be exposed and will rebound on those who practise them (vv. 18-28; Matt 23:27; Luke 12:2; Ps 7:15-16).

The dog that returns to its vomit (v. 11) shows that folly cannot cure itself, and the man wise in his own eyes (v. 12) shows that it will not ask for a cure. Both need what the chapter cannot give: a new heart. That is the gift of Christ, who became to us wisdom from God (1 Cor 1:30), and in whom The old has passed away (2 Cor 5:17).
26.examples: The chapter is a gallery: rain on the harvest, a curse that flutters and never lands, Scripture as a thorn in a drunkard's hand, a door swinging on its hinges, a passing dog grabbed by the ears, "I'm only joking!", a fire with no wood, and glaze on a cheap pot.

27.title: Iron Sharpens Iron
27.text: <sup>1</sup>Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring.<sup>2</sup>Let another praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips.<sup>3</sup>A stone is heavy, and sand is weighty, but a fool's provocation is heavier than both.<sup>4</sup>Wrath is cruel, anger is overwhelming, but who can stand before jealousy?<sup>5</sup>Better is open rebuke than hidden love.<sup>6</sup>Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy.<sup>7</sup>One who is full loathes honey, but to one who is hungry everything bitter is sweet.<sup>8</sup>Like a bird that strays from its nest is a man who strays from his home.<sup>9</sup>Oil and perfume make the heart glad, and the sweetness of a friend comes from his earnest counsel.<sup>10</sup>Do not forsake your friend and your father's friend, and do not go to your brother's house in the day of your calamity. Better is a neighbor who is near than a brother who is far away.<sup>11</sup>Be wise, my son, and make my heart glad, that I may answer him who reproaches me.<sup>12</sup>The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and suffer for it.<sup>13</sup>Take a man's garment when he has put up security for a stranger, and hold it in pledge when he puts up security for an adulteress.<sup>14</sup>Whoever blesses his neighbor with a loud voice, rising early in the morning, will be counted as cursing.<sup>15</sup>A continual dripping on a rainy day and a quarrelsome wife are alike;<sup>16</sup>to restrain her is to restrain the wind or to grasp oil in one's right hand.<sup>17</sup>Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another.<sup>18</sup>Whoever tends a fig tree will eat its fruit, and he who guards his master will be honored.<sup>19</sup>As in water face reflects face, so the heart of man reflects the man.<sup>20</sup>Sheol and Abaddon are never satisfied, and never satisfied are the eyes of man.<sup>21</sup>The crucible is for silver, and the furnace is for gold, and a man is tested by his praise.<sup>22</sup>Crush a fool in a mortar with a pestle along with crushed grain, yet his folly will not depart from him.<sup>23</sup>Know well the condition of your flocks, and give attention to your herds,<sup>24</sup>for riches do not last forever; and does a crown endure to all generations?<sup>25</sup>When the grass is gone and the new growth appears and the vegetation of the mountains is gathered,<sup>26</sup>the lambs will provide your clothing, and the goats the price of a field.<sup>27</sup>There will be enough goats' milk for your food, for the food of your household and maintenance for your girls.
27.overview: Tomorrow, self-praise, the faithful wounds of a friend, and the worth of a near neighbour (vv. 1-10). People sharpen and reveal one another; the eyes are never satisfied, and praise tests a man (vv. 11-22). A closing poem: know well your flocks, for riches do not last (vv. 23-27).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Tomorrow, Praise and Faithful Wounds
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: None of us owns tomorrow (v. 1). Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy (v. 6). Keep old friends and near neighbours (vv. 9-10).
verseByVerse.theology: Honest friends who wound us are worth more than flatterers who kiss us, and none of us owns tomorrow.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring. Let another praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not boast about tomorrow. Everyone knows this and almost everyone forgets it: tomorrow is not ours. We make plans, schedule meetings, book holidays, and talk about next year as if it were certain. But any day may bring a phone call, a diagnosis, an accident, a blessing no one saw coming.

This is not a call to stop planning. It is a call to plan humbly. James takes up the same point: you do not know what tomorrow will bring. What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes (Jas 4:14), and he tells believers to say, "If the Lord wills." Is there something you are postponing, a reconciliation, a conversation about Christ, an apology, on the assumption that there will be a tomorrow?

Let another praise you. Everyone discounts self-praise; praise from a stranger with no reason to flatter means something. Let your work speak. For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends (2 Cor 10:18).

The social media age has made self-promotion a way of life. The proverb still stands.

verseByVerse.quote: A stone is heavy, and sand is weighty, but a fool's provocation is heavier than both. Wrath is cruel, anger is overwhelming, but who can stand before jealousy?
verseByVerse.commentary:
A fool's provocation. A provoking fool is heavier than stone or wet sand. The constant needling, the unreasonable demands, the pointless arguments: they wear a person down more than physical labour. The proverb is a kind of sympathy for anyone who lives or works with such a person.

Who can stand before jealousy? Anger is destructive, but it often burns out. Jealousy is worse. It settles in and does not let go. A jealous husband, a jealous rival, a jealous colleague will pursue a grievance for years. No one can stand before it. And the Song of Songs says, jealousy is fierce as the grave (Song 8:6).

verseByVerse.quote: Better is open rebuke than hidden love. Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Open rebuke. A friend who sees you walking into disaster and says nothing, because he loves you and does not want to upset you, has not really loved you. Love that will not risk the friendship to tell the truth is not strong enough.

The wounds of a friend. A friend's wounds are faithful: they come from loyalty. They hurt, and they heal. An enemy's kisses are profuse: many, warm, and false. The most notorious kiss in the Bible was an enemy's. Judas, would you betray the Son of Man with a kiss? (Luke 22:48).

Nathan wounded David faithfully: You are the man! (2 Sam 12:7), and it brought him to repentance. Who in your life has wounded you faithfully? Thank them. And is there a friend who needs you to be that faithful, rather than comfortable?

verseByVerse.quote: One who is full loathes honey, but to one who is hungry everything bitter is sweet. Like a bird that strays from its nest is a man who strays from his home.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One who is full loathes honey. Appetite changes how everything tastes. The wealthy person surrounded by luxuries can lose the ability to enjoy them. The person who has little is often more grateful for a simple meal than the rich are for a banquet.

That is a warning against the dullness abundance can bring, and a hint about contentment. Paul had learned the secret of facing plenty and hunger, abundance and need (Phil 4:12). It applies spiritually too. People who feel full of themselves find the gospel tasteless. People who know they are starving find it sweeter than honey.

A bird that strays. A bird away from its nest leaves its young unprotected and is itself exposed; so does a man who wanders from his family, responsibilities and community. Some men stray physically; others stray by being absent while present. Where is your nest, and are you in it?

verseByVerse.quote: Oil and perfume make the heart glad, and the sweetness of a friend comes from his earnest counsel. Do not forsake your friend and your father's friend, and do not go to your brother's house in the day of your calamity. Better is a neighbor who is near than a brother who is far away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Oil and perfume. The ESV notes the line may be read, "and so does the sweetness of a friend that comes from his earnest counsel". A friend's advice, given sincerely, is like perfume in a room.

Do not forsake your friend. First, keep old friends, including family friends who knew your father. Long friendships are precious and irreplaceable.

Second, when disaster strikes, a brother who is far away, geographically or emotionally, may not be the one to run to. Third, a neighbor who is near is often more help than a relative who is distant. The church, the Christian community close at hand, can be closer than family in the day of calamity. Who is near you? Invest in those relationships before the calamity comes.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another (v. 17). The heart reflects the man, the eyes are never satisfied, and A man is tested by his praise (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: People shape and reveal one another, and how a man handles praise tests him as fire tests silver.

verseByVerse.quote: Be wise, my son, and make my heart glad, that I may answer him who reproaches me. The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and suffer for it. Take a man's garment when he has put up security for a stranger, and hold it in pledge when he puts up security for an adulteress.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Make my heart glad. A father's reputation is partly in his son's hands. If people criticise the father, the best answer is a son who turns out wise. The son's life becomes the father's defence. John wrote, I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth (3 John 4).

The prudent sees danger. This is word for word the same as 22:3, perhaps because it is so easily forgotten: see the danger coming, and take cover.

Take a man's garment. Nearly identical to 20:16. The ESV notes that the Hebrew says "a foreign woman", and that a slight change yields "foreigners", as in 20:16. Either way, do not lend to a man with such poor judgment without security.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever blesses his neighbor with a loud voice, rising early in the morning, will be counted as cursing. A continual dripping on a rainy day and a quarrelsome wife are alike; to restrain her is to restrain the wind or to grasp oil in one's right hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With a loud voice. Blessings shouted at your window at dawn feel like a curse. Good words at the wrong time, in the wrong way, or with too much noise become irritating, and people suspect a motive behind such loud flattery.

A continual dripping. The dripping roof of 19:13 returns, with a second picture. Trying to restrain constant quarrelling is like trying to hold back the wind or grip oil in your fist: it slips through your fingers. The proverb speaks of a wife, but the same is true of a husband, a parent or a colleague. Contentiousness cannot be controlled from outside; it has to change from inside.

verseByVerse.quote: Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another. Whoever tends a fig tree will eat its fruit, and he who guards his master will be honored.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Iron sharpens iron. A blade becomes sharp when it is rubbed against another piece of iron. There is friction, heat and sparks, and both pieces are changed. People are like that. The ESV notes the Hebrew is "sharpens the face of another": face to face, in real encounter, people make each other sharper.

That means Christian friendship is not meant to be comfortable only. There will be friction: disagreement, challenge, questions, correction. A friend who never disagrees with you is not sharpening you. Encourage one another and build one another up (1 Thess 5:11).

Who sharpens you? Do you have a friend who will ask you the hard questions about your marriage, your money, your prayer life, your temper? And whom are you sharpening?

Whoever tends a fig tree. A fig tree takes years of patient care before it fruits well; so the servant who faithfully looks after his master's interests will be honoured. Faithful service is rewarded, even if slowly. It is the hard-working farmer who ought to have the first share of the crops (2 Tim 2:6).

verseByVerse.quote: As in water face reflects face, so the heart of man reflects the man. Sheol and Abaddon are never satisfied, and never satisfied are the eyes of man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Face reflects face. As water gives back a face, so the heart gives back the man: what he truly is, is found in his heart, not in his appearance or reputation.

The verse can also be read another way: as you look into another person's heart, you find it reflects your own. People are more alike inside than they appear. The temptations, fears and longings you see in others are in you too. The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it? (Jer 17:9). Looking honestly into your heart is like looking into water: you may not like the face you see, and only God can change it.

Never satisfied. The grave always has room for more, and human eyes are the same. We see something and want it; we get it and see something else. The eye is not satisfied with seeing (Eccl 1:8). John names the desires of the eyes among the things that are not from the Father (1 John 2:16).

That is why no amount of acquiring ever brings contentment. The only thing that fills that emptiness is God himself, who gives himself to us in Christ: whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst (John 6:35).

verseByVerse.quote: The crucible is for silver, and the furnace is for gold, and a man is tested by his praise. Crush a fool in a mortar with a pestle along with crushed grain, yet his folly will not depart from him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tested by his praise. The first half repeats 17:3, where the LORD tests hearts. But here the fire that tests a man is praise. We usually think of hardship as the test, but success and applause reveal character just as surely. Some people handle criticism well and are ruined by praise. They begin to believe what is said about them, grow proud, and stop listening. How you respond when you are praised shows what you are made of.

Crush a fool in a mortar. You can grind a fool as fine as flour, and his folly will still be in there. Suffering alone does not make a fool wise. Only a changed heart does, and that is God's work (Ezek 36:26).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Know well the condition of your flocks, for riches do not last forever (vv. 23-24); faithful care yields enough (vv. 25-27).
verseByVerse.theology: Attentive care for what has been entrusted to you outlasts wealth, and it feeds the household.

verseByVerse.quote: Know well the condition of your flocks, and give attention to your herds, for riches do not last forever; and does a crown endure to all generations?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Know well the condition. A small closing poem to a herdsman, and its counsel is attention. Know well the state of your animals: which sheep is limping, which lamb is not feeding, which ewe is ready to lamb. A good shepherd does not leave the flock to others and hope for the best.

Few readers today keep sheep, but everyone has a flock: children, employees, finances, a congregation, students, a small business, a household. The command is to know them well, personally, not from a distance. Paul told church elders, Pay careful attention to yourselves and to all the flock (Acts 20:28), and Peter, shepherd the flock of God that is among you (1 Pet 5:2).

And every such shepherd follows the Good Shepherd, who said, I know my own and my own know me (John 10:14). He knows the condition of every one of his sheep, and where we have neglected our flocks, he has tended his perfectly, and tends us still.

Does a crown endure? Money can vanish and even royal dynasties end. What lasts is the steady, attentive care of what has been entrusted to you. Wealth is fragile; a well-tended flock renews itself year after year.

verseByVerse.quote: When the grass is gone and the new growth appears and the vegetation of the mountains is gathered, the lambs will provide your clothing, and the goats the price of a field. There will be enough goats' milk for your food, for the food of your household and maintenance for your girls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The new growth appears. If the herdsman has been attentive, the flock provides for him through the seasons. Faithful care is rewarded with provision that keeps coming, season after season.

Enough goats' milk. And the chapter ends on enough: enough milk for the family and for the young women who work in the household. Not extravagant wealth, but steady sufficiency. That is the reward of diligent, attentive, faithful work.

After a chapter full of warnings about boasting, flattery, jealousy and restless eyes, it closes on a quiet picture of contentment: a shepherd who knows his flock, a household fed, a life not grasping but tending. That is a picture worth living toward, in the strength the Good Shepherd gives by his Spirit.

27.theology:
Human beings do not control tomorrow (v. 1; Jas 4:14). True love tells the truth even when it wounds (vv. 5-6; 2 Sam 12:7). Believers sharpen one another through honest relationship (v. 17; 1 Thess 5:11).

The heart reveals the person and is deeply flawed (v. 19; Jer 17:9); human desire is insatiable apart from God (v. 20; 1 John 2:16). Praise tests character (v. 21). Faithful, attentive stewardship is rewarded, and it reflects the Good Shepherd who knows his flock (vv. 23-27; John 10:14; Acts 20:28).
27.examples:
The chapter's people are easy to recognise: the one putting off a reconciliation until tomorrow, the self-promoter online, Nathan with his faithful wound and Judas with his false kiss, the starving man to whom bitter food tastes sweet, and the man ruined not by hardship but by praise.

Its hopeful pictures are the near neighbour in the day of calamity, iron striking sparks to make a sharper blade, and the shepherd who knows which lamb is limping.

28.title: He Who Confesses and Forsakes Them Will Obtain Mercy
28.text: <sup>1</sup>The wicked flee when no one pursues, but the righteous are bold as a lion.<sup>2</sup>When a land transgresses, it has many rulers, but with a man of understanding and knowledge, its stability will long continue.<sup>3</sup>A poor man who oppresses the poor is a beating rain that leaves no food.<sup>4</sup>Those who forsake the law praise the wicked, but those who keep the law strive against them.<sup>5</sup>Evil men do not understand justice, but those who seek the LORD understand it completely.<sup>6</sup>Better is a poor man who walks in his integrity than a rich man who is crooked in his ways.<sup>7</sup>The one who keeps the law is a son with understanding, but a companion of gluttons shames his father.<sup>8</sup>Whoever multiplies his wealth by interest and profit gathers it for him who is generous to the poor.<sup>9</sup>If one turns away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer is an abomination.<sup>10</sup>Whoever misleads the upright into an evil way will fall into his own pit, but the blameless will have a goodly inheritance.<sup>11</sup>A rich man is wise in his own eyes, but a poor man who has understanding will find him out.<sup>12</sup>When the righteous triumph, there is great glory, but when the wicked rise, people hide themselves.<sup>13</sup>Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy.<sup>14</sup>Blessed is the one who fears the LORD always, but whoever hardens his heart will fall into calamity.<sup>15</sup>Like a roaring lion or a charging bear is a wicked ruler over a poor people.<sup>16</sup>A ruler who lacks understanding is a cruel oppressor, but he who hates unjust gain will prolong his days.<sup>17</sup>If one is burdened with the blood of another, he will be a fugitive until death; let no one help him.<sup>18</sup>Whoever walks in integrity will be delivered, but he who is crooked in his ways will suddenly fall.<sup>19</sup>Whoever works his land will have plenty of bread, but he who follows worthless pursuits will have plenty of poverty.<sup>20</sup>A faithful man will abound with blessings, but whoever hastens to be rich will not go unpunished.<sup>21</sup>To show partiality is not good, but for a piece of bread a man will do wrong.<sup>22</sup>A stingy man hastens after wealth and does not know that poverty will come upon him.<sup>23</sup>Whoever rebukes a man will afterward find more favor than he who flatters with his tongue.<sup>24</sup>Whoever robs his father or his mother and says, "That is no transgression," is a companion to a man who destroys.<sup>25</sup>A greedy man stirs up strife, but the one who trusts in the LORD will be enriched.<sup>26</sup>Whoever trusts in his own mind is a fool, but he who walks in wisdom will be delivered.<sup>27</sup>Whoever gives to the poor will not want, but he who hides his eyes will get many a curse.<sup>28</sup>When the wicked rise, people hide themselves, but when they perish, the righteous increase.
28.overview: A clear conscience makes the righteous bold, seeking the LORD clears moral sight, and a heart that refuses God's law cannot pray (vv. 1-11). Concealed sin rots, but confessed and forsaken sin obtains mercy (vv. 12-18). Faithfulness, honest rebuke, trust in the LORD rather than one's own mind, and an open hand to the poor (vv. 19-28).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Righteous Are Bold as a Lion
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The wicked flee when no one pursues, but the righteous are bold as a lion (v. 1). Law, justice, integrity and wealth, and the prayer of one who will not hear (vv. 2-11).
verseByVerse.theology: A clear conscience makes a person bold, and a heart that refuses God's word cannot pray.

verseByVerse.quote: The wicked flee when no one pursues, but the righteous are bold as a lion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A psychological portrait in a line. A guilty conscience makes every knock at the door sound like the police, every raised eyebrow like an accusation, every unread email like exposure. The law described that very curse: you shall flee when none pursues you (Lev 26:17).

The righteous are the opposite: bold as a lion. A lion does not look over its shoulder. A person with a clear conscience before God can face threats, criticism and even danger without panic. When the apostles were threatened, they prayed for boldness, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and continued to speak the word of God with boldness (Acts 4:31).

Much fear in life is really guilt. The way to lion-like boldness is not bravado, but a conscience cleansed by the blood of Christ (Heb 9:14) and kept clean by honesty. Is there something you keep running from that no one is actually chasing?

verseByVerse.quote: When a land transgresses, it has many rulers, but with a man of understanding and knowledge, its stability will long continue. A poor man who oppresses the poor is a beating rain that leaves no food.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When a land transgresses. National sin brings political instability: coups, rapid changes of government, factions fighting for power. Israel's northern kingdom saw one dynasty after another overthrown. A single wise and understanding leader, by contrast, brings long stability.

A poor man who oppresses the poor. When a poor man gains a little power and uses it to crush other poor people, as a foreman, a minor official, a landlord of one room, he is that storm: rain that should have watered the crops flattens them instead. Sometimes the cruellest oppressors are those who have just escaped oppression themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: Those who forsake the law praise the wicked, but those who keep the law strive against them. Evil men do not understand justice, but those who seek the LORD understand it completely.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who forsake the law. Your relationship to God's law shows in whom you admire. People who have abandoned God's standards end up praising wicked people: celebrating the ruthless businessman, the unfaithful celebrity, the cruel ruler. People who keep God's law cannot help opposing wickedness. Whom do you find yourself admiring?

Evil men do not understand justice. Evil blinds the mind. People committed to evil genuinely cannot see what justice requires; they have rationalised everything. But those who seek the LORD understand it completely, because justice is part of who God is. The closer a person draws to God, the clearer his moral vision becomes. The spiritual person judges all things (1 Cor 2:15).

verseByVerse.quote: Better is a poor man who walks in his integrity than a rich man who is crooked in his ways. The one who keeps the law is a son with understanding, but a companion of gluttons shames his father. Whoever multiplies his wealth by interest and profit gathers it for him who is generous to the poor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Better is a poor man. Almost identical to 19:1, but now the contrast is explicitly with a rich man. Wealth gained or kept crookedly is worth less than poverty with integrity. That is a hard truth in a culture that measures people by their income.

A son with understanding. Keeping God's law is what makes a son wise, and running with gluttons brings his father shame. The prodigal son's older brother said the younger had devoured your property with prostitutes. Company reveals character.

Interest and profit. The ESV notes that this means "profit that comes from charging interest to the poor". The law forbade exploiting a poor Israelite with interest: you shall not be like a moneylender to him, and you shall not exact interest from him (Exod 22:25). The man who grows rich by squeezing the desperate is, without knowing it, collecting money for someone else. God will see to it that his wealth ends up with a person who will give it back to the poor.

verseByVerse.quote: If one turns away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer is an abomination. Whoever misleads the upright into an evil way will fall into his own pit, but the blameless will have a goodly inheritance. A rich man is wise in his own eyes, but a poor man who has understanding will find him out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even his prayer is an abomination. If a person refuses to listen to God, why should God listen to him? Prayer is not a one-way channel for getting what we want. Someone who deliberately closes his ears to God's word while asking God for favours is not really praying. Isaiah said God would hide his eyes from those who prayed with bloody hands (Isa 1:15), and the psalmist: If I had cherished iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have listened (Ps 66:18).

That is not a threat against struggling believers who pray while fighting sin. It is a warning against the person who wants God's help while refusing God's word. Open your ears to God; he hears those who come humbly to him.

Whoever misleads the upright. There is a special judgment for those who lead good people astray: the false teacher, the corrupt mentor, the friend who talks a believer into sin. They dig a pit and fall into it. Jesus spoke of the millstone for whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to sin (Matt 18:6).

Wise in his own eyes. Wealth tends to make people think they are wise; after all, look how successful they are. But a poor man with real understanding sees straight through him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter's centre: Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy (v. 13). Tender and hardened hearts, wicked rulers, and integrity (vv. 14-18).
verseByVerse.theology: Hidden sin rots; confessed and forsaken sin is met with mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: When the righteous triumph, there is great glory, but when the wicked rise, people hide themselves. Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the righteous triumph. Good rulers bring freedom and something like a public celebration; under the wicked, people keep their heads down. The saying returns at verse 28.

Whoever conceals his transgressions. This is one of the great gospel verses of the Old Testament. Every human being has sins. The question is what he does with them. He can conceal them: hide them, deny them, excuse them, blame others, pretend they are not there. And he will not prosper. Hidden sin festers. David described what it did to him: For when I kept silent, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long (Ps 32:3).

Or he can "confess and forsake" them. Both verbs matter. Confession alone, admitting the sin while intending to keep doing it, is not enough. Forsaking alone, quietly changing without acknowledging the wrong to God, is not enough. Confess and forsake. And the promise is certain: he will obtain mercy. David again: I said, "I will confess my transgressions to the LORD," and you forgave the iniquity of my sin (Ps 32:5).

The New Testament gives the same promise: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness (1 John 1:9). The tax collector who beat his breast and said God, be merciful to me, a sinner! went down to his house justified (Luke 18:13-14). Why can God be called just in forgiving? Because the sins confessed have been paid for: Christ is the propitiation for our sins, the sacrifice that turns away God's wrath (1 John 2:2). Mercy for the confessing sinner is not God overlooking sin; it is God honouring the cross.

Is there something you have been concealing? The way out is not to hide it better. It is to bring it into the light, to God and where appropriate to those you have wronged, and to turn from it. Mercy is waiting.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed is the one who fears the LORD always, but whoever hardens his heart will fall into calamity. Like a roaring lion or a charging bear is a wicked ruler over a poor people. A ruler who lacks understanding is a cruel oppressor, but he who hates unjust gain will prolong his days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fears the LORD always. The ESV notes that the Hebrew lacks the words the LORD. Literally: blessed is the one who fears always. It describes a person with a tender, careful conscience, who always takes sin seriously. The opposite is the one who hardens his heart, who stops feeling guilt, stops listening, stops caring. Hebrews warns that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin (Heb 3:13). Tenderness toward God is a blessing; hardness leads to calamity.

A roaring lion. A wicked ruler over a poor people is as dangerous as a wild beast: tyranny preys on the weak, who have nowhere to hide and nothing to fight with.

A ruler who lacks understanding. A foolish ruler soon becomes a cruel one, while the ruler who hates unjust gain lasts. Integrity in leadership is not only right but durable.

verseByVerse.quote: If one is burdened with the blood of another, he will be a fugitive until death; let no one help him. Whoever walks in integrity will be delivered, but he who is crooked in his ways will suddenly fall.
verseByVerse.commentary:
