The blood of another. A murderer carries the weight of blood. He will be a fugitive until death; the ESV notes the Hebrew is "until the pit". The proverb tells others not to shield him from justice. Murder is not a crime that should be covered up by sympathetic friends.

That is about justice in human society. It is not a statement that a murderer is beyond God's mercy. Moses and David both had blood on their hands, and Paul had helped kill Christians, and all found mercy. But the gospel's mercy does not remove the rightful demands of human justice.

Whoever walks in integrity. Integrity is safe ground. Crookedness looks solid until, suddenly, it gives way. Many people's collapse looked sudden to outsiders, but it had been building for years on a crooked foundation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–28 — Whoever Trusts in the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Faithfulness and haste, partiality and flattery, and the deepest divide: The one who trusts in the LORD will be enriched, but Whoever trusts in his own mind is a fool (vv. 25-26).
verseByVerse.theology: The deepest divide is between trusting yourself and trusting the LORD, and it shows in how you handle money and the poor.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever works his land will have plenty of bread, but he who follows worthless pursuits will have plenty of poverty. A faithful man will abound with blessings, but whoever hastens to be rich will not go unpunished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever works his land. Nearly the same as 12:11, with a sharp twist. The diligent man has plenty of bread; the dreamer chasing worthless schemes has plenty of poverty.

A faithful man. Faithfulness is steady and honest over the long haul. Haste to be rich almost always involves cutting corners, taking shortcuts, and sooner or later doing wrong. It will not go unpunished.

verseByVerse.quote: To show partiality is not good, but for a piece of bread a man will do wrong. A stingy man hastens after wealth and does not know that poverty will come upon him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For a piece of bread. The second line shows how cheaply integrity can be sold. For a piece of bread, a tiny bribe, a small advantage, a person will abandon justice. Most corruption is not for fortunes; it is for crumbs. What is the smallest price at which you would bend the truth?

A stingy man. The ESV notes the Hebrew is "A man whose eye is evil", the opposite of the good eye of the generous. He rushes after money, and his very grasping leads to poverty, in his wallet or in his soul, and he does not see it coming.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever rebukes a man will afterward find more favor than he who flatters with his tongue. Whoever robs his father or his mother and says, "That is no transgression," is a companion to a man who destroys.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever rebukes a man. Flattery wins favour now; honest rebuke loses it. But afterward, when the consequences of the flattered man's folly arrive, or when the rebuked man comes to his senses, the one who told the truth is valued more. Real friends are remembered for their honesty, not their compliments (compare 27:5-6).

"That is no transgression." The son who helps himself to his parents' money and tells himself "It'll be mine anyway" is using a destroyer's excuse, and the proverb puts him in a destroyer's company. Jesus condemned religious leaders who found clever ways to avoid supporting their parents, thus making void the word of God by your tradition (Mark 7:13). Taking advantage of elderly parents, financially or otherwise, is not a small thing.

verseByVerse.quote: A greedy man stirs up strife, but the one who trusts in the LORD will be enriched. Whoever trusts in his own mind is a fool, but he who walks in wisdom will be delivered.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who trusts in the LORD. Greed produces conflict: in families over inheritances, in businesses over profits, between nations over resources. The contrast is striking: not the generous man, but the one who trusts in the LORD. The root of greed is lack of trust. The person who trusts God to provide does not need to grab, and he is the one who is truly enriched. The LORD is my strength and my shield; in him my heart trusts, and I am helped (Ps 28:7).

Whoever trusts in his own mind. That is the definition of a fool: not low intelligence, but self-reliance. The heart is not trustworthy. The heart is deceitful above all things (Jer 17:9), and Cursed is the man who trusts in man (Jer 17:5). The wise walk in a wisdom that comes from outside themselves, and are delivered.

Put these two verses together and you have the whole book of Proverbs: trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding (3:5).

Does trusting the LORD bring wealth? “Enriched” is a general pattern of God’s blessing, not a guarantee of money; Proverbs also says Better is a poor man who walks in his integrity than a rich man who is crooked (28:6).

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever gives to the poor will not want, but he who hides his eyes will get many a curse. When the wicked rise, people hide themselves, but when they perish, the righteous increase.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever gives to the poor. God sees to the generous. And the one who hides his eyes, who deliberately looks away from the beggar, crosses the street, changes the channel, will be cursed. The law said, you shall not harden your heart or shut your hand against your poor brother, but you shall open your hand to him (Deut 15:7-8). Looking away is a choice. Where have you been hiding your eyes?

When the wicked rise. The chapter ends as verse 12 ended, leading into the next chapter. Wickedness does not last forever. God's people may have to hide for a season. But the season ends, and the righteous increase.

Is “will not want” a promise that the generous will never be in need? It is a principle of God’s care for the generous (2 Cor 9:8–10; Phil 4:19), not a formula; and giving in order to get is not generosity.

28.theology:
A guilty conscience breeds fear, and a cleansed one boldness (v. 1). Seeking the LORD clears moral sight (v. 5), while refusing his word makes prayer unacceptable (v. 9). At the chapter's centre, concealed sin brings ruin, but confessed and forsaken sin receives mercy (v. 13), and a tender conscience is blessed (v. 14).

The fundamental choice is between trusting the LORD and trusting oneself (vv. 25-26; 3:5; Jer 17:5, 9). God opposes the exploitation of the poor and rewards generosity (vv. 8, 27; Exod 22:25; Deut 15:7-8).
28.examples:
The guilty hear every knock at the door as the police; the poor foreman crushes the poor; integrity is sold for a piece of bread; and the beggar is avoided by crossing the street. Each is a picture of a heart trusting itself.

Against them stands David, whose bones wasted away while he kept silent, until he confessed and was forgiven. Both verbs matter: confess and forsake, and mercy is waiting.

29.title: The Fear of Man Lays a Snare
29.text: <sup>1</sup>He who is often reproved, yet stiffens his neck, will suddenly be broken beyond healing.<sup>2</sup>When the righteous increase, the people rejoice, but when the wicked rule, the people groan.<sup>3</sup>He who loves wisdom makes his father glad, but a companion of prostitutes squanders his wealth.<sup>4</sup>By justice a king builds up the land, but he who exacts gifts tears it down.<sup>5</sup>A man who flatters his neighbor spreads a net for his feet.<sup>6</sup>An evil man is ensnared in his transgression, but a righteous man sings and rejoices.<sup>7</sup>A righteous man knows the rights of the poor; a wicked man does not understand such knowledge.<sup>8</sup>Scoffers set a city aflame, but the wise turn away wrath.<sup>9</sup>If a wise man has an argument with a fool, the fool only rages and laughs, and there is no quiet.<sup>10</sup>Bloodthirsty men hate one who is blameless and seek the life of the upright.<sup>11</sup>A fool gives full vent to his spirit, but a wise man quietly holds it back.<sup>12</sup>If a ruler listens to falsehood, all his officials will be wicked.<sup>13</sup>The poor man and the oppressor meet together; the LORD gives light to the eyes of both.<sup>14</sup>If a king faithfully judges the poor, his throne will be established forever.<sup>15</sup>The rod and reproof give wisdom, but a child left to himself brings shame to his mother.<sup>16</sup>When the wicked increase, transgression increases, but the righteous will look upon their downfall.<sup>17</sup>Discipline your son, and he will give you rest; he will give delight to your heart.<sup>18</sup>Where there is no prophetic vision the people cast off restraint, but blessed is he who keeps the law.<sup>19</sup>By mere words a servant is not disciplined, for though he understands, he will not respond.<sup>20</sup>Do you see a man who is hasty in his words? There is more hope for a fool than for him.<sup>21</sup>Whoever pampers his servant from childhood will in the end find him his heir.<sup>22</sup>A man of wrath stirs up strife, and one given to anger causes much transgression.<sup>23</sup>One's pride will bring him low, but he who is lowly in spirit will obtain honor.<sup>24</sup>The partner of a thief hates his own life; he hears the curse, but discloses nothing.<sup>25</sup>The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe.<sup>26</sup>Many seek the face of a ruler, but it is from the LORD that a man gets justice.<sup>27</sup>An unjust man is an abomination to the righteous, but one whose way is straight is an abomination to the wicked.
29.overview: The stiff neck that breaks, the joy or groaning of a people under its rulers, flattery, the rights of the poor, and the wise man who holds back his spirit (vv. 1-11). Rulers, discipline, and the restraint only God's word provides (vv. 12-18). Anger and pride, and the snare of the fear of man, from which whoever trusts in the LORD is safe (vv. 19-27).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Stiff Necks and Quiet Restraint
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He who is often reproved, yet stiffens his neck, will suddenly be broken beyond healing (v. 1). Righteous and wicked rule, flattery, the poor, and a wise man quietly holds it back (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: A heart that will not bend to correction breaks, and a wise heart holds itself back.

verseByVerse.quote: He who is often reproved, yet stiffens his neck, will suddenly be broken beyond healing. When the righteous increase, the people rejoice, but when the wicked rule, the people groan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Often reproved. The picture is of an ox that will not bow its neck to the yoke. It is corrected often, again and again, and each time it stiffens. And then one day the neck does not bend; it breaks. Suddenly, and beyond healing, the same words used of the troublemaker in 6:15.

It is a solemn warning, because it describes a pattern many people are living in. The warnings come: a friend's concern, a doctor's report, a wife's tears, a sermon that lands, a conscience that speaks. And each time, the neck stiffens. The history of Judah ended this way: God sent persistently to them by his messengers, But they kept mocking the messengers of God, until there was no remedy (2 Chr 36:15-16).

Correction is a sign of God's patience. It will not continue forever. If you have been warned about the same thing many times, today is the day to bend.

When the righteous increase. The same truth as 28:12 and 28:28. That is a reason to pray for leaders, and for Christians in any position of authority to remember how many people their character touches. On leadership in every sphere, from the home to the nation, see on Ephesians 5:21.

Can someone pass the point of no return? This describes the settled hardening of a person who refuses correction again and again. True believers who stumble are kept by Christ (John 10:28), and anyone troubled by this warning shows they are not yet hardened. The call is to respond today (Heb 3:13).

verseByVerse.quote: He who loves wisdom makes his father glad, but a companion of prostitutes squanders his wealth. By justice a king builds up the land, but he who exacts gifts tears it down.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who loves wisdom. A son who loves wisdom gladdens his father; one who keeps company with prostitutes squanders everything. The prodigal's brother said exactly this of him: this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes (Luke 15:30). What a young man loves determines where his money and his future go.

By justice a king. The one who exacts gifts may be the ruler who "taxes heavily", as the ESV notes. Corruption and oppressive taxation drain a land of its strength. The same principle applies on a smaller scale to any leader: justice builds, extraction destroys.

verseByVerse.quote: A man who flatters his neighbor spreads a net for his feet. An evil man is ensnared in his transgression, but a righteous man sings and rejoices. A righteous man knows the rights of the poor; a wicked man does not understand such knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man who flatters. The flatterer spreads a net for his neighbour's feet, whether he means to or not. Excessive praise is dangerous, and wise people are wary of it, both giving and receiving.

Ensnared in his transgression. The evil man is caught in his own sin, while the righteous man, free of that trap, sings. There is a joy in a clean conscience that the wicked never know. Paul and Silas were singing hymns in prison about midnight, beaten and in the stocks, but free inside (Acts 16:25).

The rights of the poor. A righteous person pays attention to the poor: he knows their situation, their legal rights, what is owed to them. Job could say, I was a father to the needy, and I searched out the cause of him whom I did not know (Job 29:16). The wicked man does not merely ignore such things; he does not understand them. Caring for the poor is a form of knowledge that only righteousness has.

verseByVerse.quote: Scoffers set a city aflame, but the wise turn away wrath. If a wise man has an argument with a fool, the fool only rages and laughs, and there is no quiet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Scoffers set a city aflame. A few mockers can inflame a whole city; the wise calm it down. Every community has both kinds of people, and it matters enormously which ones are listened to. In the conflicts around you, are you pouring on fuel or turning away wrath?

An argument with a fool. The wise man brings arguments; the fool rages, then laughs, then rages again. There is no resolution, no quiet. Sometimes the wise thing is to recognise that the argument cannot be won and to step away (compare 26:4).

verseByVerse.quote: Bloodthirsty men hate one who is blameless and seek the life of the upright. A fool gives full vent to his spirit, but a wise man quietly holds it back.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bloodthirsty men. Violent men do not merely ignore good people; they hate them. The blameless man's goodness is an accusation against them. That is why the righteous are often persecuted: not for what they have done wrong, but because their lives expose what others have done. The ESV notes the second line may be read, "but the upright seek his soul": the upright seek to protect the one the violent want to kill.

A fool gives full vent. The fool pours out every feeling and calls it honesty. The wise man feels the same things, but does not let them rule his tongue. Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger; for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God (Jas 1:19-20).

There is a modern idea that expressing everything you feel is healthy. Proverbs disagrees. Holding back is not repression; it is wisdom, and the self-control the Spirit grows in believers (Gal 5:23).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–18 — Rulers, Children and the Word of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Lying rulers, the one Giver of light to poor and oppressor, discipline that brings rest, and Where there is no prophetic vision the people cast off restraint (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: Nations, families and hearts all come apart without the restraint God's word provides.

verseByVerse.quote: If a ruler listens to falsehood, all his officials will be wicked. The poor man and the oppressor meet together; the LORD gives light to the eyes of both. If a king faithfully judges the poor, his throne will be established forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A ruler listens to falsehood. A leader sets the tone. If he rewards flattery and lies, the people around him learn that lying is how to get ahead, and soon they are all doing it. Honest people leave or are pushed out. A corrupt culture in any organisation usually starts at the top.

The poor man and the oppressor. Nearly the same as 22:2: the LORD gives both sight, life and breath. God is patient and generous even to oppressors. Jesus said the Father makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good (Matt 5:45). But the verse is also a reminder to the oppressor: every morning he opens his eyes, it is by the gift of the God who made his victim too.

Faithfully judges the poor. What establishes a throne? Not military strength, but faithful justice for those who cannot pay for it. That is a test for every government and every leader. And it points forward to the King whose throne will indeed be established forever, who came preaching good news to the poor.

verseByVerse.quote: The rod and reproof give wisdom, but a child left to himself brings shame to his mother. When the wicked increase, transgression increases, but the righteous will look upon their downfall. Discipline your son, and he will give you rest; he will give delight to your heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rod and reproof. A child left to himself does not grow into wisdom naturally. Folly is bound up in his heart (22:15). Without correction, he brings shame, and the proverb notes that it lands especially on his mother. Loving discipline and verbal correction together, the rod and reproof, are how wisdom is formed.

When the wicked increase. Wickedness spreads, but it does not last. The righteous will see its end. That is a word of patience for believers living in a culture where sin seems to be winning.

Discipline your son. The discipline that feels exhausting now brings rest later. A parent who does the hard work of correcting a young child will one day enjoy peace, and even delight, in a grown son or daughter. A parent who avoids it now will have no rest later.

The rod here, as at 13:24, is a real rod. Loving, consistent correction is required; whether to use measured physical correction with young children is left to wise parents, and where it is used it comes with reproof, never in anger or to injure (Eph 6:4). Anything that frightens or harms a child is abuse.

verseByVerse.quote: Where there is no prophetic vision the people cast off restraint, but blessed is he who keeps the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is one of the most misused verses in the Bible. It is often quoted in an older translation, "Where there is no vision, the people perish", and applied to leadership strategy: a church or company needs a vision statement, a clear plan for the future. That is not what the verse is about.

The ESV makes the meaning plain: prophetic vision. The word refers to revelation from God, the word of the LORD given through his prophets. When God's word is absent, or ignored, people cast off restraint, like a crowd running wild. The ESV notes it may also mean "the people are discouraged". And the second line confirms the meaning: blessed is he who keeps the law. The contrast is not between having a plan and having none. It is between having God's word and not having it.

Scripture describes such times. In the days of Eli, the word of the LORD was rare in those days; there was no frequent vision (1 Sam 3:1), and Israel was in moral chaos. Amos warned of a famine, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD (Amos 8:11).

This verse argues for faithful preaching and personal Bible reading. A society, a church, a family or a heart that neglects God's word will lose its restraint. And the blessing belongs to those who keep it. The law of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul (Ps 19:7).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–27 — The Snare and the Safe Place
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Stubbornness, hasty words, anger and pride, and the chapter's key: The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: Fearing people traps us; trusting the LORD sets us in a safe place.

verseByVerse.quote: By mere words a servant is not disciplined, for though he understands, he will not respond. Do you see a man who is hasty in his words? There is more hope for a fool than for him. Whoever pampers his servant from childhood will in the end find him his heir.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By mere words. A servant may understand exactly what is required and still not do it. That is true of stubborn employees, and of stubborn hearts. Understanding is not the same as obedience.

Hasty in his words? The second line is word for word from 26:12, where it was said of the man wise in his own eyes. Now it is said of the man who speaks too quickly. At least a fool might learn. The hasty talker is too busy talking.

Whoever pampers his servant. The ESV notes that the meaning of the word rendered his heir is uncertain, but the point is clear enough: over-indulgence produces entitlement. The same is true of children, and of our own appetites. What we pamper will eventually try to rule.

verseByVerse.quote: A man of wrath stirs up strife, and one given to anger causes much transgression. One's pride will bring him low, but he who is lowly in spirit will obtain honor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man of wrath. Anger does not only cause arguments; it causes much transgression. Words said in anger, violence, broken relationships, bitterness in others: an angry man leaves a trail of sin behind him, his own and other people's.

One's pride. The great reversal again. Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will exalt you (Jas 4:10). It is a law of God's kingdom, and Christ himself lived it perfectly, going down to the cross and being raised to the highest place.

verseByVerse.quote: The partner of a thief hates his own life; he hears the curse, but discloses nothing. The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The partner of a thief. The thief's accomplice hears the curse pronounced over the crime, and stays silent, and so brings the curse on himself. By protecting the thief, he destroys himself. Complicity is not neutral.

The fear of man. Few verses in the book touch everyday Christian life more often. The fear of man is the power other people's opinions have over us: the need for approval, the dread of criticism, the terror of looking foolish, the desire to fit in. And it lays a snare. It traps people into compromise, silence, people-pleasing and sin.

Many believed in Jesus, but for fear of the Pharisees they did not confess it, for they loved the glory that comes from man more than the glory that comes from God (John 12:42-43). Paul refused that snare: If I were still trying to please man, I would not be a servant of Christ (Gal 1:10).

The answer is not to stop caring about people. It is to fear God more. Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell (Matt 10:28). The one who trusts in the LORD is safe, out of the snare's reach. The LORD is on my side; I will not fear. What can man do to me? (Ps 118:6).

Whose opinion has too much power over you? Where has the fear of man kept you silent when you should have spoken, or made you speak when you should have kept silent? Bring it to the LORD, who has already accepted you in Christ; his is the approval that lasts.

verseByVerse.quote: Many seek the face of a ruler, but it is from the LORD that a man gets justice. An unjust man is an abomination to the righteous, but one whose way is straight is an abomination to the wicked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many seek the face of a ruler. The ruler is not the final source of justice; the LORD is. It is right to appeal to earthly authorities. It is foolish to trust them as if they were the last word. The one who has the LORD's favour does not need to fear any ruler's frown.

An unjust man. The Hezekiah collection ends with mutual repulsion: the two cannot finally be at ease with each other. That is why believers should not be surprised when living straight provokes hostility. What is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God (Luke 16:15), and the reverse is also true: what God loves, the world often hates.

But the division is not permanent for any individual. The gospel takes people who once found righteousness abominable and gives them new hearts that love it.

29.theology:
Repeated refusal of correction leads to sudden ruin (v. 1; 2 Chr 36:15-16). God's revealed word is essential restraint for a people; without it, they run wild (v. 18; 1 Sam 3:1; Amos 8:11).

Leadership shapes whole societies and is judged by its treatment of the poor (vv. 2, 4, 12, 14). Self-control and humility are wise (vv. 11, 23; Jas 1:19-20; 4:10).

The fear of man is a snare broken only by trust in and fear of God (v. 25; Matt 10:28; John 12:42-43; Gal 1:10; Ps 118:6). Christ broke that snare for us, enduring the cross and despising the shame (Heb 12:2), so that those who trust him need no longer live for the approval of others. Final justice comes from the LORD (v. 26).
29.examples:
An ox that will not bow to the yoke, and believers who kept silent for fear of the Pharisees, show the two traps of this chapter: the stiff neck and the fear of man. Against them stand Paul and Silas singing in prison at midnight, free because they feared God and not their jailers.

And the chapter's most misused verse is a warning for every church: "Where there is no vision" is not about a strategy document but about the famine that comes when God's word is not heard.

30.title: The Words of Agur: What Is His Son's Name?
30.text: <sup>1</sup>The words of Agur son of Jakeh. The oracle. The man declares, I am weary, O God; I am weary, O God, and worn out.<sup>2</sup>Surely I am too stupid to be a man. I have not the understanding of a man.<sup>3</sup>I have not learned wisdom, nor have I knowledge of the Holy One.<sup>4</sup>Who has ascended to heaven and come down? Who has gathered the wind in his fists? Who has wrapped up the waters in a garment? Who has established all the ends of the earth? What is his name, and what is his son's name? Surely you know!<sup>5</sup>Every word of God proves true; he is a shield to those who take refuge in him.<sup>6</sup>Do not add to his words, lest he rebuke you and you be found a liar.<sup>7</sup>Two things I ask of you; deny them not to me before I die:<sup>8</sup>Remove far from me falsehood and lying; give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the food that is needful for me,<sup>9</sup>lest I be full and deny you and say, "Who is the LORD?" or lest I be poor and steal and profane the name of my God.<sup>10</sup>Do not slander a servant to his master, lest he curse you, and you be held guilty.<sup>11</sup>There are those who curse their fathers and do not bless their mothers.<sup>12</sup>There are those who are clean in their own eyes but are not washed of their filth.<sup>13</sup>There are those—how lofty are their eyes, how high their eyelids lift!<sup>14</sup>There are those whose teeth are swords, whose fangs are knives, to devour the poor from off the earth, the needy from among mankind.<sup>15</sup>The leech has two daughters: Give and Give. Three things are never satisfied; four never say, "Enough":<sup>16</sup>Sheol, the barren womb, the land never satisfied with water, and the fire that never says, "Enough."<sup>17</sup>The eye that mocks a father and scorns to obey a mother will be picked out by the ravens of the valley and eaten by the vultures.<sup>18</sup>Three things are too wonderful for me; four I do not understand:<sup>19</sup>the way of an eagle in the sky, the way of a serpent on a rock, the way of a ship on the high seas, and the way of a man with a virgin.<sup>20</sup>This is the way of an adulteress: she eats and wipes her mouth and says, "I have done no wrong."<sup>21</sup>Under three things the earth trembles; under four it cannot bear up:<sup>22</sup>a slave when he becomes king, and a fool when he is filled with food;<sup>23</sup>an unloved woman when she gets a husband, and a maidservant when she displaces her mistress.<sup>24</sup>Four things on earth are small, but they are exceedingly wise:<sup>25</sup>the ants are a people not strong, yet they provide their food in the summer;<sup>26</sup>the rock badgers are a people not mighty, yet they make their homes in the cliffs;<sup>27</sup>the locusts have no king, yet all of them march in rank;<sup>28</sup>the lizard you can take in your hands, yet it is in kings' palaces.<sup>29</sup>Three things are stately in their tread; four are stately in their stride:<sup>30</sup>the lion, which is mightiest among beasts and does not turn back before any;<sup>31</sup>the strutting rooster, the he-goat, and a king whose army is with him.<sup>32</sup>If you have been foolish, exalting yourself, or if you have been devising evil, put your hand on your mouth.<sup>33</sup>For pressing milk produces curds, pressing the nose produces blood, and pressing anger produces strife.
30.overview: Agur, a weary man, confesses how little he knows of the Holy One, asks the name of God's son, trusts every word of God, and prays for neither poverty nor riches (vv. 1-9). A generation never satisfied (vv. 10-17), things too wonderful and too heavy (vv. 18-23), and small, stately and silent wisdom (vv. 24-33).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — A Weary Man, a Riddle and a Prayer
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Agur owns how little he knows, asks a question the Old Testament leaves open (v. 4), rests on God's tested word, and prays for truth and daily bread (vv. 5-9).
verseByVerse.theology: Wisdom begins where Agur begins: admitting what he does not know, trusting God's word, and asking only for what he needs.

verseByVerse.quote: The words of Agur son of Jakeh. The oracle. The man declares, I am weary, O God; I am weary, O God, and worn out. Surely I am too stupid to be a man. I have not the understanding of a man. I have not learned wisdom, nor have I knowledge of the Holy One.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The words of Agur. A new voice. The ESV notes that he may be "the man of Massa", perhaps a place outside Israel, and that the traditional Hebrew text reads the end of the verse as names: "to Ithiel, to Ithiel and Ucal", which the KJV keeps. The ESV follows a revocalization, a different choice of vowels for the same Hebrew letters, that gives something striking: a man who begins his words of wisdom by saying he is weary and worn out.

That is an unusual opening for a wise man. He does not start with credentials. He starts with exhaustion, and he says it to God twice. Anyone who has searched hard for answers about God and life and come to the end of his strength will recognise the voice.

Too stupid to be a man. Agur goes further. The psalmist said something similar when he saw how little he understood of God's ways: I was brutish and ignorant; I was like a beast toward you (Ps 73:22).

This is not false modesty. It is the beginning of wisdom. Agur has seen how far beyond him God is, and he admits he does not have knowledge of the Holy One, the very phrase from 9:10. The fool in Proverbs is always sure of himself. The wise man, having looked honestly at God, knows how much he does not know. Every real encounter with God begins with this kind of humility.
verseByVerse.note: Nothing is known of Agur except what is in this chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: Who has ascended to heaven and come down? Who has gathered the wind in his fists? Who has wrapped up the waters in a garment? Who has established all the ends of the earth? What is his name, and what is his son's name? Surely you know!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who has ascended to heaven? Now Agur asks a series of questions, like the questions God asked Job: Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth? (Job 38:4). Isaiah asks the same: Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand (Isa 40:12)? Who holds the wind in his fist, wraps the oceans like a cloak, and fixed the boundaries of the world?

The obvious answer is: no human being. Only God. Agur's point is that human beings cannot climb up to heaven to get wisdom. If we are to know God, God must come down.

What is his son's name? And then come two remarkable questions: what is the name of the one who rules heaven and earth, and what is his son's name? Agur may be speaking ironically, as God did to Job: if you know so much, tell me who he is. But the question stands open in the Old Testament, waiting for an answer.

In the Old Testament God's "son" can be Israel (Exod 4:22) or David's royal heir (Ps 2:7), and Agur may mean no more than that. But the New Testament, without quoting Agur, answers his question in his own terms. Jesus said, No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man (John 3:13). Paul says, He who descended is the one who also ascended far above all the heavens (Eph 4:10). And Jesus said, no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him (Matt 11:27). The one who came down from heaven to bring the knowledge of the Holy One that Agur longed for has a name. The Father's name is revealed by the Son, and the Son's name is Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: Every word of God proves true; he is a shield to those who take refuge in him. Do not add to his words, lest he rebuke you and you be found a liar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every word of God proves true. Agur cannot climb to heaven, but he has God's word, tested like metal in the fire and found pure. David said almost the same thing: the word of the LORD proves true; he is a shield for all those who take refuge in him (Ps 18:30).

That is where the weary seeker finds rest. Not in his own understanding, which he has confessed is too small, but in God's word, which is tested and true, and in God himself, who is a shield. And it is every word, not only the parts we like.

Do not add to his words. And because God's word is perfectly true, it must not be tampered with. Moses said, You shall not add to the word that I command you, nor take from it (Deut 4:2), and the last chapter of the Bible repeats the warning (Rev 22:18-19). Adding human rules and treating them as God's, or claiming God said what he did not, makes a person a liar. That is a sober word for every preacher, teacher, and anyone who says "God told me".

verseByVerse.quote: Two things I ask of you; deny them not to me before I die: Remove far from me falsehood and lying; give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the food that is needful for me, lest I be full and deny you and say, "Who is the LORD?" or lest I be poor and steal and profane the name of my God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two things I ask. Proverbs seldom speaks to God directly; here a man does, and the prayer is short, honest and wise.

Neither poverty nor riches. First, truth: far from the lies he might tell and the lies he might believe. Second, enough: daily bread. Jesus taught his disciples the same prayer: Give us this day our daily bread (Matt 6:11). And Paul: if we have food and clothing, with these we will be content (1 Tim 6:8).

"Who is the LORD?". The reason is the wisest part. Agur is not asking for moderation because wealth is evil or poverty holy. He knows himself. If he is rich, he may grow comfortable and forget God. Moses warned of exactly that: when you have eaten and are full, then your heart be lifted up, and you forget the LORD your God (Deut 8:12, 14). And if he is poor, he may be tempted to steal and bring shame on God's name.

Both extremes carry temptations. So he asks God not to put him in either. It is a prayer version of lead us not into temptation (Matt 6:13).

Few people pray this prayer, because most of us would quite like to be rich. But it is a searching question: would more money draw you closer to God, or further from him? Could you pray Agur's prayer honestly today?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — Generations That Are Never Satisfied
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A generation that curses parents, is clean in its own eyes, proud and predatory (vv. 10-14), and things that never say Enough (vv. 15-17).
verseByVerse.theology: Pride and greed are bottomless; they never say enough.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not slander a servant to his master, lest he curse you, and you be held guilty. There are those who curse their fathers and do not bless their mothers. There are those who are clean in their own eyes but are not washed of their filth. There are those—how lofty are their eyes, how high their eyelids lift! There are those whose teeth are swords, whose fangs are knives, to devour the poor from off the earth, the needy from among mankind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not slander a servant. A servant is vulnerable; a word against him to his master could ruin him. The powerless have a defender, and the one who wrongs them will be held guilty.

Those who curse their fathers. The ESV notes that the Hebrew is "There is a generation", in this verse and the next three. Agur describes a whole generation, a kind of people, marked by four things. The first is contempt for parents. Paul lists the same among the marks of the last days: disobedient to their parents, ungrateful, unholy (2 Tim 3:2).

Clean in their own eyes. The second mark is self-righteousness: they see a clean person, and God sees filth never washed. The Pharisee in the temple prayed, God, I thank you that I am not like other men (Luke 18:11). The most dangerous sin is the one a person cannot see in himself, and the only cleansing is the one he does not think he needs.

How lofty are their eyes. The third mark is pride, and Agur describes it by the face: eyes raised, eyelids lifted, looking down on everyone else.

Teeth are swords. The fourth mark is predatory cruelty. Contempt for parents, self-righteousness, pride, and exploitation of the weak: it is a portrait that fits every generation, including our own.

verseByVerse.quote: The leech has two daughters: Give and Give. Three things are never satisfied; four never say, "Enough": Sheol, the barren womb, the land never satisfied with water, and the fire that never says, "Enough." The eye that mocks a father and scorns to obey a mother will be picked out by the ravens of the valley and eaten by the vultures.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Give and Give. Agur's numerical sayings begin with a grotesque, memorable image: the leech's two suckers named as daughters. The ESV notes it may read, "'Give, give,' they cry". The leech never stops sucking. Some people are like that: always taking, never satisfied, never saying thank you.

Sheol, the barren womb. The grave always has room. A woman longing for a child aches without end. Agur names that ache as real, not as a reproach; the childless are seen by God, who heard Hannah (1 Sam 1:10–20) and promised the barren woman a joy of her own (Isa 54:1). Dry land soaks up rain and is thirsty again. Fire consumes whatever it is given and wants more. None of them ever says Enough.

Set beside the leech, the lesson is plain: greed is like the grave and the fire. Feed it and it grows. The only thing that can say "enough" to a human heart is contentment in God.

The eye that mocks a father. The contemptuous eye ends up unburied, food for birds. In the ancient world there was no worse end than to lie unburied. Contempt for parents leads to disgrace and death. God takes the fifth commandment seriously.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–23 — Too Wonderful and Too Heavy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Four mysteries, ending in the way of a man with a virgin (v. 19), set against the adulteress who says I have done no wrong (v. 20); and four reversals that make the earth tremble (vv. 21-23).
verseByVerse.theology: Some things in God's world are beyond understanding, and some upheavals are more than the earth can bear.

verseByVerse.quote: Three things are too wonderful for me; four I do not understand: the way of an eagle in the sky, the way of a serpent on a rock, the way of a ship on the high seas, and the way of a man with a virgin. This is the way of an adulteress: she eats and wipes her mouth and says, "I have done no wrong."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Too wonderful for me. Agur, who confessed that he knew so little, now marvels at things he cannot explain.

The way of an eagle. Four mysteries of movement, each leaving no trace: an eagle soaring through the air, a snake gliding across bare rock without legs, a ship finding its way on the open sea with no road. And the fourth, the climax, is the way of a man with a virgin, the mystery of love between a man and a woman, attraction, courtship, the joining of two lives.

Agur finds it wonderful, and it is. Love between a man and a woman is one of the great mysteries of God's creation. Paul said of marriage, This mystery is profound, and that it points to Christ and the church (Eph 5:32). It is not to be treated casually or cynically.

The way of an adulteress. Straight after the wonder of love, its opposite: the adulteress treats sex like a snack. The mystery that Agur stood in awe of has become as ordinary to her as a meal. And her conscience is so dulled that she sees nothing wrong.

The contrast between verse 19 and verse 20 is the contrast between a biblical view of sexuality and a casual one. One stands in wonder; the other wipes its mouth.

verseByVerse.quote: Under three things the earth trembles; under four it cannot bear up: a slave when he becomes king, and a fool when he is filled with food; an unloved woman when she gets a husband, and a maidservant when she displaces her mistress.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The earth trembles. Four upheavals of the social order, described with humour, are more than the earth can bear.

A slave when he becomes king. A servant suddenly given supreme power, with no preparation and no character to carry it, often becomes a tyrant. A fool who has eaten well becomes insufferable: comfortable, loud, satisfied with himself.

An unloved woman. A woman who has been disliked, once she finally marries, may lord it over others. A servant girl who takes her mistress's place can become proud and bitter. In each case, a sudden reversal of position reveals character that could not handle it.

The lesson is not that people's positions should never change. It is that power, comfort and status test people, and those who receive them without the character to bear them make the ground shake for everyone.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Four small, wise creatures, four stately ones, and the last word to the proud: put your hand on your mouth (vv. 24-33).
verseByVerse.theology: God's creatures preach wisdom, and the last word to the proud is: stop talking.

verseByVerse.quote: Four things on earth are small, but they are exceedingly wise: the ants are a people not strong, yet they provide their food in the summer; the rock badgers are a people not mighty, yet they make their homes in the cliffs; the locusts have no king, yet all of them march in rank; the lizard you can take in your hands, yet it is in kings' palaces.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Exceedingly wise. God's world is full of lessons, often from the least likely teachers.

The ants. The ant is the one the sluggard was sent to study in 6:6-8: weak, but wise, because she plans ahead.

The rock badgers. The defenceless rock badger lives among the rocks, where predators cannot reach it. Its wisdom is knowing where to hide. That is the believer's wisdom too: we are not strong, so we shelter in the Rock.

The locusts have no king. Locusts have no commander, and yet a swarm moves together like a disciplined army. Wisdom is not only for leaders. Ordinary people, working together in order, can accomplish what no individual could.

The lizard. A lizard is so small you can catch it in your hand, yet it gets into the king's palace, climbing walls and slipping through gaps where guards and walls keep others out.

Four small things, each wise in a different way: preparation, refuge, cooperation and persistence. God delights to use the small. God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong (1 Cor 1:27). No reader is too small to be wise.

verseByVerse.quote: Three things are stately in their tread; four are stately in their stride: the lion, which is mightiest among beasts and does not turn back before any; the strutting rooster, the he-goat, and a king whose army is with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stately in their tread. From the small to the stately: creatures that move with confidence and dignity.

The lion. The lion retreats from nothing. Beside it walk the rooster strutting in the yard; the ESV notes the word is uncertain, perhaps "the magpie" or "the greyhound", literally "girt-of-loins". the he-goat leading the flock; and a king at the head of his army, which the ESV notes may mean a king "against whom there is no rising up".

There is humour in the list: the lion's majesty sits next to a strutting rooster. Some confidence is real strength; some is just strutting. And the wise can tell the difference. The next two verses will speak to the strutters.

verseByVerse.quote: If you have been foolish, exalting yourself, or if you have been devising evil, put your hand on your mouth. For pressing milk produces curds, pressing the nose produces blood, and pressing anger produces strife.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you have been foolish. If you have been strutting like the rooster, or plotting wrong, stop. Say nothing more. When Job finally saw God, he said, Behold, I am of small account; what shall I answer you? I lay my hand on my mouth (Job 40:4).

The chapter that began with Agur confessing his ignorance ends with the same humility. Sometimes the wisest thing a person can do is stop talking.

Pressing milk. The ESV uses the same word three times: pressing. Churn milk and you get curds. Squeeze a nose and you get blood. Press anger, keep pushing it, stirring it, provoking it, and you get strife.

So the counsel is to stop pressing. Put the hand over the mouth. Let the argument go. Agur, the weary man who knew he was not wise, ends up giving some of the wisest advice in the book.

30.theology:
No one can climb to heaven to know God; the knowledge of the Holy One must come down, and it has, in the Son who descended and reveals the Father (vv. 2-4; John 3:13; Eph 4:9-10; Matt 11:27).

Every word of God is true and sufficient, and must not be added to (vv. 5-6; Ps 18:30; Deut 4:2; Rev 22:18-19). Wealth and poverty both carry temptations, and contentment with daily bread is wise (vv. 7-9; Matt 6:11, 13; 1 Tim 6:8). Self-righteousness blinds (v. 12; Luke 18:11). Greed is insatiable (vv. 15-16). God uses the small and weak (vv. 24-28; 1 Cor 1:27).
30.examples:
Agur is a wise man who begins by saying he is worn out, and ends with his hand over his mouth. Between those two points he asks who has gone up to heaven and come down, and prays for neither poverty nor riches.

His pictures teach without explaining themselves: a leech with two daughters called Give and Give, an eagle's path through the sky, a woman who wipes her mouth and says she has done no wrong, a rock badger sheltering in the cliffs, and a rooster strutting beside a lion.

31.title: A Woman Who Fears the LORD Is to Be Praised
31.text: <sup>1</sup>The words of King Lemuel. An oracle that his mother taught him:<sup>2</sup>What are you doing, my son? What are you doing, son of my womb? What are you doing, son of my vows?<sup>3</sup>Do not give your strength to women, your ways to those who destroy kings.<sup>4</sup>It is not for kings, O Lemuel, it is not for kings to drink wine, or for rulers to take strong drink,<sup>5</sup>lest they drink and forget what has been decreed and pervert the rights of all the afflicted.<sup>6</sup>Give strong drink to the one who is perishing, and wine to those in bitter distress;<sup>7</sup>let them drink and forget their poverty and remember their misery no more.<sup>8</sup>Open your mouth for the mute, for the rights of all who are destitute.<sup>9</sup>Open your mouth, judge righteously, defend the rights of the poor and needy.<sup>10</sup>An excellent wife who can find? She is far more precious than jewels.<sup>11</sup>The heart of her husband trusts in her, and he will have no lack of gain.<sup>12</sup>She does him good, and not harm, all the days of her life.<sup>13</sup>She seeks wool and flax, and works with willing hands.<sup>14</sup>She is like the ships of the merchant; she brings her food from afar.<sup>15</sup>She rises while it is yet night and provides food for her household and portions for her maidens.<sup>16</sup>She considers a field and buys it; with the fruit of her hands she plants a vineyard.<sup>17</sup>She dresses herself with strength and makes her arms strong.<sup>18</sup>She perceives that her merchandise is profitable. Her lamp does not go out at night.<sup>19</sup>She puts her hands to the distaff, and her hands hold the spindle.<sup>20</sup>She opens her hand to the poor and reaches out her hands to the needy.<sup>21</sup>She is not afraid of snow for her household, for all her household are clothed in scarlet.<sup>22</sup>She makes bed coverings for herself; her clothing is fine linen and purple.<sup>23</sup>Her husband is known in the gates when he sits among the elders of the land.<sup>24</sup>She makes linen garments and sells them; she delivers sashes to the merchant.<sup>25</sup>Strength and dignity are her clothing, and she laughs at the time to come.<sup>26</sup>She opens her mouth with wisdom, and the teaching of kindness is on her tongue.<sup>27</sup>She looks well to the ways of her household and does not eat the bread of idleness.<sup>28</sup>Her children rise up and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praises her:<sup>29</sup>"Many women have done excellently, but you surpass them all."<sup>30</sup>Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised.<sup>31</sup>Give her of the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her in the gates.
31.overview: King Lemuel's mother warns him against women and wine, and charges him to open his mouth for those who have no voice (vv. 1-9). An acrostic poem portrays an excellent wife: trustworthy, industrious, shrewd and generous (vv. 10-22), praised by her family and in the gates, because she fears the LORD (vv. 23-31).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — What a Mother Taught a King
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A mother's teaching for a king: keep from women and wine, and Open your mouth for the mute (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: Power is for protecting the helpless, and a king must keep himself clear-headed and pure to use it well.

verseByVerse.quote: The words of King Lemuel. An oracle that his mother taught him: What are you doing, my son? What are you doing, son of my womb? What are you doing, son of my vows?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The words of King Lemuel. The last chapter of Proverbs opens with a king, and with his mother. The ESV notes that the verse may read "king of Massa", perhaps the same people as Agur's (30:1). But what stands out is who taught him: not a court philosopher, not a prophet, but his mother. The book that began with a father saying forsake not your mother's teaching (1:8) ends with a mother's teaching written down for all time.

That is a great encouragement to every mother who wonders whether the words she speaks to her children are making any difference. Lemuel's mother taught a boy, and the boy became a king, and her words became Scripture.

What are you doing, my son? The ESV notes that the Hebrew is simply "What, my son?", three times. It is the cry of a mother's heart, almost wordless. My son, the boy she raised. Son of my womb, the child she carried. Son of my vows, the one she prayed for and dedicated to God, as Hannah did with Samuel. She is not lecturing a stranger. Everything she is about to say comes out of that love.

Correction has the most power when it comes from someone who has plainly loved you first.
verseByVerse.note: King Lemuel is otherwise unknown; these are his mother’s words.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not give your strength to women, your ways to those who destroy kings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Her first warning is about sexual indulgence, which destroyed many kings. The law had said of Israel's king, he shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away (Deut 17:17). David's adultery brought violence into his house. Solomon's many wives turned his heart to other gods.

Your strength is the energy, attention and vigour a man has. It is limited. Spend it on lust, and it will not be there for the work God has given. Many gifted leaders have lost everything here.

verseByVerse.quote: It is not for kings, O Lemuel, it is not for kings to drink wine, or for rulers to take strong drink, lest they drink and forget what has been decreed and pervert the rights of all the afflicted. Give strong drink to the one who is perishing, and wine to those in bitter distress; let them drink and forget their poverty and remember their misery no more.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is not for kings. Her second warning is about alcohol. Others might drink; a king must not be drunk, because his responsibility is too great.

Lest they drink and forget. The reason is about other people. A drunk king forgets the law and makes bad judgments, and the ones who suffer are the afflicted, the people who most depend on a just ruler. A leader's self-indulgence is never private. Its cost falls on the weakest. The same is true for a father, a pastor, a surgeon, a pilot: people depend on your clear head. Do not get drunk with wine (Eph 5:18).

Give strong drink. Wine has a place, she says, but it is with those who are dying, and those the ESV notes are "bitter in soul". In the ancient world, strong drink was the commonest pain relief, given to the dying and the desperate to dull their agony. The king's calling is to keep his mind clear for justice; the sufferer may be given relief. Scripture recognises a proper medicinal use: Paul told Timothy to use a little wine for the sake of your stomach (1 Tim 5:23).

And there is a remarkable moment in the Gospels. At the crucifixion, when Jesus was the one perishing and in bitter distress, they offered him wine mixed with myrrh, but he did not take it (Mark 15:23). The one person entitled by this verse to dull his suffering refused, and went to the cross with his mind clear, bearing the full weight of our sin. He did not forget his misery; he bore it for us.

Does verse 6 permit drink as a comfort for the depressed or grieving? It speaks of easing the last hours of the dying and the desperate, in an age without painkillers; some read it as ironic, set against the king’s duty to stay sober. It is no licence to drink away sorrow (23:29–35; Eph 5:18), and today the grieving need care, counsel and medicine, not drink.

verseByVerse.quote: Open your mouth for the mute, for the rights of all who are destitute. Open your mouth, judge righteously, defend the rights of the poor and needy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Open your mouth for the mute. Her third instruction is the positive one, and it is the reason for the other two. A king must keep himself from lust and drunkenness so that he can do this: speak up for those who cannot speak for themselves. The mute are people with no voice: no money, no lawyer, no influence, no platform. The ESV notes that all who are destitute is literally "all who are sons of passing away", people who are vanishing, who could disappear and no one would notice.

Defend the rights of the poor. Open your mouth, twice. Silence in the face of injustice is not neutrality. The one with a voice must use it for those without one. Isaiah said, seek justice, correct oppression; bring justice to the fatherless, plead the widow's cause (Isa 1:17). James says true religion is to visit orphans and widows in their affliction (Jas 1:27).

Few readers are kings. But most have some voice somewhere: at work, in a church, in a community, online, at the ballot box. Who in your world has no voice, and could use yours?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–22 — An Excellent Wife Who Can Find?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: An excellent wife who can find? She is far more precious than jewels (v. 10). Trusted, hard-working, shrewd and strong, and She opens her hand to the poor (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: The poem is an alphabet of wisdom lived: strong, industrious, shrewd, generous and utterly trustworthy.

verseByVerse.quote: An excellent wife who can find? She is far more precious than jewels. The heart of her husband trusts in her, and he will have no lack of gain. She does him good, and not harm, all the days of her life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An excellent wife who can find? Here begins one of the most famous poems in the Bible. Its acrostic form (see the note) makes it an A to Z of a woman of wisdom. Whether it continues the words of Lemuel's mother or stands on its own, it is a fitting close to the book.

An excellent wife is a woman of strength and worth; the Hebrew phrase is often rendered "a woman of valour". The same description was used at 12:4, An excellent wife is the crown of her husband. Ruth is called a worthy woman by Boaz (Ruth 3:11), and she is a living picture of this poem: loyal, hard-working, generous and faithful to God. And the question, who can find?, says such a woman is rare and precious, far more precious than jewels, the very comparison the book used for wisdom herself (3:15; 8:11).

That is the key to reading the poem. The book began with Wisdom portrayed as a woman calling in the streets. It ends with a real woman in whom wisdom has taken flesh and blood, in a home.

The heart of her husband. The first thing said of her is not what she does but that she can be trusted. He does not worry about what she is doing when he is away, or whether she will waste what they have. Trust is the foundation of a marriage.

She does him good. She does it not only in the early years of romance, but in sickness, hard times and old age, all the days of her life. That is the kind of faithfulness every spouse can aim at.
verseByVerse.note: Verses 10–31 are an acrostic poem, each verse beginning with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: She seeks wool and flax, and works with willing hands. She is like the ships of the merchant; she brings her food from afar. She rises while it is yet night and provides food for her household and portions for her maidens.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Willing hands. She works gladly, not grudgingly. Wool for warm clothing, flax for linen: she provides for her family through skill and effort.

Like the ships of the merchant. Merchant ships sailed to far ports and returned with goods that could not be found locally. She goes out of her way to find the best for her household, looking beyond the nearest and easiest option.

She rises while it is yet night. She is up before dawn to feed her family, and she also looks after the women who work for her, giving them their portions. Her care reaches beyond her own children to those under her authority.

A word of care is needed here. This poem is not a checklist that every woman must match in every detail to be acceptable to God, and it was never meant to crush tired mothers. It is a portrait of wisdom lived out, a picture to admire and grow toward, not a standard of performance. Its heart is in verse 30.

verseByVerse.quote: She considers a field and buys it; with the fruit of her hands she plants a vineyard. She dresses herself with strength and makes her arms strong. She perceives that her merchandise is profitable. Her lamp does not go out at night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She considers a field. She is a businesswoman: she weighs a purchase carefully, and plants a vineyard, an investment that takes years to return. She is shrewd, forward-looking and capable. The Bible's portrait of the ideal wife is not of a woman confined to insignificance, but of a woman of real ability and enterprise.

She dresses herself with strength. The ESV notes that the Hebrew is "She girds her loins", the picture of someone tucking up her robe to work hard or to run. She is strong, physically and in character.

Her lamp does not go out. She knows the value of what she produces; she is not naive about business. And her lamp does not go out at night. That may mean she works late, or that her household is so well provided that its lamp never runs out of oil. Either way, her house is never dark. Compare the lamp of the wicked, which will be put out (13:9; 24:20).

May a wife work outside the home or run a business? This woman buys land, plants a vineyard and trades (vv. 16, 24), and her husband trusts her (v. 11). Nothing here forbids a wife’s enterprise or paid work. What the poem assumes is a household ordered in love, in which she looks well to the ways of her household (v. 27), and in which, as the New Testament teaches, her husband leads in love (Eph 5:22–33) and the care of the home is honoured (Titus 2:5).

verseByVerse.quote: She puts her hands to the distaff, and her hands hold the spindle. She opens her hand to the poor and reaches out her hands to the needy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The distaff. The distaff and spindle were tools for spinning thread: the most ordinary daily work.

She opens her hand to the poor. The same hands open wide to the poor. Her industry is not selfish. She works hard so that she has something to give. That is exactly what Paul told believers: work honestly so that he may have something to share with anyone in need (Eph 4:28).

The early church had a woman like this. Now there was in Joppa a disciple named Tabitha, who was full of good works and acts of charity (Acts 9:36). When she died, the widows stood weeping, showing the garments she had made for them.

verseByVerse.quote: She is not afraid of snow for her household, for all her household are clothed in scarlet. She makes bed coverings for herself; her clothing is fine linen and purple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not afraid of snow. Winter does not frighten her, because she has prepared. Her household is dressed warmly in good clothes; the ESV notes scarlet may be "in double thickness". She has looked ahead to the cold season and made ready. That is the wisdom of the ant, applied to a whole family.

Fine linen and purple. Fine linen and purple were expensive, royal fabrics. The Bible does not despise beauty or quality. Her appearance reflects dignity.

And there is a lovely echo at the end of the Bible. The church, the Bride of Christ, is given fine linen, bright and pure, for the fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints (Rev 19:8). Many Christians have seen in the excellent wife a small picture of the Bride that Christ is preparing for himself, though the poem's own subject is a real woman in a real home.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–31 — Her Children Call Her Blessed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Strength and dignity, wisdom and kindness, the praise of her family, and the poem's heart: Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised (v. 30).
verseByVerse.theology: The book ends where it began, with the fear of the LORD, now lived out in a home and honoured in the city.

verseByVerse.quote: Her husband is known in the gates when he sits among the elders of the land. She makes linen garments and sells them; she delivers sashes to the merchant. Strength and dignity are her clothing, and she laughs at the time to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Known in the gates. Her husband is a respected leader, sitting with the elders at the city gate where decisions were made. And the placement of this verse in the middle of her portrait suggests her part in it. A wise and capable wife frees her husband for public responsibility and adds to his good name. As 12:4 says, she is his crown.

Linen garments. She makes garments and sells them to the merchants, so her influence reaches beyond her household into the economy of her town.

Strength and dignity. Verse 22 described her clothes; this is her real clothing. Then one of the most beautiful phrases in the poem: she laughs at the time to come. She is not anxious about the future. She has prepared, but more deeply, she trusts. The simple who refused wisdom in chapter 1 meet calamity with terror (1:26-27); this woman faces the unknown future with laughter.

That is a gift worth praying for, for any reader. Not a carefree ignorance of what might go wrong, but a settled confidence in the God who holds tomorrow.

verseByVerse.quote: She opens her mouth with wisdom, and the teaching of kindness is on her tongue. She looks well to the ways of her household and does not eat the bread of idleness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The teaching of kindness. After her hands, her mouth: she teaches, and she teaches kindly, a rare combination. Some people are wise but harsh; some are kind but have nothing to say. Her words are both true and gracious.

Paul tells older women to teach what is good, and so train the young women (Titus 2:3-4). This is the kind of woman whose teaching younger women seek out.

The ways of her household. She pays attention to what is happening in her home, knowing its ways, just as the good herdsman of 27:23 knew the condition of his flock. And she is never idle. The sluggard who filled so many chapters of this book is her opposite.

verseByVerse.quote: Her children rise up and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praises her: "Many women have done excellently, but you surpass them all."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Her children rise up. Here is the reward, and it comes from the people who know her best. Her children, who have seen her at her worst and most tired, rise up and call her blessed. Her husband, who has lived with her for years, praises her. Public praise is easy to get; praise from your own family is earned over a lifetime.

A husband reading this should ask whether he praises his wife, out loud, often. Children should ask whether they have ever risen up and called their mother blessed.

You surpass them all. Her husband's words. To him, she is the best of all. That is not a statistical claim; it is the language of love and gratitude, the way every husband should see the wife God gave him.

verseByVerse.quote: Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised. Give her of the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her in the gates.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A woman who fears the LORD. And here is the heart of the poem, and the key to the whole book. After all the praise of her skill, strength and generosity, the poet names what made her who she is.

The book of Proverbs began with its motto: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge (1:7). It ends here, with a woman who fears the LORD. Everything in between has been an unfolding of what that fear looks like in real life. This woman is what it looks like: in the kitchen before dawn, in the marketplace, at the spinning wheel, with her hands open to the poor, with wisdom and kindness on her tongue. Her industry and generosity were not the root; they were the fruit.

That is why the poem is good news and not a burden. The standard is not an impossible list of accomplishments. It is the fear of the LORD, and the Spirit grows it in every woman who belongs to Christ, single or married, rich or poor, gifted or ordinary. Peter says the lasting adornment is the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which in God's sight is very precious (1 Pet 3:4). Paul speaks of women adorned with good works (1 Tim 2:10).

What if I look nothing like this woman? Hear three things. First, the poem may well continue a mother's counsel to her son about what to prize in a wife (31:1), and it gathers the fruit of a whole lifetime into one portrait; no woman lives every line at once, in every season. Second, many faithful women are single, widowed, childless, unwell, or married to a husband who never praises them, and none of them is shut out of verse 30. Third, a woman's standing before God never rested on her output. It rests on Christ, whose perfect life and death are counted to all who trust him, and his Well done is spoken to the faithful, not to the impressive.

Give her of the fruit. Let her enjoy the fruit of what she has done, and let her works speak for her. She is to be honoured publicly, in the gates, where the elders sat and where Wisdom first called out in chapter 1.

And her Lord will say the same on the last day: Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a little; I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your master (Matt 25:21).

So the book of Proverbs closes. It began with a father teaching his son to fear the LORD. It ends with a woman who did. And behind both stands the one who is himself the wisdom of God, who loved the church and gave himself up for her, so that he might present the church to himself in splendor (Eph 5:25, 27). The fear of the LORD begins wisdom; Christ completes it; and every life that fears him will be praised in the gates.

31.theology:
Power is given to protect the powerless, and leaders must keep themselves free of indulgence for the sake of those who depend on them (vv. 1-9; Deut 17:17; Isa 1:17).

The book closes as it opened, with the fear of the LORD (v. 30; 1:7). Wisdom, personified as a woman in chapters 1-9, is embodied in a real woman whose industry, generosity, strength, speech and faithfulness are the fruit of reverence for God. True beauty is inward (1 Pet 3:3-5). Many Christians have also heard in it an echo of the Bride Christ prepares for himself (Eph 5:25-27; Rev 19:7-8).
31.examples:
A mother's anxious "What, my son?" becomes Scripture, and her charge to keep a clear head for the sake of the afflicted is met most fully in Jesus, who refused the wine mixed with myrrh. Every reader with any voice is asked to lend it to those who have none.

Then the poem shows the same hands at the spindle and open to the poor, a woman laughing at the time to come, and children rising to call their mother blessed. Charm and beauty fade; the fear of the LORD remains.
